docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This is Volume 3 of the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā: Darśana Darpaṇa: Schools of Indian Philosophy. It introduces the classical schools of Indian philosophy — Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pūrva Mīmāṃsā and Vedānta, together with the philosophy of the Grammarians — and the traditions that Brahmanical authors called nāstika: the materialist Cārvāka, and Buddhist and Jain philosophy. A chapter on Śaiva philosophy — the dualist Śaiva Siddhānta and the non-dualist school of Recognition (pratyabhijñā) — follows, with an account of its Tamil form, and a final chapter compares the schools’ theories of knowledge (pramāṇa), error and debate and draws the volume’s conclusions.

The book tries to present each school on its own terms and in its own best arguments, and to give the reader a sense of the long debate among them. Dates are given according to mainstream academic scholarship, with traditional dates identified as such. Quotations from primary texts are limited to passages whose wording and reference could be checked; claims that ancient texts anticipated modern science have been avoided, and comparisons with modern philosophy are offered as analogies. The social setting of philosophy, including restrictions of learning by caste and gender, is noted where it bears on the subject.

This edition has been revised to correct errors found in an earlier draft, and the Buddhist and Jain chapters in particular have been expanded. Later additions are the chapter on Śaiva philosophy and accounts of Advaita after Śaṅkara, of the method of Navya-Nyāya and its early-modern successors, and of the theory of debate; in the latest revision, sections that treated the same topic twice were merged, the arguments of the Cārvākas and the Vaiśeṣikas were set out more fully, and the volume’s omissions — above all Indo-Islamic thought and much regional-language philosophy — are stated in the Introduction. It remains an introduction: specialists will find simplifications, and every primary-text quotation should be checked against a critical edition; the editions used are listed at the end, with a chronology and a guide to further reading.

Transliteration and abbreviations. Sanskrit, Pali and Prakrit are given in the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration (IAST): long vowels are marked with a macron (ā, ī, ū), retroflex consonants with a dot below (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ), the palatal sibilant as ś, anusvāra as ṃ and visarga as ḥ; vocalic r is ṛ. Tamil follows the transliteration of the Tamil Lexicon (so ḻ, ṉ, ṟ). Names of modern authors and places are given in their usual English spelling. References to primary texts are by chapter and verse or sūtra; in a few tables NS, VS, MS and ṚV stand for the Nyāya Sūtra, Vaiśeṣika Sūtra, Mīmāṃsā Sūtra and Ṛgveda. Dates are CE unless marked BCE.

Nikhil Kumar Rajput Ramanujan College, University of Delhi Guru Pūrṇimā, 2026

docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction — The Panorama of Indian Philosophy
1.1 The Meaning of Darśana
docs.text:
The Sanskrit word darśana is derived from the verbal root dṛś — “to see”, “to perceive”, “to envision”. In later doxographies such as Haribhadra’s Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya (8th century CE) and Mādhava’s Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha (14th century CE), darśana means a “point of view” or “system” of philosophy. Traditional interpreters often gloss it more strongly as a “vision of truth” (tattva-darśana); the technical usage, however, is simply “doctrine” or “school”.

A mature darśana usually offers an account of what there is (tattva), an account of how it can be known (pramāṇa), and an account of the highest human good and the way to it. The proportions differ greatly. Nyāya is mostly epistemology and logic, Vaiśeṣika mostly ontology, Pūrva Mīmāṃsā mostly the interpretation of injunctions, and the Grammarians’ system mostly a philosophy of language.

Most classical Indian systems present themselves as oriented towards mokṣa — liberation from suffering — or towards the highest good (niḥśreyasa). This should not be overstated. A great deal of Indian philosophy, especially in logic, epistemology, grammar and hermeneutics, was pursued with a technical rigour that has no obvious soteriological payoff, and the materialist Cārvāka rejected liberation altogether. Equally, ancient Greek philosophy was itself often understood as a way of life rather than a merely intellectual exercise. The contrast between “spiritual India” and “rational West” is therefore a stereotype that modern scholarship has largely abandoned (Matilal 1986; Ganeri 2001).

docs.title: 1.2 Characteristic Features of Indian Philosophical Inquiry
docs.text: Four features recur across the schools, though none is peculiar to India.

docs.title: 1.2.1 Appeal to Experience and Authority
docs.text: Brahmanical tradition regards the Vedic seers (ṛṣi) as mantra-draṣṭā — “seers” of the mantras rather than their authors — and several schools (Yoga, Buddhism, Jainism) give a central place to the perception of advanced practitioners (yogi-pratyakṣa, the omniscience of the Jina or the Buddha). At the same time, the classical systems argued for their positions with explicit criteria of valid knowledge, and much of their literature is rigorous argument rather than report of experience.

docs.title: 1.2.2 The Question of the Highest Good
docs.text: Most darśanas ask what the highest good for a human being is, and even Cārvāka, which rejects rebirth and liberation, answers the question — with happiness in this life. That the question is asked does not mean that every argument serves it: much of the technical literature on inference, meaning or validity can be read, and was often written, for its own sake.

docs.title: 1.2.3 Commentary as a Form of Innovation
docs.text: Philosophical writing typically took a layered form. A terse foundational text (sūtra), traditionally ascribed to the founder of the system, was explained in a commentary (bhāṣya), which was in turn defended and extended in a sub-commentary (vārttika) and glossed again in further commentaries (ṭīkā); alongside these stood independent treatises on particular topics (prakaraṇa). The form encouraged an author to present a new theory as the right reading of an old text. Innovation was real — Navya-Nyāya and late Advaita are very different from the sūtras they claim to explain — but it was seldom announced as such.

docs.title: 1.2.4 The Culture of Debate (Vāda)
docs.text: Indian philosophy has a well-developed tradition of formal debate. The Nyāya Sūtra (1.2.1–3) distinguishes three kinds of discussion (kathā) — honest inquiry (vāda), disputation for victory (jalpa) and mere refutation (vitaṇḍā) — and Buddhist and Jain logicians wrote their own codes of debate (see Chapter 13, Table 13.5).

docs.title: 1.3 The Classification of Darśanas
docs.text:
The most fundamental classification of Indian philosophical schools is the division into Āstika (orthodox) and Nāstika (heterodox) systems. This classification, however, must be understood with care.

Āstika and Nāstika — What Do They Really Mean?

The terms Āstika and Nāstika are often loosely translated as “theistic” and “atheistic,” but this is misleading. In the technical philosophical usage:

  • Āstika (from asti, “there is”) originally meant one who affirms that there is another world, karmic retribution and the like (Pāṇini 4.4.60, asti-nāsti-diṣṭaṃ matiḥ, as the grammatical commentators explain it); in later Brahmanical usage it came to mean a system that accepts the authority (prāmāṇya) of the Vedas.

  • Nāstika (from nāsti, “there is not”) correspondingly meant a denier of the other world, and later a system that does not accept Vedic authority.

Classical Sāṃkhya, counted as āstika, is non-theistic (nirīśvara), and Pūrva Mīmāṃsā — the most Vedic of all schools — explicitly argues against a creator God. Buddhists and Jains, classed as nāstika by Brahmanical authors, accept rebirth, karma and liberation. The classification is therefore about attitudes to Vedic authority, not about belief in God; it is also a Brahmanical classification, which Buddhists and Jains did not use of themselves.

docs.title: 1.3.1 The Six Āstika Darśanas
docs.text:
The six orthodox schools are conventionally grouped into three pairs of allied systems (samānatantra). The list of exactly “six” āstika systems is itself a late, doxographical convention; earlier authors also treated Vyākaraṇa (grammar), Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava theologies, and others as darśanas.

  1. Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika — Logic-Atomism pair

  2. Sāṃkhya and Yoga — Enumeration-Practice pair

  3. Pūrva Mīmāṃsā and Uttara Mīmāṃsā (Vedānta) — Ritual-Knowledge pair

Each pair shares many assumptions while differing in emphasis and method (Figure 1.1).

Figure 1.1. The conventional classification of Indian philosophical schools, with the founders named by tradition; the six āstika schools are shown in their three allied pairs

docs.title: 1.3.2 The Three Nāstika Darśanas
docs.text: The three schools that reject Vedic authority set much of the agenda for the others. The materialist Cārvāka or Lokāyata accepted perception as the primary (for its early adherents, the only) means of knowledge and denied any self or world beyond the body. Buddhist philosophy, built on the teaching of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), produced the Abhidharma schools, the Madhyamaka and the Yogācāra, and the epistemology of Dignāga and Dharmakīrti. Jain philosophy combined a realist metaphysics of soul (jīva) and non-soul (ajīva) with the doctrine that reality is many-sided (anekāntavāda).

docs.title: 1.3.3 The Limits of the Āstika/Nāstika Scheme
docs.text:
The “six plus three” scheme is a convenient map, and this volume follows it, but it is not a neutral description of Indian thought. Four limits should be kept in mind.

First, the two words changed their meaning. In the older sense recorded by the grammarians, an āstika is one who holds that there is another world and a moral order beyond this life; by that test Buddhists and Jains are āstikas, and only the materialists are nāstika. Buddhist and Jain authors themselves used nāstika in this sense for the materialists. The Brahmanical legal tradition narrowed the term: the Manusmṛti (2.11) calls a twice-born man who, relying on the science of argument (hetuśāstra), disparages the two roots of dharma, Veda and tradition (smṛti), a nāstika and a “reviler of the Veda” (vedanindaka). The second, scriptural sense is the one that produced the modern classification, and it is a judgement made from one side of the debate.

Second, membership of the āstika group did not guarantee orthodoxy in any other respect. Classical Sāṃkhya placed Vedic ritual on a level with ordinary remedies (Chapter 4); Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika built their systems largely by independent argument; and Kumārila complained at the opening of his Ślokavārttika that Mīmāṃsā itself had been turned into a kind of Lokāyata and needed to be brought back to the āstika path.

Third, the number and membership of the “six” varied. The Jain Haribhadra’s Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya (8th century) also counts six systems — Buddhist, Nyāya, Sāṃkhya, Jain, Vaiśeṣika and Mīmāṃsā — adding Lokāyata for readers who treat Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika as one; in this count the Buddhists and Jains are among the “āstikas”, and only the Lokāyata is not. Mādhava’s Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha (14th century) reviews sixteen systems, including Pāśupata, Śaiva, Pratyabhijñā, the alchemical Raseśvara school and the Grammarians. The fixed textbook list of six āstika and three nāstika schools owes much to late doxographers such as Vijñānabhikṣu and Madhusūdana Sarasvatī (16th century) and to 19th- and 20th-century presentations of “Hindu philosophy” (Halbfass 1988; Nicholson 2010).

Fourth, the scheme leaves out a great deal: Kaśmīrī Śaiva philosophy and Śaiva Siddhānta, the theologies of the bhakti movements, the Grammarians (treated in Chapter 6), and the śramaṇa movements other than Buddhism and Jainism, of which the Ājīvikas are the most important. The scheme is used in this book as a map of the main lines of argument, not as a ranking of schools.

Other doxographies drew the map differently. The Tamil Buddhist poem Maṇimēkalai (usually placed about the sixth century, though estimates vary) has its heroine hear, in the city of Vañci, the exponents of a series of systems — Vedic interpreters and teachers of the means of knowledge, Śaivas, Vaiṣṇavas, Ājīvikas, Jains, Sāṃkhyas, Vaiśeṣikas and materialists — before she receives the Buddhist teaching, including an account of perception and inference close to that of the Buddhist logicians. It is one of the earliest surveys of Indian philosophy in any language, and it orders the systems as a Buddhist would (Zvelebil 1973).

A more radical criticism came from the philosopher Daya Krishna (1924–2007). In Indian Philosophy: A Counter Perspective (1991) and in earlier essays he argued that the familiar picture — a fixed set of “schools”, each a closed system oriented to liberation — is largely a modern construction, which hides a tradition of open-ended argument in which positions were constantly revised in debate (Daya Krishna 1991). One need not accept all of his conclusions to see the force of the point. This volume keeps the conventional chapter divisions for the sake of orientation, but it tries throughout to show the schools arguing with one another, and it returns to Daya Krishna’s challenge in its conclusion (Section 13.10).

docs.title: 1.3.4 Other Śramaṇa Schools: The Ājīvikas
docs.text:
The Buddha and Mahāvīra were two among many wandering teachers (śramaṇas) in the eastern Ganges plain. The Pali Sāmaññaphala Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya 2) summarises the doctrines of six of them: Pūraṇa Kassapa, who denied that actions bring merit or demerit; Makkhali Gosāla, who taught that everything is governed by destiny (niyati); Ajita Kesakambalī, the materialist discussed in Chapter 9; Pakudha Kaccāyana, who held that a person is made of seven eternal, unchanging bodies, so that a sword passing through them kills no one; Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, that is, Mahāvīra; and Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, who refused to commit himself to any answer. The reports are hostile and schematic, but they show that the debates about action, causation and the self that the classical schools later systematised were already lively in the Buddha’s time.

The most durable of these movements was that of the Ājīvikas, associated above all with Makkhali Gosāla (Sanskrit Maskarin Gośāla). According to the Buddhist report, Gosāla taught that beings have no power of their own to change their destiny: they are shaped by destiny, by circumstance and by their own nature, and are purified only by passing through a fixed, immense number of rebirths, as a ball of thread unwinds to its end when thrown. Human effort, on this view, can neither hasten nor delay liberation. The Ājīvikas were nevertheless known for severe asceticism, and their determinism was a serious philosophical position, not mere fatalism: Buddhist and Jain authors devoted considerable effort to refuting it because it denied the efficacy of moral action on which their own paths depended. The Jain Bhagavatī Sūtra (book 15) gives a long and hostile account of Gosāla, who is said to have been a companion of Mahāvīra for some years before they quarrelled.

The Ājīvikas were a recognised order in the Mauryan period: Aśoka and his grandson Daśaratha dedicated rock-cut caves to them in the Barābar and Nāgārjunī hills of Bihar. They are mentioned in Tamil literature (the Maṇimēkalai summarises their doctrine) and in South Indian inscriptions into the second millennium CE, after which they disappear. No Ājīvika text survives; everything we know comes from their rivals, as with the Cārvākas. A.L. Basham’s monograph remains the standard study, and more recent work has used the Ājīvikas to reconstruct the wider śramaṇa culture of “Greater Magadha” from which Buddhism, Jainism and the yogic and ascetic strands of Brahmanical thought all drew (Basham 1951; Bronkhorst 2007).

docs.title: 1.4 The Historical Development of Philosophical Thought
1.4.1 The Vedic Period (c. 1500–500 BCE)
docs.text:
Philosophical questioning begins in the Ṛg Veda itself. The Nāsadīya Sūkta (ṚV 10.129) opens with a negation (nāsad āsīn no sad āsīt, “there was then neither non-being nor being”) and ends by wondering whether even the overseer in the highest heaven knows how the world arose; it is a speculative poem rather than a doctrine, and it is discussed in its Vedic setting in Vol. 1, Veda Prakāśa. What matters for the later darśanas is the habit it displays: asking what lies behind the plurality of things, and admitting the limits of the answer.

The period of the early Upaniṣads (c. 800–300 BCE) saw the crystallization of fundamental philosophical concepts — Brahman, Ātman, Karma, Mokṣa — that would become the common inheritance of all subsequent Indian thought.

docs.title: 1.4.2 The Sūtra Period (c. 300 BCE – 500 CE)
docs.text:
Over several centuries the āstika schools codified their doctrines in foundational sūtra texts. The dates below are the approximate ranges accepted in mainstream scholarship; most sūtra texts grew in layers, and the founders are largely figures of tradition (Frauwallner 1973; Potter 1977); see Table 1.1.

Table 1.1. Foundational Sūtra Texts of the Six Orthodox Schools School Founder Sūtra Text Approximate Date Nyāya Akṣapāda Gautama Nyāya Sūtra compiled c. 2nd–3rd cent. CE (older layers) Vaiśeṣika Kaṇāda Vaiśeṣika Sūtra c. 1st cent. BCE – 1st cent. CE Sāṃkhya Kapila (legendary) Sāṃkhyakārikā of Īśvarakṛṣṇa\(^{*}\) c. 350–450 CE Yoga Patañjali Pātañjala Yogaśāstra (Sūtra with Bhāṣya) c. 325–425 CE (Maas) Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Jaimini Mīmāṃsā Sūtra c. 2nd cent. BCE (range 3rd–1st BCE) Vedānta Bādarāyaṇa Brahma Sūtra final form c. 1st–5th cent. CE (estimates vary)

\(^{*}\)No early sūtra text of Sāṃkhya survives; the Sāṃkhyasūtra ascribed to Kapila is late (see Chapter 4).

docs.title: 1.4.3 The Age of Commentaries (c. 200–1000 CE)
docs.text:
This period saw the composition of the great bhāṣyas (commentaries), vārttikas (sub-commentaries), and independent treatises that elaborated, defended, and often transformed the original sūtra traditions. It was a period of intense debate among Buddhist, Jaina and Brahmanical schools; the Buddhist logicians Dignāga and Dharmakīrti in particular reshaped the agenda of every school that came after them.

Its principal figures include the Buddhist Nāgārjuna (c. 2nd century CE), founder of the Madhyamaka, and the Yogācāra systematisers Asaṅga and Vasubandhu (c. 4th–5th century); the Jain authors Umāsvāti and Kundakunda (dates disputed, c. 2nd–6th century); the Brahmanical commentators Vātsyāyana on Nyāya, Praśastapāda on Vaiśeṣika, Īśvarakṛṣṇa on Sāṃkhya, “Vyāsa” on the Yoga Sūtra (possibly Patañjali himself) and Śabara on Mīmāṃsā; the Grammarian Bhartṛhari (5th century); Dignāga (c. 480–540) and Dharmakīrti (6th–7th century, often given as c. 600–660); and Śaṅkara (c. 700–750 in most recent scholarship; the older conventional dates are 788–820). A chronology of these and later thinkers is given at the end of the volume.

docs.title: 1.4.4 The Scholastic Period (1000–1700 CE)
docs.text: This era was marked by the rise of Navya-Nyāya (“New Logic”), founded by Gaṅgeśa of Mithilā (14th century) and developed at Navadvīpa in Bengal; by the Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja, 11th–12th century) and Dvaita (Madhva, 13th century) schools of Vedānta; by Śaiva philosophy, both the dualist Siddhānta and the Kaśmīrī non-dualism of Utpaladeva (c. 925–975) and Abhinavagupta (c. 950–1016) (Chapter 12); by the dialectical Advaita of Śrīharṣa and Madhusūdana Sarasvatī; and, until the decline of Buddhism in northern India in the 12th–13th centuries, by continuing Buddhist–Brahmanical debate.

docs.title: 1.4.5 The Modern Period (1800 CE – Present)
docs.text:
The encounter with Western philosophy and colonialism led to creative reinterpretations of Indian philosophical traditions by thinkers such as Svāmī Vivekānanda, Sri Aurobindo, Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, K.C. Bhattacharyya and B.R. Ambedkar (whose The Buddha and His Dhamma, 1957, recast Buddhism as a philosophy of social liberation); their Vedāntic reinterpretations are discussed in Chapter 8.

After independence, academic philosophy in India took a different turn. K.C. Bhattacharyya’s son Kalidas Bhattacharyya, and later J.N. Mohanty, B.K. Matilal and Daya Krishna, read the classical texts with the tools of phenomenology and analytic philosophy and argued that their arguments could be assessed as arguments, not only as documents of a culture (Matilal 1986; Mohanty 2000). Matilal’s studies of perception, logic and language, Mohanty’s work on the theory of knowledge, and Daya Krishna’s Saṃvāda experiment of the 1980s — in which traditional paṇḍits and university philosophers debated Navya-Nyāya and modern logic face to face — are the immediate background of much recent scholarship, including that on which this volume draws.

docs.title: 1.5 The Philosophical Questions
docs.text:
All Indian philosophical schools, despite their divergences, address a common set of fundamental questions (Table 1.2):

Table 1.2. Core Philosophical Questions Across Indian Schools Domain Central Questions Metaphysics (Tattva-Mīmāṃsā) What is ultimately real? What is the nature of the Self, the world, and God? Epistemology (Pramāṇa-Śāstra) How do we know? What are the valid means of knowledge? Ethics (Dharma-Śāstra) What is the right way to live? What is dharma? Soteriology (Mokṣa-Śāstra) What is liberation? How is it attained? Logic (Tarka-Śāstra) What constitutes valid reasoning? How should arguments be structured?

docs.title: 1.6 Epistemological Foundations: The Pramāṇas
docs.text: Each school defines the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇas) it accepts, and much inter-school debate turns on their number and nature. The lists range from one (perception alone, for the early Cārvākas) to six (for the Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsakas and the Advaitins, who add comparison, postulation and non-apprehension to perception, inference and testimony). The disagreement is not merely about counting. To accept testimony as an independent means of knowledge is to allow that a text such as the Veda can tell us what no perception or inference could; to reduce it to inference, as the Buddhist and Vaiśeṣika epistemologists did, is to make every word answerable to reasons. A single table of which school accepts which means of knowledge is given in Chapter 13 (Table 13.1), where the disputes are compared.

docs.title: 1.7 The Integrative Vision
docs.text:
The Indian philosophical tradition is best understood not as a collection of isolated systems but as a long conversation — often a sharp and polemical one — in which each school defined itself against its rivals.

The Rig Vedic Spirit of Inquiry

ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti That which is one, the inspired poets call by many names. — Ṛg Veda 1.164.46

This Vedic line, which in context speaks of one divine reality called Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni and so on, is often quoted today as a motto of pluralism. It should not be read back into the classical schools, which argued vigorously that their rivals were wrong. The present volume, Darśana Darpaṇa, tries to present each school on its own terms, including the points on which the schools could not all be right.

docs.title: 1.8 The Concept of Tattva: Reality in Indian Thought
docs.text:
The Sanskrit term tattva (literally “that-ness” or “the reality of that”) is a central concept in all darśanas. Each school provides its own enumeration of tattvas — the fundamental principles that constitute reality (Table 1.3).

Table 1.3. Number of Tattvas Enumerated by Different Schools School Number of Tattvas Key Features Sāṃkhya 25 Puruṣa and Prakṛti with 23 evolutes Yoga 25 Sāṃkhya’s 25, with īśvara as a special puruṣa (sometimes counted as a 26th) Vaiśeṣika 6 (later 7) Six categories (padārtha); absence (abhāva) added as a seventh from c. 10th century Nyāya 16 Sixteen epistemological-logical categories Advaita Vedānta 1 Brahman alone is ultimately real Śaiva Siddhānta 36 Śiva Tattva through Pṛthivī Tattva Jainism 7 Jīva, Ajīva, Āsrava, Bandha, Saṃvara, Nirjarā, Mokṣa Buddhism Varies Dharmas (75 in Sarvāstivāda; 100 in Yogācāra)

docs.title: 1.8.1 Tattva as Ontological Foundation
docs.text: The enumeration of tattvas is not a mere intellectual exercise; in several schools it is tied to liberation. In Sāṃkhya, understanding the 25 tattvas and discriminating Puruṣa from Prakṛti is itself the means of liberation; the Nyāya Sūtra (1.1.1) likewise promises the highest good from true knowledge (tattvajñāna) of its sixteen categories. In Advaita Vedānta, recognizing that only Brahman is ultimately real dissolves the apparent multiplicity.

docs.title: 1.9 The Puruṣārthas and Philosophical Inquiry
docs.text: The Brahmanical scheme of the puruṣārthas, the goals of human life, gives a convenient way of locating the schools. The older scheme had three goals (trivarga): dharma (right conduct and religious duty), artha (prosperity and power) and kāma (pleasure); liberation (mokṣa) was added later as a fourth and, for most schools, as the highest. Mīmāṃsā, at least in its earlier formulations, gives primacy to dharma; the Cārvākas, as their opponents report them, recognised only pleasure, with wealth as its means, and rejected both dharma and mokṣa; Vedānta, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika make liberation the supreme goal. The scheme is a Dharmaśāstra and epic framework, which holds that worldly goals are legitimate when pursued within dharma; the Bhagavad Gītā offers one influential synthesis, in which action, devotion and knowledge can all lead to liberation. Buddhist and Jain authors used frameworks of their own, centred on the path to nirvāṇa or mokṣa.

docs.title: 1.10 The Common Doctrinal Heritage
docs.text: Despite their differences, the Indian philosophical schools share a set of common doctrines and presuppositions that form the background of their mutual engagement. Understanding these shared assumptions is essential for appreciating the nature of their disagreements.

docs.title: 1.10.1 The Doctrine of Karma and Rebirth
docs.text:
All Indian schools except Cārvāka accept some form of the doctrine of karma (action and its results) and punarjanma (rebirth). This doctrine provides the existential context for philosophical inquiry: the human being is trapped in an endless cycle of birth, death, and rebirth (saṃsāra), and philosophy offers the means of escape (Table 1.4).

Table 1.4. Interpretations of Karma Across Indian Schools School Understanding of Karma Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika Karma produces adṛṣṭa (unseen merit/demerit) inhering in the ātman; God dispenses results Sāṃkhya-Yoga Karma creates saṃskāras (impressions) in the citta; effects manifest through prakṛti Mīmāṃsā Ritual karma produces apūrva (transcendent potency) that yields results independently Advaita Vedānta Karma operates within the realm of māyā; ultimately transcended by jñāna Buddhism Karma is cetana (intention); no permanent self undergoes rebirth; continuity through consciousness-stream Jainism Karma is subtle material particles (kārmaṇa pudgala) that physically bind to the jīva Cārvāka Karma and rebirth are rejected as unverifiable and as priestly fabrications

docs.title: 1.10.2 The Problem of Duḥkha (Suffering)
docs.text: The starting point of most Indian philosophical systems is the recognition of duḥkha — the pervasiveness of suffering in conditioned existence. The Sāṃkhyakārikā opens with the inquiry provoked by “the torment of the threefold suffering” (Chapter 4); the Buddha’s first sermon proclaims the Noble Truth of Suffering (Chapter 10); and even the Nyāya Sūtra (1.1.22) defines liberation (apavarga) as complete release from pain.

docs.title: 1.10.3 The Concept of Mokṣa (Liberation)
docs.text:
While all schools (except Cārvāka) affirm the possibility of liberation, they differ significantly in their understanding of its nature (Table 1.5):

Table 1.5. Conceptions of Mokṣa (Liberation) Across Indian Philosophical Schools School Conception of liberation Nyāya Cessation of suffering; the ātman exists without any qualities Sāṃkhya Kaivalya: isolation of Puruṣa from Prakṛti Yoga Kaivalya: consciousness established in its own nature Advaita Identity with Brahman; realization of “I am Brahman” Viśiṣṭādvaita Eternal blissful communion with Nārāyaṇa Dvaita Eternal blissful servitude to Lord Viṣṇu; souls retain individuality Buddhism Nirvāṇa: cessation of craving and the cycle of becoming Jainism Infinite knowledge, perception, bliss, and energy of the pure jīva

docs.title: 1.11 The Methodology of Philosophical Inquiry
docs.text: Indian philosophical inquiry follows a methodology that combines reverence for tradition with rigorous rational analysis.

docs.title: 1.11.1 The Anubandha-catuṣṭaya
docs.text:
Many commentators, above all in later Advaita Vedānta (for example Sadānanda’s Vedāntasāra), open a work by stating its anubandha-catuṣṭaya — the four “connected factors” that justify undertaking the study of a śāstra:

The Four Connected Factors (Anubandha-catuṣṭaya)

  1. Viṣaya (Subject Matter) — What is the text about?

  2. Prayojana (Purpose) — What benefit does the study yield?

  3. Adhikārī (Qualified Student) — Who is fit to study this text?

  4. Sambandha (Connection) — How is the text related to its subject and its purpose?

The question of the qualified student (adhikārī) is also where restrictions of caste and gender entered the definition of who might study (see Section 1.14).

docs.title: 1.11.2 Tarka: The Role of Reasoning
docs.text:
While all Indian schools accept some form of reasoning (tarka), they differ on its scope and authority. A recurring theme is the distinction between independent reasoning (śuṣka-tarka, “dry reasoning”) and reasoning guided by scripture:

The Limits of Mere Reasoning

tarko ’pratiṣṭhaḥ śrutayo vibhinnā naiko ṛṣir yasya mataṃ pramāṇam Reasoning is unstable; the scriptures differ among themselves; there is no single sage whose opinion is authoritative. — Mahābhārata, Āraṇyakaparvan (Yudhiṣṭhira’s answers to the Yakṣa; vulgate reading, Bombay/Calcutta 3.313.117; not in the constituted text of the Critical Edition, which relegates it to an appended passage after 3.297.61)

The epic verse goes on to recommend following “the path the great have taken”. It expresses a widespread suspicion of unaided reasoning; the Nyāya, Buddhist and Jain logicians, by contrast, built elaborate theories of when reasoning is reliable.

docs.title: 1.12 The Darśanas in Comparative Perspective
docs.text:
Table 1.6 sets the nine conventional schools side by side on two questions: what is ultimately real, and what, if anything, frees a person from suffering. Their answers to the question of how anything is known are compared in Chapter 13.

Table 1.6. Comparative Overview of the Nine Major Darśanas Darśana Ultimate Reality Means to Liberation Nyāya Pluralistic: selves, God, atoms and other substances Right knowledge of the sixteen categories Vaiśeṣika Pluralistic: nine substances, including atoms; God from Praśastapāda onwards Knowledge of the categories Sāṃkhya Dualistic: many selves (puruṣa) and one primordial nature (prakṛti) Discriminative knowledge (viveka) Yoga Sāṃkhya’s dualism, with īśvara as a special self The eight-limbed discipline Mīmāṃsā Pluralistic realism; no creator God Performance of Vedic dharma Advaita Vedānta Non-dual: Brahman alone Knowledge of the self’s identity with Brahman Cārvāka Materialist: four elements No liberation; happiness in this life Buddhism Dependent origination; no permanent self; emptiness (Madhyamaka) or mind only (Yogācāra) The eightfold path; insight (prajñā) Jainism Pluralistic: infinitely many souls and five kinds of non-soul Right faith, knowledge and conduct together

docs.title: 1.13 Modern Uses of the Darśanas
docs.text: The classical schools are also read today for purposes their authors did not have in view, and it is worth being clear about the difference. Philosophers of mind compare Sāṃkhya’s separation of consciousness from the intellect, or Buddhist debates on reflexive awareness, with modern theories of consciousness (Ganeri 2001); logicians have studied the precision of Navya-Nyāya (Ingalls 1951; Matilal 1968); philosophers of language have taken up Bhartṛhari’s holism and Dignāga’s theory of exclusion (Matilal 1990). These are legitimate uses, and recent work has shown that Indian arguments can be engaged on their merits (Matilal 1986; Siderits 2007). Other uses are looser. Jain non-violence is invoked in environmental ethics, though its classical purpose was the purification of the soul, and modern mindfulness programmes borrow from Buddhist and yogic analyses of the mind while changing their aims. This volume does not argue for or against such adaptations; it tries to state what the classical texts themselves held, so that the reader can judge how far a modern use is faithful to them.

docs.title: 1.14 The Guru-Śiṣya Paramparā in Philosophical Transmission
docs.text: The transmission of philosophical knowledge in India took place largely within teacher–student lineages (guru-śiṣya paramparā), in Brahmanical households and maṭhas, and in Buddhist and Jain monasteries. Innovation was common, but it was usually presented as the correct interpretation of an earlier authority rather than as a break with it.

docs.title: 1.14.1 The Structure of Philosophical Education
docs.text:
The traditional model of philosophical learning involved several stages. The student (adhikārī) first had to demonstrate the requisite qualifications, which typically included a command of Sanskrit grammar (vyākaraṇa), familiarity with the Vedic corpus, and the moral and intellectual discipline necessary for sustained inquiry. In Brahmanical institutions eligibility was also defined by birth and gender: Vedic study, and hence the formal study of Mīmāṃsā and Vedānta, was restricted to twice-born males (see below). The guru would then guide the student through the foundational texts of the chosen darśana, beginning with the sūtras and proceeding through the commentarial literature.

Study usually proceeded from memorising the foundational text, through critical examination of its arguments — learning to state the opponent’s position (pūrvapakṣa) before the established conclusion (siddhānta) — to practice in debate as proponent and opponent, and finally, for a few, to the composition of new works.

docs.title: 1.14.2 Major Centres of Philosophical Learning
docs.text:
Throughout Indian history, certain centres emerged as focal points for philosophical study and debate. These institutions fostered the development and refinement of the various darśanas (Table 1.7).

Table 1.7. Historical Centres of Philosophical Learning in India Centre Period Philosophical Traditions Takṣaśilā c. 5th c. BCE – 5th c. CE A city with renowned private teachers (grammar, medicine) according to Jātakas and other texts; not an institutional university Nālandā c. 5th – 12th c. CE Buddhist monastic university; Madhyamaka, Yogācāra, pramāṇa Vikramaśilā c. 8th – 12th c. CE Vajrayāna Buddhism; Tantric philosophy Kāśī (Vārāṇasī) Ancient – present All six āstika darśanas; Vedānta; Vyākaraṇa Mithilā c. 11th – 18th c. CE Nyāya (Udayana), Navya-Nyāya (Gaṅgeśa); Dharmaśāstra Navadvīpa c. 15th – 18th c. CE Navya-Nyāya; Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism Kāñcīpuram Ancient – present Buddhist, Jain and later Vaiṣṇava and Advaita learning Śṛṅgerī medieval – present Advaita Vedānta (founding by Śaṅkara is traditional)

The places in Table 1.7, with Kashmir, where much of the Śaiva and later Nyāya literature was written, are shown in Figure 1.2.

docs.title: 1.14.3 The Culture of Inter-School Engagement
docs.text: A notable feature of the Indian philosophical landscape was the sustained engagement between rival schools. Philosophers were expected to master not only their own tradition but also the positions of competing schools. The pūrvapakṣa-siddhānta method — in which a philosopher first presents the strongest version of the opponent’s argument before offering a refutation — ensured intellectual honesty and depth. This practice is found throughout the commentarial literature, from Uddyotakara’s defence of Nyāya against Dignāga to Śaṅkara’s refutation of Sāṃkhya, Buddhism and Jainism in the Brahmasūtrabhāṣya, and Buddhists such as Śāntarakṣita who surveyed and criticised every rival school in the Tattvasaṅgraha.

docs.title: 1.15 The Philosophical Vocabulary of Darśana
docs.text:
A proper understanding of Indian philosophy requires familiarity with a set of key technical terms that recur across all the darśanas. These terms constitute the shared vocabulary of Indian philosophical discourse (Table 1.8).

Table 1.8. Essential Philosophical Terms Across Indian Darśanas Sanskrit Term Translation Philosophical Significance Dravya Substance The substratum that bears qualities and undergoes change Guṇa Quality, attribute Properties that inhere in substances Karma Action, deed Both physical action and its unseen moral consequences Kāraṇa Cause That which produces an effect; classified into material, efficient, and instrumental Kārya Effect The product of a causal process Svabhāva Inherent Nature The essential nature of a thing Padārtha Category A fundamental kind of being; the basic ontological unit Sambandha Relation The connection between two entities; a key topic of analysis

docs.title: 1.15.1 The Problem of Philosophical Translation
docs.text: Terms like dharma, karma, māyā and brahman carry layers of meaning that resist simple translation, and the same term may mean different things in different schools. Dharma is “that which is enjoined by the Veda” in Mīmāṃsā, the “medium of motion” in Jain ontology, “merit” (a quality of the self) in Vaiśeṣika, and both “the teaching” and a “basic element of existence” in Buddhism. Even pramāṇa shifts: Nyāya counts four, the Mīmāṃsakas five or six, and the Buddhist epistemologists two, defining perception in a radically different way as free from conceptual construction. The reader should always ask which school’s usage is in play.

docs.title: 1.16 Philosophy, the Other Sciences and Society
1.16.1 Darśana and the Śāstric Tradition
docs.text: The philosophical schools supplied concepts and methods to many other Indian śāstras (systematic disciplines). The logical methods of Nyāya were used in many other fields of learning, from grammar to law. Categories close to those of Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika appear in the theory of Āyurveda. The hermeneutical principles of Mīmāṃsā shaped the interpretation of legal texts in Dharmaśāstra. The psychological vocabulary of Yoga was widely shared by later religious and medical literature.

docs.title: 1.16.2 The Darśanas and Social Order
docs.text:
The philosophical schools also addressed questions of social organization and individual conduct. The Mīmāṃsā emphasis on dharma as revealed through Vedic injunctions provided a philosophical basis for the performance of social duties. The Nyāya arguments for the existence of God and the moral law supported the traditional understanding of cosmic justice.

The philosophical schools were not neutral on social hierarchy. Vedic learning — and hence formal training in Mīmāṃsā and Vedānta — was restricted to twice-born men. The Brahmasūtra (1.3.34–38) denies śūdras eligibility (adhikāra) for Vedic knowledge, and Śaṅkara’s commentary on these sūtras, citing the Dharmaśāstras, endorses severe penalties for a śūdra who hears or recites the Veda, while allowing that śūdras may attain liberation through the epics and Purāṇas. Women’s access was similarly restricted, though the Upaniṣads remember women such as Gārgī and Maitreyī as participants in philosophical debate. Buddhist texts criticised claims of brahmin superiority by birth (for example in the Assālāyana and Vāseṭṭha Suttas), and both Buddhist and Jain orders admitted members of all castes and women as renunciants, although monastic rules subordinated nuns to monks. Devotional movements and, in the modern period, B.R. Ambedkar drew on these resources in criticising caste (Ambedkar 1957; Olivelle 2005).

docs.title: 1.16.3 Women and Philosophical Tradition
docs.text: What the sources say about women in philosophy is limited, and what they leave out is telling. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad remembers Gārgī Vācaknavī, who questions Yājñavalkya in a public contest, and Maitreyī, to whom he teaches the doctrine of the self. The Mahābhārata (Śāntiparvan) gives the female ascetic Sulabhā a debate with King Janaka, in which she argues that he has not attained the freedom he claims. Buddhist nuns’ verses survive in the Therīgāthā (Chapter 10), and the Jain sects disagreed about whether a woman can attain liberation at all (Chapter 11). The later Advaita hagiographies make Ubhayabhāratī, wife of Maṇḍana Miśra, the judge of his debate with Śaṅkara, but this is legend, not history. Women’s voices are clearer in devotional poetry — the Tamil Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār and Āṇṭāḷ, the Kannada Akka Mahādēvi, the Kashmiri Lalleśvarī (Lal Ded) — than in the śāstric literature of the schools, where almost no surviving systematic treatise is known to be by a woman. The silence reflects the restrictions on Vedic and śāstric education described above, not an absence of thought; and it means that the philosophy surveyed in this book is very largely the philosophy of men of a few social groups.

docs.title: 1.17 Organization and Scope of This Volume
docs.text: Chapters 2–6 treat five of the six āstika schools — Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Sāṃkhya, Yoga and Pūrva Mīmāṃsā — the last together with the Grammarian philosophy of language of Bhartṛhari, its chief rival on the nature of words. Chapters 7 and 8 treat Vedānta and its many schools. Chapters 9–11 treat the three schools that Brahmanical authors called nāstika: Cārvāka, Buddhist and Jain philosophy. Chapter 12 treats Śaiva philosophy — the Śaiva Siddhānta, including its Tamil form, and the Pratyabhijñā of Somānanda, Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta. Chapter 13 compares the schools’ theories of knowledge, error and debate and draws the volume’s conclusions. Most chapters cover, in roughly this order, history and texts, doctrines and the arguments for them, the school’s theory of knowledge, its debates with rivals, and its later influence. Readers new to the subject may read the chapters in order; others can follow the cross-references. A chronology of thinkers, a list of abbreviations, a guide to editions and further reading, and a glossary are given at the end.

docs.title: 1.17.1 What This Volume Leaves Out
docs.text: A book with this title should say plainly what it does not cover. First, Indo-Islamic and Indo-Persian thought is absent. From the thirteenth century onwards India had a rich tradition of Islamic philosophy, theology and logic in Arabic and Persian: the rational sciences were taught in the madrasas, and the eighteenth-century theologian Shāh Walī Allāh of Delhi wrote systematic works on metaphysics and ethics. The meeting of Islamic and Indian thought produced texts that are philosophical by any reasonable definition, such as the Mughal prince Dārā Shikōh’s Majma‘ al-Baḥrayn (“The Mingling of the Two Oceans”, 1655), which sets the categories of Sufism beside those of Vedānta, and his Persian translation of fifty Upaniṣads (1657). The series plan lists Indo-Islamic and Indo-Persian knowledge as a gap that no volume yet fills, and this volume shares that gap. Second, Tamil and other regional-language philosophy is treated only in part: the Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta is described in Chapter 12, the Maṇimēkalai’s survey of the systems above, and the Tamil devotional background of Rāmānuja in Chapter 7; the thought of the Āḻvār and Nāyaṉmār poets, of the Vīraśaiva vacanas in Kannada and of the Sikh scriptures is not covered. Third, modern Indian philosophy after K.C. Bhattacharyya receives only the brief account given above. Finally, the volume concentrates on Sanskrit and Pali sources and on argument; the religious and institutional history of the traditions belongs to other volumes of the series — Buddhist and Jain traditions to Volume 4 (Buddha–Jina Prabhā), yoga practice to Volume 5 (Yoga Taraṅgiṇī), Śaiva scripture and ritual to Volume 6 (Tantra–Āgama), grammar to Volume 10 (Śabda Vidyā), the medical use of Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika categories to Volume 13 (Āyurveda) and Mīmāṃsā in law to Volume 18 (Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra).

docs.title: Chapter 2: Nyāya — The Science of Logic and Epistemology
docs.text:
The Opening Sūtra

pramāṇa-prameya-saṃśaya-prayojana-dṛṣṭānta-siddhāntāvayava-tarka-nirṇaya-vāda-jalpa-vitaṇḍā-hetvābhāsa-cchala-jāti-nigrahasthānānāṃ tattva-jñānān niḥśreyasādhigamaḥ By the true knowledge of the sixteen categories — means of knowledge, objects of knowledge, doubt, purpose, example, established doctrine, members of a syllogism, reasoning, ascertainment, debate, sophistry, cavil, fallacies, quibbles, futile rejoinders, and clinchers — one attains the highest good. — Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.1

docs.title: 2.1 Historical Background
docs.text:
The Nyāya school, one of the most influential systems of Indian philosophy, takes its name from the Sanskrit word nyāya (from the root i, “to go”, with the prefix ni), “that by which one is led” to a conclusion; Vātsyāyana defines it as the examination of an object by the means of knowledge (pramāṇair arthaparīkṣaṇaṃ nyāyaḥ, on NS 1.1.1). It is also known as Tarka-Śāstra (the science of reasoning), Pramāṇa-Śāstra (the science of valid knowledge), Hetu-Vidyā (the science of reasons), and Ānvīkṣikī (the science of critical inquiry). The term ānvīkṣikī is already used in the Arthaśāstra (1.2) for a discipline of reasoned investigation — there exemplified by Sāṃkhya, Yoga and Lokāyata — which Vātsyāyana later identified with Nyāya (Matilal 1998; Phillips 2012).

Historical Note: The Founder — Akṣapāda Gautama

The foundational text of Nyāya is the Nyāya Sūtra, attributed to the sage Akṣapāda Gautama (not to be confused with Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha). The name Akṣapāda (“eyes on his feet”) is explained by a late legend that Gautama, absorbed in thought, fell into a well, after which he was granted “eyes in his feet.” The Nyāya Sūtra is a layered text: some of its material on debate may go back to the last centuries BCE, but the work as we have it is generally dated to c. 2nd–3rd century CE, since it already responds to Madhyamaka arguments of Nāgārjuna’s period (Frauwallner 1973; Potter 1977).

docs.title: 2.1.1 Key Texts and Commentators
docs.text:
Table 2.1 lists the principal texts and commentators.

Table 2.1. Major Texts of the Nyāya Tradition Text Author Date (approx.) Significance Nyāya Sūtra Gautama c. 2nd–3rd c. CE (older layers) Foundational aphorisms Nyāya Bhāṣya Vātsyāyana (Pakṣilasvāmin) c. 5th c. CE First surviving commentary Nyāya Vārttika Uddyotakara c. late 6th c. CE Defence against Dignāga’s critique Tātparyaṭīkā Vācaspati Miśra 9th or 10th c. CE Sub-commentary Nyāyamañjarī Jayanta Bhaṭṭa late 9th c. CE Independent treatise, written in Kaśmīr Tātparyapariśuddhi; Nyāyakusumāñjali Udayana late 10th – 11th c. CE Systematic defence of Nyāya theism Tattvacintāmaṇi Gaṅgeśa 14th c. CE Foundation of Navya-Nyāya

docs.title: 2.2 The Sixteen Categories (Padārthas)
docs.text:
The Nyāya Sūtra opens with an enumeration of sixteen topics (padārthas) whose correct understanding is said to lead to the highest good. Unlike the Vaiśeṣika categories, they are not kinds of being: most of them are topics of epistemology and debate, while the second, prameya, contains the metaphysics (Figure 2.1).

Figure 2.1. The Sixteen Categories (Padārthas) of the Nyāya System

docs.title: 2.2.1 Means and Objects of Knowledge
docs.text: The first category, the means of knowledge (pramāṇa), sets the agenda of the system. Nyāya accepts four: perception (pratyakṣa), cognition arising from the contact of a sense organ with its object; inference (anumāna), knowledge preceded by perception and proceeding through a mark (liṅga); comparison (upamāna), knowledge of what a word refers to through similarity with something already known; and testimony (śabda), knowledge from the words of a trustworthy person (āpta). Each is treated below. The second category, the objects of knowledge (prameya), is a list of twelve items whose right understanding matters for liberation: the self, the body, the sense organs, their objects, cognition, the mind, activity, the defects (desire, aversion and delusion), rebirth, the fruit of action, suffering, and release (apavarga). The list begins with the self and ends with release, and it shows that Nyāya’s epistemology was meant to serve an account of bondage and freedom. The remaining fourteen categories — doubt, purpose, example, established doctrine, the members of an argument, suppositional reasoning, ascertainment, and the kinds and faults of debate — describe how an inquiry or a debate proceeds from doubt to settled knowledge.

docs.title: 2.3 The Nyāya Theory of Perception (Pratyakṣa)
docs.text:
The sūtra’s definition of perception is short, but each of its terms was argued over for a thousand years:

Definition of Perception

indriyārtha-sannikarṣotpannaṃ jñānam avyapadeśyam avyabhicāri vyavasāyātmakaṃ pratyakṣam Perception is that cognition which arises from the contact of a sense organ with its object, which is non-verbal (avyapadeśya), non-errant (avyabhicāri), and of a determinate character (vyavasāyātmaka). — Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.4

Later Nyāya, from Vācaspati Miśra onwards, read the terms avyapadeśya and vyavasāyātmaka as marking two stages of perception. Indeterminate perception (nirvikalpaka) is the first, pre-conceptual grasp of an object together with its qualifiers, before they are related to one another in a judgement; determinate perception (savikalpaka) is the cognition that follows, in which the object is grasped as a thing of a certain kind, with certain qualities and a name. The distinction was Nyāya’s answer to Dignāga, for whom only the first, conceptless stage is perception at all (Chapter 10): the Naiyāyikas granted that there is such a stage, but denied that what follows it is mere construction. Navya-Nyāya, systematising earlier ideas, also admitted three “extraordinary” (alaukika) kinds of sense-contact: the perception of a universal through an individual (sāmānyalakṣaṇā), perception mediated by an earlier cognition, as when one “sees” that sandalwood is fragrant (jñānalakṣaṇā), and the perception of yogins (yogaja). The first of these was put to work in the theory of inference, as a way of knowing that all smoke, and not only the smoke one has seen, is accompanied by fire.

docs.title: 2.4 The Nyāya Theory of Inference (Anumāna)
docs.text: Inference is defined in the Nyāya Sūtra (1.1.5) as knowledge “preceded by that” (tatpūrvaka), i.e. by perception, and it proceeds through a logical mark (liṅga or hetu). Nyāya inference is not a formal logic in the modern sense: its validity rests on an observed, exceptionless relation (vyāpti) between the mark and what is to be proved (Matilal 1998).

docs.title: 2.4.1 The Five-Membered Syllogism (Pañcāvayava)
docs.text:
The hallmark of Nyāya logic is the five-membered syllogism (pañcāvayava nyāya). Unlike the Aristotelian three-membered syllogism, the Nyāya syllogism includes explicit citation of an example and application (Figure 2.2).

Figure 2.2. The Five-Membered Nyāya Syllogism (Pañcāvayava Nyāya)

docs.title: 2.4.2 The Terms of an Inference and Their Conditions
docs.text: Every inference has three terms: the subject about which something is inferred (pakṣa, the hill), the property to be proved (sādhya, fire), and the reason or mark (hetu or liṅga, smoke). The validity of the inference depends on the relation between the reason and the property to be proved, which Nyāya calls pervasion (vyāpti): wherever there is smoke, there is fire.

docs.title: 2.4.3 Classification of Inference
docs.text:
The Nyāya Sūtra (1.1.5) names three types of inference. Their meaning was already disputed by Vātsyāyana, who offers two different interpretations; the readings below are the most common (Table 2.2):

Table 2.2. Types of Nyāya Inference Type Sanskrit Description “Like the earlier” Pūrvavat From cause to effect (seeing dark clouds, inferring rain) “Like the remainder” Śeṣavat From effect to cause (seeing a swollen river, inferring past rain) “Seen in general” Sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa From a generally observed correlation (inferring the sun’s motion from its change of position)

In later Nyāya a valid reason is said to have five features (pañcarūpa), which extend the three features (trairūpya) of the Buddhist logicians (Chapter 10). It must be present in the subject (the hill must actually have smoke); present in at least one similar case (the kitchen, which has both smoke and fire); absent from all dissimilar cases (a lake, which has neither); its conclusion must not be contradicted by a stronger means of knowledge; and there must be no equally strong counter-reason. The last two conditions show what Nyāya added to the Buddhist scheme: an inference is assessed not only by its internal form but against everything else one knows.

docs.title: 2.5 The Nyāya Theory of Fallacies (Hetvābhāsa)
docs.text:
The Nyāya Sūtra (1.2.4–9) enumerates five types of hetvābhāsa (pseudo-reasons); later authors renamed and refined them:

Five Fallacies in Nyāya Logic

  1. Savyabhicāra (Irregular) — The hetu is found in both sapakṣa and vipakṣa

  2. Viruddha (Contradictory) — The hetu proves the opposite of the thesis

  3. Prakaraṇasama (Counterbalanced) — The hetu has an equally strong counter-reason

  4. Sādhyasama (Unproved) — The hetu itself stands in need of proof

  5. Kālātīta (Mistimed; later bādhita, “contradicted”) — The hetu is put forward for a conclusion already ruled out by stronger evidence

docs.title: 2.6 The Nyāya Theory of Comparison (Upamāna)
docs.text:
Upamāna (comparison or analogy) is the third pramāṇa accepted by Nyāya. It is defined as the knowledge of the relation between a name and a thing through the perception of similarity with a known object.

Definition of Upamāna

prasiddha-sādharmyāt sādhya-sādhanam upamānam Upamāna is the means of establishing the thing to be known through its similarity to a well-known object. — Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.6

The classic example: A person who has never seen a gavaya (a wild bovine, probably the gayal or nilgai) is told by a reliable person, “A gavaya resembles a cow.” Later, encountering an animal in the forest that resembles a cow, the person recognizes: “This is the animal called gavaya.” The knowledge “This is a gavaya” arises not from perception alone (the person has never seen one before), nor from inference, nor from testimony (which only said it resembles a cow) — but from comparison.

The status of comparison as an independent means of knowledge was contested. Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika reduced it to inference or perception, and the Buddhists rejected it. Mīmāṃsā accepted it but defined it differently, as the knowledge that the remembered cow is similar to the animal now seen, rather than as knowledge of a word’s referent; the Jain logicians treated it as a form of recognition (pratyabhijñā). The Naiyāyikas’ reason for keeping it separate is that its result — “this is what the word gavaya means” — links a word to a thing, which neither perception nor inference alone accomplishes.

docs.title: 2.7 The Nyāya Theory of Verbal Testimony (Śabda)
docs.text:
Śabda (verbal testimony) is the fourth means of knowledge. It is defined as the knowledge arising from the sentence of a trustworthy person (āpta), one who knows the matter, wishes to convey it truthfully and is able to express it. For a sentence to produce knowledge, its words must also satisfy three conditions, which Nyāya shared with Mīmāṃsā (Chapter 6): syntactic expectancy (ākāṅkṣā), by which each word calls for the others that complete its meaning; semantic fitness (yogyatā), which “fire is cold” lacks; and contiguity (sannidhi or āsatti), the utterance of the words without long interruption. Later Nyāya added a fourth, the speaker’s intention (tātparya), which decides between possible readings of an ambiguous sentence: “bring the saindhava” means salt at dinner and a horse before a journey. The role given to intention invites comparison with H.P. Grice’s account of speaker meaning, although the Indian theory was developed in a different framework (Matilal 1990).

Nyāya distinguishes secular testimony (laukika), the statements of trustworthy persons about worldly matters, from Vedic testimony (vaidika). The Nyāya Sūtra (2.1.68) compares the Veda’s reliability to that of medical and mantra texts, whose effectiveness is known; later Nyāya grounds it in the omniscience of its author, God. This sets Nyāya sharply against Mīmāṃsā, which holds the Veda to be authorless (apauruṣeya) and therefore free of the faults of any author.

docs.title: 2.8 Nyāya Theory of Causation
docs.text:
Nyāya upholds the doctrine of asatkāryavāda or ārambhavāda — the view that the effect is a new creation, not pre-existent in the cause. This stands in opposition to Sāṃkhya’s satkāryavāda.

Nyāya’s Three Types of Causes

  1. Samāvāyi-kāraṇa (Material / Inherent Cause) — The material out of which the effect is produced, in which the effect inheres by the relation of samavāya. E.g., threads are the inherent cause of cloth.

  2. Asamavāyi-kāraṇa (Non-inherent Cause) — That which resides in the material cause and helps produce the effect. E.g., the conjunction (saṃyoga) of the threads is the non-inherent cause of cloth.

  3. Nimitta-kāraṇa (Efficient / Instrumental Cause) — The agent or instrument that brings about the effect. E.g., the weaver and the loom are efficient causes of cloth.

The Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika argument against satkāryavāda proceeds as follows: if the effect already exists in the cause, then production is meaningless; there would be no difference between the caused and the uncaused; and the activity of the agent would be purposeless.

docs.title: 2.9 The Self (Ātman)
docs.text:
The Nyāya school gives one of the most careful defences of a self in Indian philosophy, worked out above all against the Buddhist denial of the self (anātman). The sūtra names the self’s marks:

The Self as the Substrate of Experience

icchā-dveṣa-prayatna-sukha-duḥkha-jñānāny ātmano liṅgam Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition are the marks of the self. — Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.10

The argument behind this sūtra can be reconstructed in three steps. First, desire, effort, pleasure, pain and cognition are qualities, and every quality inheres in a substance. Secondly, they cannot inhere in the body, since a corpse has a body but none of them; nor in the senses, since each sense grasps only its own objects, whereas the same subject both sees and touches one and the same thing — the argument with which the third book of the Nyāya Sūtra opens (3.1.1); nor in the mind (manas), which is atomic and serves only as an instrument of attention. Thirdly, they must inhere in one enduring subject, since I desire now what I enjoyed before: desire presupposes the memory of past pleasure, and memory presupposes that the one who remembers is the one who experienced, for no one remembers what another has seen. That subject is the self (Table 2.3).

Table 2.3. Nyāya Arguments for the Existence of Ātman Argument Reasoning Buddhist Counter From memory Memory of “I experienced X” requires a continuing subject Memory is a new mental event, not proof of continuing self From desire “I want X again” presupposes identity of the desirer and the past experiencer Desire arises from causal chain, not from a persistent self From moral responsibility Karma requires an enduring agent who reaps what it sows Karmic continuity through consciousness-stream suffices From recognition “This is the same object I saw before” requires a persisting recognizer Recognition is a fresh cognition arising from saṃskāras From the unity of experience One subject perceives through five senses; this requires a unifier The mind coordinates sense data without a self

The Buddhist reply, given in the right-hand column, does not deny the facts of memory and desire but explains them differently. What makes my memory mine is not a persisting substance but a causal series: an experience leaves a trace in a stream of momentary events, and a later event of the same stream is the recollection. Uddyotakara and his successors answered that a series is not one thing and cannot be the single subject that “I” refers to; the Buddhists answered that “I” refers to the series only conventionally. The dispute lasted as long as Buddhism remained in India, and Udayana’s Ātmatattvaviveka is its most elaborate Nyāya statement (Matilal 1986).

The self that emerges is eternal, all-pervading and many — each living being has its own — and it is a substance. Consciousness, however, is not its nature but an adventitious quality (āgantuka guṇa), which arises only when the self is joined to a body, senses and mind. This distinguishes the Nyāya self from the self of Advaita, which is consciousness, and from the Sāṃkhya puruṣa, which is essentially conscious. In liberation the Nyāya self exists without any qualities, including consciousness, and Vedāntin critics mocked such a liberation as the existence of a stone (pāṣāṇavat). The Naiyāyika’s reply was that the absence of all pain is worth having even at the price of all pleasure, since pleasure is always mixed with pain.

docs.title: 2.10 God (Īśvara)
docs.text:
The Nyāya Sūtra itself says little about God (4.1.19–21), and Vātsyāyana’s theism is modest. Systematic arguments were developed later, largely in response to Buddhist critiques. Udayana’s Nyāyakusumāñjali (“A Handful of Flowers of Logic”, late 10th or 11th century) is the most systematic Indian treatise arguing for the existence of God. It answers Buddhist and Mīmāṃsaka objections, and its fifth chapter opens with a verse listing eight grounds of proof: kāryāyojanadhṛtyādeḥ padāt pratyayataḥ śruteḥ / vākyāt saṅkhyāviśeṣāc ca sādhyo viśvavid avyayaḥ (5.1; Figure 2.3).

Figure 2.3. The eight grounds for the existence of īśvara listed in Udayana’s Nyāyakusumāñjali 5.1 (glosses simplified)

The first and best-known of these grounds was put in the standard form of a Nyāya inference: the earth and other such things have a maker, because they are effects, as a pot is. That they are effects was argued from their having parts: whatever is composed of parts is produced and perishes. That an effect needs a maker who knows its material was taken from experience: no pot without a potter. Buddhist critics, above all Dharmakīrti and later Śāntarakṣita in the Tattvasaṅgraha, replied that the reason is ambiguous. The kind of “effect” that shows a maker, as a pot does, is something we have seen being made; mountains and trees are not like that, and the wider sense in which they are “effects” — things that arise from causes — does not imply a maker at all. Jain critics and Mīmāṃsakas such as Kumārila added that there is no evidence that the world ever had a beginning (Potter 1977). Udayana’s answer was to defend each step of the inference against these objections and to argue that the concept of God is not empty, since God is the subject of the very inferences the opponent tries to refute. Modern readers have compared the argument from effects with cosmological arguments, and the argument from the ordering of atoms with design arguments; but Udayana’s arguments are inferences within a Vaiśeṣika ontology, and their strength depends on it.

docs.title: 2.11 Navya-Nyāya — The New Logic
docs.text:
The Navya-Nyāya (New Logic) school was founded by Gaṅgeśa Upādhyāya of Mithilā (14th century CE) with his Tattvacintāmaṇi, which is organised by the four Nyāya means of knowledge. It built on Udayana and absorbed the Vaiśeṣika ontology, so that the combined school is often called Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika (Ingalls 1951; Potter 1977). Its distinctive contribution was a technical language for stating cognitions and definitions with great precision, together with refined theories of universals, relations and absence. Figure 2.4 summarises the main phases of the tradition.

Figure 2.4. Historical development of the Nyāya tradition (simplified)

docs.title: 2.11.1 The Metalanguage of Navya-Nyāya
docs.text:
Navya-Nyāya developed a highly technical philosophical language characterized by:

  1. Avacchedaka (Limitor/Delimiter) — A property or relation that fixes exactly how another property is to be taken. In “the hill has fire”, fireness (vahnitva) is the limitor of the property-to-be-proved (sādhyatāvacchedaka): what is to be proved is fire in general, not some particular fire.

  2. Nirūpaka (Describer/Relator) — A property that determines the form of a relation. When we say “x has knowledge of y,” the knowledge-relation is described by the object y.

  3. Pratiyogin and Anuyogin — The two relata in a relation of absence. In “the absence of a pot on the floor,” the pot is the pratiyogin (the absentee) and the floor is the anuyogin (the locus).

  4. Svarūpa-sambandha (Self-linking Relation) — A relation that links directly to its relatum without requiring a further relation (avoiding infinite regress).

docs.title: 2.11.2 Navya-Nyāya Analysis of Absence (Abhāva)
docs.text:
One of the most refined contributions of Navya-Nyāya is its analysis of negation and absence (Table 2.4):

Table 2.4. Navya-Nyāya Classification of Absence Type Sanskrit Definition and Example Prior absence Prāg-abhāva Absence of an entity before its production; beginningless but terminable (e.g., absence of the pot before it is made) Posterior absence Dhvaṃsa-abhāva Absence of an entity after its destruction; has a beginning but is endless (e.g., absence of the pot after it is broken) Absolute absence Atyantābhāva Absence that holds for all time; both beginningless and endless (e.g., absence of colour in air) Mutual absence Anyonyābhāva The difference of one entity from another (e.g., the pot is not the cloth)

docs.title: 2.11.3 A Worked Analysis: Gaṅgeśa on Pervasion
docs.text:
The technical language is easiest to understand in use. Its most famous application is the definition of pervasion (vyāpti), the relation between reason and property-to-be-proved on which every inference depends. The chapter on pervasion in Gaṅgeśa’s Tattvacintāmaṇi begins by considering and rejecting five provisional definitions (the vyāptipañcaka, “five on pervasion”), then states and refines his own; with the commentaries of Raghunātha and Mathurānātha this became the most intensively studied text of the Navadvīpa school (Ingalls 1951; Goekoop 1967).

The first definition. The first provisional definition says that the reason is pervaded by the property to be proved when the reason does not occur in anything that possesses the absence of that property (sādhyābhāvavad-avṛttitva). Take the standard inference, “the hill has fire, because it has smoke”. The things that possess the absence of fire include a lake; smoke does not occur in a lake; and so on for every fireless place. The definition is satisfied, and the inference is valid. Now reverse it: “the hill has smoke, because it has fire”. Among the things that possess the absence of smoke is a red-hot iron ball, and fire does occur in it. The definition is not satisfied, and the inference is rightly rejected: fire is not pervaded by smoke (Figure 2.5).

Figure 2.5. Testing two inferences against the first provisional definition of pervasion in Gaṅgeśa’s Tattvacintāmaṇi

Why limitors are needed. Stated loosely, the definition already goes wrong. The hill has the fire that is on it, but it lacks the fire in the kitchen; so the hill itself “possesses an absence of fire”, and smoke occurs on the hill. Taken literally, the definition would reject the standard inference. Navya-Nyāya removes the difficulty by specifying which absence is meant: the absence whose counterpositive (pratiyogin, the thing absent) is fire as limited by fireness (vahnitva) — the absence of fire in general, not of this or that fire. In the technical idiom, the counterpositiveness of the absence must be limited by the property that limits the property-to-be-proved (sādhyatāvacchedaka), and by the relation in which that property is to be proved, here contact. A parallel specification, spelled out by the commentators, is needed on the side of the reason. Smoke inheres in its own parts, and the parts of smoke contain no fire; if “occurrence” could be by any relation, smoke would occur, by inherence, in something that lacks fire. So the reason’s non-occurrence must be taken in the relation by which it serves as the reason, which is again contact. Each of these qualifications is a limitor (avacchedaka), and the analysis shows why Navya-Nyāya needed them: a general statement about properties is ambiguous until the property-bearer, the property-limiting property and the relation are all fixed.

Why the provisional definitions fail. Even when refined in this way, all five provisional definitions fail for one kind of inference, the “purely positive” (kevalānvayin), whose property to be proved is present everywhere — for example, “this is nameable, because it is knowable”. Nothing lacks nameability, so there is nothing that “possesses the absence of the property to be proved”; a definition framed in terms of such things has nothing to apply to, and fails to cover a valid inference. Gaṅgeśa therefore turns the definition round. On his own account, pervasion is the reason’s co-occurrence with a property to be proved that, taken under its limiting property, is not the counterpositive of any absolute absence found in the loci of the reason. Since no absence of nameability exists, nameability is not the counterpositive of any absence, and the purely positive inference is covered.

A further refinement. Gaṅgeśa’s definition contains one more qualification, and it shows the school’s care with “partial occurrence” (avyāpyavṛtti). The commentators explain it with a standard example. A monkey sits on the top branch of a tree. The tree has contact with the monkey, but at its roots it lacks that contact; so the absence of monkey-contact occurs in the same tree. If the definition were left as it stands, the inference “this has monkey-contact, because it is this tree” would be wrongly rejected. The definition therefore requires that the absence considered be one that does not occur in the same locus as its own counterpositive (pratiyogy-asamānādhikaraṇa): the absence of monkey-contact in the tree, which shares its locus with monkey-contact, is set aside. The full definition is long, but every clause in it answers a specific counter-example. That is the characteristic method of Navya-Nyāya: a definition is tested against cases until it neither over-extends nor under-extends, and the results are stated in a vocabulary of properties, limitors and relations precise enough to make the test decidable (Matilal 1968; Ganeri 2001). Much of the stimulus for this method, it has been argued, came from the Advaitin Śrīharṣa’s attack on Nyāya definitions (Section 7.4).

docs.title: 2.11.4 Cognition, Inference and Meaning in the New Logic
docs.text:
The same precision was applied to every part of the theory. Gaṅgeśa’s Tattvacintāmaṇi contains a section on pakṣatā, the condition that makes something a proper subject of inference. The older view was that inference applies where the property to be proved is still in doubt. Gaṅgeśa points out that one can infer what one already knows, and that one need not doubt in order to infer. He therefore defines pakṣatā negatively: it is the absence of certainty that the subject has the property, unless that certainty is accompanied by a desire to infer it (sisādhayiṣā). Inference is blocked only where one already knows the conclusion and has no wish to prove it.

The analysis of verbal understanding (śābdabodha) was treated in the same way. Navya-Nyāya described the cognition produced by a sentence as a structure of qualifiers and qualificands joined by relations, each fixed by its limitor, so that complex and ambiguous sentences could be disambiguated exactly (Table 2.5).

Table 2.5. Navya-Nyāya Analysis of Sentential Meaning Component Sanskrit Technical Term Function Qualifier Viśeṣaṇa The property that determines or specifies another entity Qualificand Viśeṣya The entity that is determined or specified Relation Saṃsarga The connection between qualifier and qualificand Limitor Avacchedaka The property that restricts the scope of a relation Describer Nirūpaka The property that determines the form of a relation

docs.title: 2.11.5 The Early-Modern Logicians
docs.text:
Between about 1450 and 1700 the logicians of Mithilā and, above all, Navadvīpa in Bengal made Navya-Nyāya the common technical language of Sanskrit learning. Raghunātha Śiromaṇi (c. 1460–1540) is its most original figure. His commentary on the Tattvacintāmaṇi, the Dīdhiti, repeatedly corrects Gaṅgeśa, and his short Padārthatattvanirūpaṇa reopened the Vaiśeṣika list of categories itself, arguing, among other things, that space and time need not be counted as substances distinct from God and that some items the old list ignored, such as causal power, deserve a place of their own. His successors Jagadīśa Tarkālaṅkāra and Gadādhara Bhaṭṭācārya (17th century) turned the method on language: Jagadīśa’s Śabdaśaktiprakāśikā and Gadādhara’s Vyutpattivāda analyse the meaning of case-endings, verbs and compounds in the terms of qualifier and relation.

The method spread beyond the school. Grammarians such as Kauṇḍa Bhaṭṭa and Nāgeśa, Mīmāṃsakas such as Khaṇḍadeva, Advaitins such as Madhusūdana Sarasvatī (Section 7.4) and Dharmaśāstra authors in Bengal and Mithilā wrote in its idiom. The Jain monk Yaśovijaya (1624–1688), who studied the new logic, restated Jain epistemology and the doctrine of many-sidedness in Navya-Nyāya terms in works such as the Jainatarkabhāṣā, so that the old Jain theory of standpoints could be argued with the same precision as its rivals. Jonardon Ganeri has argued that this period, often dismissed as one of scholastic stagnation, was in fact a time of self-consciously “new” philosophy, in which thinkers debated the methods of philosophy itself (Ganeri 2011). Scholars such as D.H.H. Ingalls, B.K. Matilal and J.N. Mohanty later analysed Navya-Nyāya with the tools of modern logic, while noting that it is a logic of cognitions and properties rather than of sentences or sets (Ingalls 1951; Matilal 1968).

docs.title: 2.12 The Nyāya Theory of Debate
docs.text:
The Nyāya theory of debate (vāda-vidhi) is an early and systematic treatment of argumentation, comparable in scope to Aristotle’s Topics and Sophistical Refutations; debate manuals with related terminology also appear in the Carakasaṃhitā (Vimānasthāna 8) and in early Buddhist texts. The fifth book of the Nyāya Sūtra is devoted to futile rejoinders and points of defeat. The three kinds of debate the sūtra recognises, and the later arguments about whether victory-seeking debate is legitimate, are discussed in Chapter 13 (Section 13.8); this section describes the apparatus itself.

The Nyāya Sūtra (5.2.1) lists twenty-two points of defeat (nigrahasthāna); the preceding chapter, 5.1, deals with twenty-four kinds of jāti, or futile rejoinder. They include not only logical errors but procedural faults, such as abandoning one’s thesis, introducing irrelevant matter or speaking out of turn (aprāptakāla). Table 2.6 gives a selection, numbered by their place in the sūtra’s list.

Table 2.6. Selected Points of Defeat (Nigrahasthāna), with Their Place in the List of Nyāya Sūtra 5.2.1 Place in NS 5.2.1 Sanskrit Name Nature of the Violation 1 Pratijñā-hāni Abandoning one’s original thesis under pressure 2 Pratijñāntara Shifting to a different thesis to avoid refutation 3 Pratijñāvirodha Contradicting one’s own stated position 5 Hetvantara Substituting a different reason from the one first stated 6 Arthāntara Introducing irrelevant matter 7 Nirarthaka Uttering meaningless sounds 15 Ajñāna Failing to understand the opponent’s argument 16 Apratibhā Inability to reply — speechlessness

The last three of the sixteen categories — quibble (chala), futile rejoinder (jāti) and point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) — deal with fallacious tactics. The sūtra identifies three kinds of quibble: verbal quibble, which exploits an ambiguous word; generic quibble, which confuses what is true of a class with what is true of its members; and figurative quibble, which takes a metaphor literally.

The theory was tested above all in the long debate with the Buddhist logicians. Nyāya authors from Uddyotakara to Udayana argued against Dignāga, Dharmakīrti and their successors on the reality of universals, which the Buddhists explained by exclusion (apoha); on the nature of perception, which Dignāga defined as free from conceptual construction; on the self; and on the form of argument, which Dignāga reduced to thesis, reason and example and Dharmakīrti to reason and pervasion alone. Each side sharpened its tools against the other (Matilal 1986; Dunne 2004).

docs.title: 2.13 The Purpose and Legacy of Nyāya
docs.text:
For the sūtra, logic was not an end in itself. Its first sūtra promises the highest good from knowledge of the sixteen categories, and its second explains how:

Liberation Through Knowledge

duḥkha-janma-pravṛtti-doṣa-mithyājñānānām uttarottarāpāye tadanantarāpāyād apavargaḥ By the successive removal of suffering, birth, activity, defects, and false knowledge — each being caused by the one following it — liberation (apavarga) is attained. — Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.2

Suffering arises from birth, birth from activity, activity from the defects of desire, aversion and delusion, and the defects from false knowledge (mithyā-jñāna); true knowledge removes the last link, and the chain unravels. How far the later logicians kept this purpose in view is another matter. Much of Navya-Nyāya reads as the pursuit of precision for its own sake, and its authors seldom mention liberation outside their opening verses.

Nyāya’s legacy lies above all in method. It gave Indian philosophy its standard form of argument, its theory of pervasion and its classification of fallacies, which rival schools adopted, adapted or argued against; its analyses of perception, inference, comparison and testimony set the terms of later epistemology; its theory of debate gave rules for honest and dishonest argument; its arguments for God became the standard Indian natural theology; and its later technical language became the idiom of grammar, law and theology. Some computer scientists have explored analogies between Navya-Nyāya’s analysis of qualifiers and absences and modern knowledge-representation languages, but these are modern analogies, not evidence of anticipation. The Vaiśeṣika ontology that Nyāya took over is the subject of Chapter 3; the Buddhist side of the debates is in Chapter 10; and the comparison of theories of knowledge is in Chapter 13.

docs.title: Chapter 3: Vaiśeṣika — Atomism and the Categories of Reality
docs.text:
Opening of Vaiśeṣika Sūtra

athāto dharmaṃ vyākhyāsyāmaḥ Now, therefore, we shall expound dharma. — Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.1

docs.title: 3.1 Historical Background and Foundational Texts
docs.text:
The Vaiśeṣika school derives its name from viśeṣa (particularity or distinction), reflecting its emphasis on the differentiation and classification of all that exists.
