It offers a systematic realist ontology and an atomic theory of matter. Indian and Greek atomism (Leucippus and Democritus, 5th century BCE) appear to have developed independently; the Vaiśeṣika form is known only from texts later than the Greek one, and claims of Indian priority are not supported by the evidence (Halbfass 1992).

Historical Note: The Founder — Maharshi Kaṇāda

The founder of Vaiśeṣika is the sage Kaṇāda (also known as Ulūka or Kaṇabhuk), whose name is usually explained as “grain-eater” (kaṇa, a grain or particle). Tradition says he lived on grains gleaned from the fields; opponents punned on the name. The Vaiśeṣika Sūtra is a layered text, usually dated in its earliest form to c. 1st century BCE – 1st century CE; its transmission is complicated, and the oldest surviving commentary (Candrānanda’s) preserves a different recension from the one used by later authors.

docs.title: 3.1.1 Major Texts and Commentators
docs.text:
Table 3.1 lists the major texts and commentators.

Table 3.1. Major Texts of the Vaiśeṣika Tradition Text Author Date Significance Vaiśeṣika Sūtra Kaṇāda c. 1st c. BCE – 1st c. CE Foundational aphorisms Padārtha­dharma­saṅgraha Praśastapāda c. 6th c. CE First systematic exposition; introduces īśvara Vyomavatī Vyomaśiva c. 10th c. CE Commentary on Praśastapāda Nyāyakandalī Śrīdhara 991 CE Commentary on Praśastapāda Kiraṇāvalī Udayana late 10th c. CE Commentary on Praśastapāda Saptapadārthī Śivāditya c. 11th c. CE Treats absence as a seventh category

docs.title: 3.2 The Seven Categories of Reality (Sapta Padārtha)
docs.text:
The Vaiśeṣika system classifies all that can be known and named into fundamental categories (padārthas). The vulgate text of the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra (1.1.4; several scholars doubt that this sūtra belonged to the earliest text) and Praśastapāda list six positive categories; absence (abhāva) was recognised as a seventh by later authors such as Śivāditya and Udayana (10th–11th century). The distinction between the six categories and the nine substances (one of the categories) should be kept clear (Halbfass 1992); see Figure 3.1.

Figure 3.1. The Seven Categories (Sapta Padārtha) of Vaiśeṣika; absence (abhāva, dashed) was added as a seventh by later authors

docs.title: 3.2.1 1. Dravya (Substance)
docs.text:
Substance (dravya) is defined as “that which possesses action and qualities and is an inherence cause” (kriyāguṇavat samavāyikāraṇam iti dravyalakṣaṇam, Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.15; numbering varies between recensions). Vaiśeṣika enumerates nine substances. Earth, water, fire and air are eternal only in their atomic form; their composite products are impermanent (Table 3.2):

Table 3.2. The Nine Dravyas (Substances) of Vaiśeṣika No. Dravya English Characteristics 1 Pṛthivī Earth Possesses smell, taste, colour, touch 2 Ap (Jala) Water Possesses taste, colour, touch; viscous 3 Tejas Fire/Light Possesses colour and touch; hot 4 Vāyu Air Possesses touch alone 5 Ākāśa Ether/Space Possesses sound; all-pervading 6 Kāla Time All-pervading; basis of temporal relations 7 Dik Direction/Space All-pervading; basis of spatial relations 8 Ātman Self/Soul All-pervading; conscious; many 9 Manas Mind Atomic in size; internal organ

Of these, the first four (earth, water, fire, air) are composed of atoms (paramāṇu), while the remaining five are non-atomic and all-pervading (except manas, which is atomic but non-material).

docs.title: 3.2.2 2. Guṇa (Quality)
docs.text: A quality is what inheres in a substance and has no qualities or motions of its own. The Vaiśeṣika Sūtra (1.1.6 in the vulgate) names seventeen qualities; Praśastapāda completed the list to the canonical twenty-four. They fall into natural groups: the five sensible qualities (colour, taste, smell, touch and sound, each the special object of one sense); the general physical qualities of number, magnitude, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness and proximity; the qualities of the self — cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion and effort, together with merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma); and heaviness (gurutva), fluidity, viscosity and “tendency” (saṃskāra), which covers impetus, elasticity and the memory-trace. That cognition and pleasure are listed alongside colour and number is characteristic: for Vaiśeṣika the mental is not a separate realm but a set of qualities of one kind of substance, the self.

docs.title: 3.2.3 3. Karma (Action)
docs.text: Action belongs to only one substance at a time and is the cause of conjunction and disjunction; unlike a quality, it is transient by nature, since it ceases once it has produced the new contact. Five kinds are distinguished — throwing upwards, throwing downwards, contraction, expansion and going — the last covering every other kind of motion. Only substances of limited size can move, so that the all-pervading substances (ether, time, space and the self) are motionless.

docs.title: 3.2.4 4. Sāmānya (Universal)
docs.text: Universals are eternal, one, and inhere in many individuals. The argument for them starts from language and cognition: we call many different animals “cow” and recognise each as a cow, and this recurrent cognition (anuvṛtti-pratyaya) needs a common object, which no single cow can provide. The highest universal is being (sattā), present in all substances, qualities and actions; below it come lower universals such as substancehood, cowness and potness. Not every general word, however, names a real universal. Udayana listed six conditions that block one, among them the existence of only one individual (there is no universal “etherness”, since there is only one ether) and the threat of an infinite regress (there is no universal of universals). The Buddhists denied universals altogether and explained common names by exclusion (apoha; Chapter 10).

docs.title: 3.2.5 5. Viśeṣa (Particularity)
docs.text: The category that gives the school its name answers a question its atomism raises. Two atoms of earth have the same qualities, the same magnitude and the same universals; yet they are two, and a yogin, according to the school, can tell them apart. What distinguishes them? Not anything they share, and not their positions, which change. Each eternal substance — each atom, each self, each mind — must therefore have its own ultimate differentiator, a particularity (viśeṣa). Why do particularities not need further particularities to distinguish them? Because, the Vaiśeṣika replies, a particularity distinguishes itself as well as its substance, as light reveals itself as well as other things. Critics asked why, if a particularity can do this, the atom could not do so directly; the doctrine was one of those that later Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika authors felt free to question.

docs.title: 3.2.6 6. Samavāya (Inherence)
docs.text: Inherence is the permanent relation between things that are never found apart (ayutasiddha): a substance and its qualities, a whole and its parts, a universal and its instances, a substance and its motion. Conjunction will not do for these, since conjunction joins things that can exist separately and can be undone. Inherence is one and eternal; Nyāya holds that it is perceived, Vaiśeṣika that it is inferred. It also faced the most famous objection to the system. If quality and substance need a third thing, inherence, to relate them, then inherence too must be related to each of them by a further relation, and so on without end; Śaṅkara pressed this regress in the Brahmasūtrabhāṣya (2.2.13). The Vaiśeṣika answer is that inherence is not a thing that needs connecting but the connecting itself: it relates its terms by its own nature, without a further relation, just as a lamp needs no second lamp to be seen. Later Nyāya generalised this into the notion of a self-linking relation (svarūpa-sambandha; Section 2.11). The opponents’ rejoinder was that if a relation can be self-linking, so can a quality, and inherence becomes superfluous; the Prābhākara Mīmāṃsakas and the Buddhists both took this line.

docs.title: 3.2.7 7. Abhāva (Non-existence)
docs.text: Later Vaiśeṣika recognised absence as a seventh category, on the ground that “there is no pot on the floor” is a true cognition and must have an object. Four kinds are distinguished: prior absence (of a pot before it is made), posterior absence (after it is destroyed), absolute absence (of colour in air, at all times) and mutual absence or difference (a pot is not a cloth). The absentee must itself be something real somewhere, so that “the hare’s horn” is not a proper example of absolute absence. The fullest analysis of absence came later, in Navya-Nyāya (Table 2.4).

docs.title: 3.3 The Atomic Theory (Paramāṇu-Vāda)
docs.text: The Vaiśeṣika atom (paramāṇu) is eternal, partless and of the smallest magnitude, a special magnitude called “globularity” (pārimaṇḍalya). There are four kinds, corresponding to the four elements earth, water, fire and air; ether, the medium of sound, is a single, all-pervading substance and not atomic.

docs.title: 3.3.1 Why There Must Be Atoms
docs.text: The argument for atoms is conceptual, not experimental. Composite things — pots, mountains, mustard seeds — have parts, and those parts have parts. Either division goes on for ever, or it stops. If it went on for ever, every composite thing would have infinitely many parts, and a mustard seed would contain as many parts as Mount Meru; but then nothing would account for the difference in their size, which is absurd. If division ended in nothing, composite things would be made of nothing, which is also absurd. So division must end in parts that have no parts, and since what has no parts cannot be broken up, these are eternal. The argument is Vaiśeṣika’s version of the reasoning of the Greek atomists, and it shares their difficulty: whether something partless can have a size at all, and how such things can combine (see below).

docs.title: 3.3.2 The Process of Atomic Combination
docs.text:
The school also explained how atoms make visible things (Figure 3.2).

Figure 3.2. The Vaiśeṣika Process of Atomic Combination

Two atoms combine to form a dyad (dvyaṇuka), which is still imperceptible; three dyads form a triad (tryaṇuka), the smallest perceptible thing, identified with the mote that dances in a sunbeam; further combinations produce gross objects. The reason for these particular numbers is ingenious. The infinitesimal magnitude of atoms cannot itself produce any larger magnitude — adding nothing to nothing gives nothing — so the magnitude of a dyad must come from something else, namely the number of its components; the duality of two atoms produces the dyad’s minute size, and the triplicity of three dyads produces the first visible size. Udayana’s eighth ground for God (Figure 2.3) depends on this doctrine, since a number such as duality was held to arise from a cognition that counts. The first motion of atoms is attributed in the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra to the unseen merit and demerit of souls (adṛṣṭa); from Praśastapāda onwards it is also said to be set going by God’s will.

docs.title: 3.4 Causation (Ārambhavāda)
docs.text: Vaiśeṣika holds that the effect is a genuinely new thing (ārambha, “beginning”), which did not exist in its cause before it was produced; the view is also called asatkāryavāda. A cloth is a new substance, a whole (avayavin) distinct from the threads that are its parts and inhering in each of them. The arguments are drawn from ordinary experience. The cloth has properties — a certain size, a pattern, the capacity to cover a body — that no thread has; it is perceived as one thing where the threads are many; if it already existed in the threads, the weaver’s work would produce nothing; and when a pot is broken, the pot ceases to exist while its potsherds remain, which shows that the whole was something over and above its parts. Against this stands Sāṃkhya’s doctrine that the effect pre-exists in its cause (Chapter 4), and Advaita’s that the effect is an appearance of the cause (Chapter 7). The Buddhists attacked the whole from the other side: if the whole is distinct from its parts, it should be perceptible apart from them, and the cloth should weigh more than all its threads together, which the scales do not show. The Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika defence of the real whole against Buddhist reductionism is one of the long-running debates of Indian metaphysics. The threefold analysis of causes — inherent, non-inherent and instrumental — is given in Chapter 2 (Section 2.8).

docs.title: 3.5 Space, Time and Mind
docs.text:
Space (dik) and time (kāla) are single, eternal, all-pervading substances, known not by perception but by inference from our judgements of “east” and “west”, “near” and “far”, “earlier” and “later”, “quick” and “slow”. Their apparent multiplicity — past, present and future, this direction and that — is imposed by their relations to changing things. Modern readers have compared this with the early modern European debate between absolute and relational views of space, but the Vaiśeṣika problem was different: how to account for the content of such judgements, given that the things judged do not contain it.

The mind (manas) is a substance too, one for each self, atomic in size and eternal, and it is the organ through which the self is joined to the senses. Its atomicity was argued from a fact of experience, the non-simultaneity of cognitions (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.16): when we seem to see and hear at once, the mind is in fact alternating very rapidly between eye and ear, for if it were large it could be in contact with several senses together. Modern readers sometimes compare this with theories of selective attention, but it is a metaphysical argument, not an empirical psychology.

docs.title: 3.6 The Vaiśeṣika Theory of Motion
docs.text:
The Vaiśeṣika analysis of motion (karma) holds that every motion requires a cause and that different types of motion have different causes. The table below summarises the causes recognised in the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra (book 5) and by Praśastapāda (Table 3.3).

Table 3.3. Vaiśeṣika Analysis of Types of Motion and Their Causes Type of Motion Sanskrit Cause and Explanation Initial motion of atoms Ādya-karma Caused by adṛṣṭa (later: directed by God) Falling Patana Caused by heaviness (gurutva) in the absence of conjunction (support) Projectile motion Vega Caused by vega (impetus), a saṃskāra produced by the initial impulse Upward flaming of fire — Attributed to adṛṣṭa (VS 5.2.13) Movement of a needle towards a magnet — Attributed to adṛṣṭa (VS 5.1.15)

The concept of vega (impetus) is particularly noteworthy. When an arrow is released from a bow, the Vaiśeṣika philosopher explains its continued motion through the notion of an impressed force (saṃskāra) that is transmitted from the bow to the arrow at the moment of release. This force gradually diminishes, causing the arrow to slow down and eventually fall. The idea is comparable to the “impetus” theories of John Philoponus (6th century) and Jean Buridan (14th century), which addressed the same problem — the continued motion of projectiles after they leave the mover. Like them, and unlike Newtonian inertia, it treats continued motion as needing a cause that wears out.

docs.title: 3.6.1 The Concept of Gurutva (Gravity)
docs.text: Vaiśeṣika treats gurutva (heaviness) as a quality of earth and water only. Unsupported bodies of these elements fall because of it, while fire and air, lacking heaviness, do not. Heaviness is imperceptible and is inferred from falling. This is close to the Aristotelian idea of natural heaviness; it is not a theory of universal gravitation, which explains the motion of all bodies, including the heavens, by mutual attraction. The common translation “gravity” is therefore misleading.

docs.title: 3.7 Adṛṣṭa, God and the Cycle of the World
docs.text:
Adṛṣṭa, “the unseen”, is the merit and demerit that accumulate in the self as a result of its actions. The Vaiśeṣika Sūtra (5.2.13 in the common numbering) attributes to it the upward flaming of fire, the sideways blowing of wind and the first motion of atoms and of the mind, as well as the approach of a needle to a magnet. It thus did two jobs at once: it linked actions to their fruits in a later life, and it filled the gaps in the school’s physics where no visible cause could be found.

The Vaiśeṣika Sūtra does not clearly discuss God, and the system may originally have been non-theistic. From Praśastapāda (c. 6th century) onwards God (īśvara, Maheśvara) became central to its cosmology, because the atomic theory left a gap. In the dissolution of the world (pralaya) the atoms lie separate and inactive, and the selves have no bodies, senses or minds. Neither the unconscious atoms nor the unconscious adṛṣṭa can begin the process of combination, and the selves cannot direct it. An intelligent agent is therefore required, who, in accordance with the adṛṣṭa of souls, sets the atoms moving — air first, then the other elements — sustains the world for a cosmic period, and dissolves composite things again into atoms. The argument became one of Udayana’s grounds for God (Section 2.10).

docs.title: 3.8 Vaiśeṣika Epistemology and Its Relation to Nyāya
docs.text:
Vaiśeṣika accepted only two means of knowledge, perception and inference; Praśastapāda explicitly reduced testimony and comparison to inference. Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika were nonetheless regarded as allied systems (samānatantra), and their roles are complementary (Table 3.4).

Table 3.4. Complementary Roles of Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika Aspect Nyāya Vaiśeṣika Primary focus Epistemology and logic Ontology and metaphysics Central question How do we know? What exists? Key categories 16 topics (mainly epistemological) 6 (later 7) categories (ontological) Pramāṇas Four Two (originally) Atomic theory Accepted (from Vaiśeṣika) Developed in detail Theism Elaborated extensively Present but less emphasized

By the medieval period, the two schools effectively merged into the composite Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika system, combining Nyāya’s logical methodology with Vaiśeṣika’s ontological categories.

docs.title: 3.9 Vaiśeṣika and the Philosophy of Science
docs.text:
Several Vaiśeṣika concepts invite comparison with later scientific ideas. Such comparisons must be handled carefully: the Vaiśeṣika concepts belong to a qualitative, non-experimental natural philosophy, and none of them anticipates a modern theory (Table 3.5).

Table 3.5. Vaiśeṣika Concepts and Modern Scientific Parallels Vaiśeṣika Concept Description Comparison and limits Paramāṇu (Atom) Indivisible, eternal, partless particles of four elemental kinds Comparable to Greek atomism; unrelated to the modern atom, which is divisible Dvyaṇuka (Dyad) Two atoms of the same element combine Superficially recalls a molecule, but dyads combine atoms of one element only Gurutva (Heaviness) An imperceptible quality of earth and water, inferred from falling A local quality of some substances, not a universal force of attraction Vega (Impetus) A “tendency” (saṃskāra) that keeps a projectile moving until exhausted Comparable to the impetus theories of Philoponus and Buridan, not to Newtonian inertia Pākaja (Qualities produced by heat) Heating produces new colours, tastes, etc. Recognises transformation by heat; no theory of chemical combination

These comparisons need care. Vaiśeṣika atomism is embedded in a moral framework that has no counterpart in modern physics: atoms are set in motion by adṛṣṭa and, later, divine will, not by impersonal laws, and the arguments for atoms are conceptual. What the system offers is a careful, systematic natural philosophy of substances, qualities and motions. Its categories were also closely related to those of Indian medicine: the Carakasaṃhitā (Sūtrasthāna 1) lists six categories corresponding to the Vaiśeṣika list, although the direction of influence is debated, and medical theory used the five elements, a list of qualities and a doctrine of transformation by heat. That use is treated in Volume 13 (Āyurveda).

The theory of heat was itself a philosophical problem. The Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika authors debated how firing changes the colour of a clay pot. On the Vaiśeṣika view, the “cooking of the atoms” (pīlupāka), heat breaks the pot down into its atoms, which acquire a new colour and recombine into a new red pot, so quickly that we do not notice. On the Nyāya view, the “cooking of the pot” (piṭharapāka), heat penetrates the pores of the whole pot and changes the colour of its atoms and of the whole without destroying it. The debate concerns the identity of composite things through change: the Vaiśeṣika view saves the doctrine that a whole’s qualities come from its parts at the cost of saying that the pot we see after firing is not the one we saw before.

docs.title: 3.10 Inter-School Debates
docs.text: Vaiśeṣika atomism had critics on every side. Sāṃkhya rejected it in favour of the continuous transformation of a single primordial nature: if the effect pre-exists in its cause, there is no need for ultimate building blocks. Śaṅkara (Brahmasūtrabhāṣya 2.2.11–17) argued that unconscious atoms cannot begin to move, that unconscious adṛṣṭa cannot direct them, and that inherence leads to the regress described above. The sharpest objection came from the Buddhist Vasubandhu (Viṃśatikā 11–14). If an atom joins six others on its six sides, it must have six parts, and so is not partless; if it has no sides, atoms joining one another would coincide, and no aggregate would be larger than a single atom. Either way, partless atoms cannot make extended bodies. The Vaiśeṣika reply was that combination is not spatial interpenetration but conjunction, a quality that does not require the conjoined things to have parts; critics found this a description of the difficulty rather than its solution. The Jains, finally, accepted atoms but held that they are all of one kind and can become any element, against the four fixed kinds of the Vaiśeṣikas.

docs.title: 3.11 Philosophical Assessment of Vaiśeṣika
docs.text:
The Vaiśeṣika system’s purpose is stated in its second sūtra:

The Purpose of Vaiśeṣika

yato ’bhyudaya-niḥśreyasa-siddhiḥ sa dharmaḥ That which leads to worldly prosperity (abhyudaya) and supreme liberation (niḥśreyasa) — that is dharma. — Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.2

Its legacy, however, lies less in this promise than in its ontology. Its atomism is, with the Greek, Jain and Buddhist theories, one of the major atomisms of the ancient world; its list of categories gave later Indian thought a common vocabulary of substance, quality, motion, universal and relation; its doctrine of particularity faced the question of individuation squarely; and its treatment of absence as a genuine object of knowledge became, in Navya-Nyāya, one of the most refined analyses of negation in any tradition. These features led modern writers to call it the most “scientific” of the Indian schools, though its methods were conceptual rather than experimental.

Its difficulties are equally clear. The atomic theory never answered Vasubandhu’s objection about how partless atoms combine. The explanatory work done by adṛṣṭa — the flaming of fire, the movement of wind and of the needle — shows the school calling on an unseen moral cause wherever its physics ran out, and the later appeal to God to start the atoms moving filled the same gap at a higher level. The relations of inherence and particularity, introduced to stop regresses, invited the charge that they were names for problems rather than solutions; and the realism about wholes that it defended so stubbornly against the Buddhists required a whole to be distinct from its parts without being separable from them. Later Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika authors, from Udayana to Raghunātha (Section 2.11.5), spent much of their effort refining exactly these points.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Sāṃkhya — The Philosophy of Cosmic Enumeration
docs.text:
The Opening Verse of the Sāṃkhyakārikā

duḥkha-trayābhighātāj jijñāsā tad-abhighātake hetau dṛṣṭe sāpārthā cen naikāntātyantato ’bhāvāt From the torment of the threefold suffering arises the inquiry into the means of removing it. If it be said that this inquiry is needless since visible means exist — not so, for those means are neither certain nor final. — Sāṃkhyakārikā 1 (Īśvarakṛṣṇa)

docs.title: 4.1 Historical Background
docs.text:
Ideas later systematised as Sāṃkhya are among the oldest in Indian philosophy: lists of principles and the distinction between the self and the evolving world appear in the Kaṭha and Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣads and in the Mokṣadharma section of the Mahābhārata. The classical system, however, is known to us only from the Sāṃkhyakārikā (c. 350–450 CE). The word sāṃkhya is usually derived from saṅkhyā (number, enumeration), since the system proceeds by enumerating the principles (tattvas) of reality; it may also mean “discrimination” or “reasoned reflection” (Larson 1979; Larson and Bhattacharya 1987).

Historical Note: Maharshi Kapila — The Primordial Philosopher

The Sāṃkhya system is attributed to the legendary sage Kapila, whom tradition reveres as one of the most ancient among the seers. The Bhagavad Gītā (10.26) declares: “siddhānāṃ kapilo muniḥ” — “Among the perfected ones, I am the sage Kapila.” The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (5.2) speaks of a “kapila seer” born in the beginning; whether this refers to the sage or simply means “the red/tawny seer” (Hiraṇyagarbha) is disputed. Kapila’s disciple Āsuri and Āsuri’s disciple Pañcaśikha are named in the tradition, but nothing of their works survives beyond fragments.

The Sāṃkhyasūtra attributed to Kapila is a late work (c. 14th–15th century CE). The earliest surviving systematic text of the school is Īśvarakṛṣṇa’s Sāṃkhyakārikā (c. 350–450 CE), in about seventy verses, which itself claims to summarise an older work, the lost Ṣaṣṭitantra.

docs.title: 4.1.1 Key Texts
docs.text:
Table 4.1 lists the key texts of the school.

Table 4.1. Major Sāṃkhya Texts Text Author Date Significance Sāṃkhyakārikā Īśvarakṛṣṇa c. 350–450 CE Classical systematic text (c. 70 verses) Chinese translation with commentary Paramārtha 6th c. CE Earliest dated witness to the Kārikā Yuktidīpikā Anonymous c. 6th–7th c. CE Most detailed early commentary Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī Vācaspati Miśra 9th or 10th c. CE Most influential commentary Sāṃkhyasūtra Kapila (trad.) c. 14th–15th c. CE Late sūtra text Sāṃkhyaprava­cana­bhāṣya Vijñāna­bhikṣu 16th c. CE Theistic, Vedāntic interpretation

An illustrative painting is reproduced in Figure 4.1.

Figure 4.1. Kapila, the legendary founder of Sāṃkhya, as imagined by a Company School painter (British Museum; illustrative, not an actual portrait) Painting: Company School, British Museum; public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 4.2 Suffering and the Inquiry
docs.text:
The Kārikā begins, as the epigraph to this chapter shows, with suffering. The commentators distinguish three kinds: suffering that arises within oneself, in body (illness) or mind (grief, desire, anger) (ādhyātmika); suffering caused by other beings, human or animal (ādhibhautika); and suffering caused by forces beyond human control, such as weather, natural calamity or supernatural beings (ādhidaivika). The same triad is used throughout later Indian literature.

The first two verses then argue that the inquiry is not idle. Visible remedies — medicine, wealth, power, social arrangements — are neither certain (ekānta) nor final (atyanta): they do not always work, and when they work the suffering returns. The Vedic means (ānuśravika, “what is heard” in the Veda) are “like the seen” (verse 2): they are tainted by impurity (aviśuddhi), which the commentators explain as the killing of animals in sacrifice, and their results decay and are unequal. Only discriminative knowledge (viveka) of the difference between the conscious self and everything material can end suffering absolutely. The argument places Sāṃkhya in open tension with Pūrva Mīmāṃsā (Chapter 6), for which Vedic ritual is the highest human pursuit. It is not that ritual is useless; its benefits belong to the realm of matter and its transformations, and so cannot touch the self, which alone needs to be freed.

docs.title: 4.3 Two Ultimate Principles: Puruṣa and Prakṛti
docs.text:
The system rests on a dualism of two irreducible kinds of reality. Puruṣa, the self, is pure consciousness: eternal, unchanging, inactive, without qualities, the witness of experience, and many in number. Prakṛti, primordial nature, is unconscious, eternal and always active; it is one, it is made of three constituents (guṇas), and it is the root cause (mūla-prakṛti) of everything manifest, including the mind. The Kārikā infers the nature of the self from its contrast with what has the three constituents:

The Nature of Puruṣa

sākṣitvam asya puruṣasya kaivalyaṃ mādhyasthyaṃ draṣṭṛtvam akartṛbhāvaś ca [From its contrast with what has the three guṇas, it is established that] this Puruṣa is a witness, isolated, neutral, a seer, and a non-agent. — Sāṃkhyakārikā 19 (excerpt)

docs.title: 4.3.1 The Arguments for Prakṛti
docs.text: Why believe in a single, unmanifest material cause? Verse 15 gives five reasons, which together form one argument. The manifest things are limited in size and number (bhedānāṃ parimāṇāt), and what is limited depends on something beyond it. They share a common nature (samanvayāt): every one of them, the Sāṃkhya holds, is pleasant, painful or deluding, which suggests a common source with that threefold nature. Effects proceed from a potency already present in their cause (śaktitaḥ pravṛtteḥ), as oil comes from sesame and not from sand. Cause and effect are distinct, as the pot is distinct from the clay (kāraṇakāryavibhāgāt). And at the dissolution of the world the variety of things merges back into an undifferentiated state (avibhāgād vaiśvarūpyasya). Tracing effects back to causes and those causes back again, one must reach a cause that is not itself an effect, and the common nature of all effects tells us what it must be like. The argument depends on the doctrine that effects pre-exist in their causes, discussed below.

docs.title: 4.3.2 The Arguments for Puruṣa
docs.text: Verse 17 argues in the same way for the self. Composite things exist for the sake of something else (saṅghātaparārthatvāt), as a bed is for a sleeper; the whole manifest world, being composite, must exist for something that is not composite. That something must lack the three constituents (triguṇādiviparyayāt), since whatever has them is itself composite and for another. There must be a controller of the body–mind complex (adhiṣṭhānāt), as a chariot has a driver; there must be an experiencer distinct from what is experienced (bhoktṛbhāvāt); and the very striving for liberation (kaivalyārthaṃ pravṛtteḥ) presupposes something that can be freed. The first argument is the most characteristic: it moves from the purposive organisation of matter to a subject for whose sake it is organised, without making that subject its maker.

docs.title: 4.3.3 Why There Are Many Selves
docs.text: Unlike Advaita, which holds that there is only one self whose apparent plurality is due to ignorance, Sāṃkhya holds that selves are really many (puruṣa-bahutva). Verse 18 gives three reasons. Birth, death and the sense capacities are allotted separately (janana-maraṇa-karaṇānāṃ pratiniyamāt): if there were one self, all would be born when one was born, and all would be blind when one was blind. Beings do not act all at once (ayugapat pravṛtteś ca). And the proportions of the three constituents differ from one being to another (traiguṇyaviparyayāt). The reasons show that experiences are many; it is less clear that they show the selves are many, since the Sāṃkhya self does not itself experience anything. Its critics pressed this point. If every self is pure, attributeless consciousness, what makes one self different from another? The Sāṃkhya answer is that they are numerically distinct though qualitatively alike, and are told apart only by their association with different intellects; the Advaitins replied that a plurality with no ground of difference is unintelligible. Modern readers have compared the problem with debates over Leibniz’s “identity of indiscernibles”. The doctrine has clear consequences: liberation is an individual affair, each self reaps only the fruits of dispositions in its own intellect, and the world never ceases, since some selves always remain bound.

docs.title: 4.4 The Three Guṇas
docs.text:
Guṇa here does not mean “quality” in the ordinary sense but a constituent strand of primordial nature. The three — sattva, rajas and tamas — are among Sāṃkhya’s most influential ideas; they were adopted by the Bhagavad Gītā, the Purāṇas, Vedānta and Āyurveda. The Kārikā defines them by their affective character, their function and their mode of interaction:

The Nature of the Guṇas

prīty-aprīti-viṣādātmakāḥ prakāśa-pravṛtti-niyamārthāḥ anyonyābhibhavāśraya-janana-mithuna-vṛttayaś ca guṇāḥ The guṇas have the nature of pleasure, pain and dejection; their purposes are illumination, activity and restraint; they mutually dominate, support, produce and pair with each other. — Sāṃkhyakārikā 12

Table 4.2. The Three Guṇas of Prakṛti Guṇa Nature Function Physical and psychological effects Sattva Light, illumination Reveals, illumines Lightness, clarity, joy, knowledge, serenity Rajas Activity, motion Activates, stimulates Restlessness, desire, effort, passion, anxiety Tamas Inertia, darkness Obstructs, veils Heaviness, dullness, confusion, sloth, sleep

The three are never found apart. Every manifest thing, physical or mental, is a particular balance of them, and change is a shift in that balance. In the state of dissolution (pralaya) they are in equilibrium (sāmyāvasthā), and nothing is manifest. When the equilibrium is disturbed, manifestation begins. What disturbs it is the system’s great puzzle. The Kārikā speaks of the “conjunction” (saṃyoga, verse 21) of the self and nature, the commentators of mere proximity (sānnidhya); the Yoga Bhāṣya (on 1.4) compares the self to a magnet, which moves iron without doing anything. Critics asked how proximity between two realities that have nothing in common — one conscious and inactive, the other unconscious and active — could start the whole process of the world, and Śaṅkara pressed the objection in the Brahmasūtrabhāṣya (2.2.1–10). The Sāṃkhya has no answer beyond the analogies, and it is the main reason later Vedāntins thought the system needed a conscious first cause.

docs.title: 4.5 The Pre-existence of the Effect (Satkāryavāda)
docs.text:
The argument for primordial nature rests on Sāṃkhya’s theory of causation, that the effect exists in its cause before it is produced:

Satkāryavāda

asad-akaraṇād upādāna-grahaṇāt sarva-sambhavābhāvāt śaktasya śakya-karaṇāt kāraṇa-bhāvāc ca satkāryam The effect pre-exists in the cause because: (1) what is non-existent cannot be produced, (2) there must be a material cause, (3) everything cannot come from everything, (4) only a potent cause produces its specific effect, (5) the effect has the nature of the cause. — Sāṃkhyakārikā 9

The five reasons are not independent; they work together against the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika view that the effect is a new thing (Chapter 3). If the effect did not exist beforehand, it would be like a hare’s horn, and nothing can make that exist. If it did not pre-exist, any cause could produce any effect; but people seek clay for pots and milk for curds, and do not get oil from sand. The best explanation of these facts, the Sāṃkhya argues, is that a cause has a determinate capacity for its effect, and that the effect is that capacity made manifest. Production is then manifestation (abhivyakti), and destruction is a return to the unmanifest. The Naiyāyika’s reply is that if the pot is already in the clay, the potter’s work is pointless and the pot should be visible before it is made; the Sāṃkhya answers that the potter’s work is needed to make the pot manifest, as a lamp is needed to show a pot already in a dark room.

Sāṃkhya’s version of the doctrine is pariṇāmavāda: causation is a real transformation of the cause into the effect, as milk becomes curds. Advaita Vedānta also holds that the effect pre-exists in the cause but treats the transformation as only apparent (vivarta; Chapter 7).

docs.title: 4.6 Manifestation: The Twenty-Five Tattvas
docs.text:
Sāṃkhya’s best-known doctrine is its enumeration of twenty-five principles (tattvas), which describes the order in which primordial nature becomes manifest (Figure 4.2). The process is often called “evolution”, but the word is misleading: it is not a history of the world in time so much as an analysis of its structure, read as a series of transformations (pariṇāma) from the subtle to the gross.

Figure 4.2. The Twenty-Five Tattvas of the Sāṃkhya System

From unmanifest nature arises first the intellect (mahat or buddhi), the principle of ascertainment; from it the “I-maker” (ahaṃkāra), the principle of individuation. From the I-maker the sequence divides in two. In its sāttvika aspect it produces the mind (manas), the five sense capacities and the five capacities of action — eleven principles; in its tāmasa aspect it produces the five subtle elements (tanmātras: sound, touch, form, taste and smell), from which the five gross elements arise — ten principles. With primordial nature, intellect and I-maker these make twenty-four; the self, which is not produced and produces nothing, is the twenty-fifth. The order is striking. The intellect and the ego come before the physical elements, and the mind is on the side of matter: what a Cartesian would call mental is, for Sāṃkhya, the subtlest part of nature.

The Kārikā also groups everything into three: the manifest (vyakta), the twenty-three products from intellect down to the gross elements; the unmanifest (avyakta), primordial nature itself, which is a cause but never an effect; and the knower (jña), the self, which is neither cause nor effect. Their characteristics are set out in Table 4.3.

Table 4.3. Characteristics of Vyakta, Avyakta, and Puruṣa Property Vyakta (Manifest) Avyakta (Unmanifest) Puruṣa (Knower) Caused? Yes (caused by Prakṛti) No (uncaused) No (uncaused) Finite? Yes (impermanent) No (eternal) No (eternal) Composed of guṇas? Yes Yes No Active? Yes (sakriya) No movement (akriya), though it transforms No (inactive) Conscious? No No Yes Many or one? Many evolutes One (single root) Many (plural selves)

The process is purposive, though no one designs it. Nature becomes manifest for the sake of the self — for its experience (bhoga) and for its liberation (apavarga) — as milk flows, unconsciously, for the calf’s nourishment (verse 57). This teleology without a designer is one of the most characteristic features of the system, and its most questionable: critics asked how an unconscious nature can act for a purpose at all.

docs.title: 4.7 Knowledge, the Inner Organ and the Theory of Reflection
docs.text:
Sāṃkhya accepts three means of knowledge: perception; inference, of the three kinds also named by Nyāya (pūrvavat, śeṣavat and sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa); and reliable testimony (āpta-vacana). Its own contribution is its account of the apparatus of knowing. The “inner instrument” (antaḥkaraṇa) has three parts: the intellect (buddhi), whose function is ascertainment (adhyavasāya) — “this is a pot”, “this is to be done”; the I-maker (ahaṃkāra), which appropriates what the intellect determines — “I know this”, “this is mine”; and the mind (manas), which organises the data of the senses and directs the organs of action. The external senses are the “gateways” through which the inner instrument meets the world. In perception the senses present an object, the mind organises the impression, the I-maker claims it, and the intellect ascertains it. All this is a process within nature: all knowing, in the ordinary sense, belongs to matter.

This creates a difficulty. The self is conscious but does nothing; the intellect does everything but is unconscious. How can there be conscious knowledge at all? The answer worked out by the commentators, Vācaspati Miśra and Vijñānabhikṣu in particular, is a theory of reflection. The intellect, the subtlest and most transparent product of nature, dominated by sattva, reflects the light of the self’s consciousness as a mirror reflects light. The intellect then appears conscious, and the self appears to know and to suffer, though in reality neither has the other’s character (Figure 4.3). Bondage is this mutual appearance; liberation is seeing through it.

Figure 4.3. The Sāṃkhya Reflection Theory of Knowledge

docs.title: 4.8 Dispositions and the Subtle Body
docs.text:
The intellect is also the seat of character. The Kārikā (23, 44–45) names eight dispositions (bhāvas) of the intellect, in four opposed pairs, each with its own result (Table 4.4).

Table 4.4. The Eight Dispositions (Bhāvas) of Buddhi Sāttvika Leads to Nature Tāmasika Leads to Nature Dharma Rise to higher states Virtue Adharma Descent to lower states Vice Jñāna Liberation Knowledge Ajñāna Bondage Ignorance Vairāgya Absorption in prakṛti Dispassion Avairāgya Continued saṃsāra Attachment Aiśvarya Unimpeded will Mastery Anaiśvarya Frustration Powerlessness

Only knowledge (jñāna) leads to liberation; virtue leads merely to a better rebirth, and even dispassion without knowledge leads only to temporary absorption in prakṛti.

These dispositions are carried from life to life by the subtle body (liṅga-śarīra), which gives Sāṃkhya its account of rebirth. While the gross body perishes at death, the subtle body persists. It is made of eighteen elements — the intellect, the I-maker and the mind, the five sense capacities, the five capacities of action and the five subtle elements — and it transmigrates from one gross body to another:

The Transmigrating Subtle Body

pūrvotpannam asaktaṃ niyataṃ mahadādisūkṣmaparyantam saṃsarati nirupabhogaṃ bhāvair adhivāsitaṃ liṅgam The subtle body, produced in the beginning, unattached, constant, consisting of the principles from mahat down to the subtle elements, transmigrates without enjoyment, perfumed by the dispositions. — Sāṃkhyakārikā 40

The components are listed in Table 4.5.

Table 4.5. Components of the Liṅga Śarīra (Subtle Body) Category Number Components Antaḥkaraṇa (Inner organ) 3 Buddhi (intellect), Ahaṃkāra (ego), Manas (mind) Jñānendriyas (Sense capacities) 5 Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching Karmendriyas (Action capacities) 5 Speaking, grasping, locomotion, excretion, reproduction Tanmātras (Subtle elements) 5 Śabda (sound), Sparśa (touch), Rūpa (form), Rasa (taste), Gandha (smell) Total 18

The subtle body requires a support (āśraya), just as a painting requires a canvas or a shadow requires a post (Sāṃkhyakārikā 41). Without a physical frame, the subtle body cannot function. Yet the subtle body itself is the carrier of bhāvas (dispositions) — the accumulated psychological tendencies of virtue and vice, knowledge and ignorance, attachment and detachment, power and powerlessness — that determine the character and destiny of the individual across lifetimes.

The impressions (saṃskāras) left by past experience and action, and the tendencies (vāsanās) that grow from them, are the content of these dispositions. The literature of Sāṃkhya and Yoga compares them to seeds, which sprout into future experience and future births unless discriminative knowledge “roasts” them. The commentators add that the subtle body lasts until the dissolution of the world, when it merges back into primordial nature, and that at each new manifestation the subtle bodies re-emerge with their dispositions.

docs.title: 4.9 Liberation (Kaivalya)
docs.text:
Liberation is kaivalya, the “aloneness” or isolation of the self from nature, and it is reached through the discriminative knowledge that the self is not the intellect, nor the I-maker, nor anything material. The Kārikā describes the association of self and nature with an analogy:

The Analogy of the Lame and the Blind

puruṣasya darśanārthaṃ kaivalyārthaṃ tathā pradhānasya paṅgvandhavad ubhayor api saṃyogas tatkṛtaḥ sargaḥ For the Puruṣa’s seeing of Pradhāna (Prakṛti), and likewise for its isolation, there is union of the two, like that of a lame man and a blind man. From this union proceeds creation. — Sāṃkhyakārikā 21

The self is like a lame man who can see, nature like a blind man who can walk; together they make the journey of experience. Liberation, on this picture, is not a new state that the self attains but the end of a confusion. In the Kārikā’s other famous image (verse 59), nature is like a dancer who stops dancing once she has been seen by the audience; when the self has seen nature for what it is, nature ceases to act with respect to that self. Strictly, the Kārikā says (verse 62), no self is ever bound or freed: it is nature, in its various forms, that is bound and is released. The claim follows from the system’s premises, but it makes liberation curiously impersonal: what the self gains is nothing, and what nature loses is one spectator.

docs.title: 4.10 The Question of God in Sāṃkhya
docs.text: Classical Sāṃkhya is non-theistic (nirīśvara). The Kārikā does not invoke God as the cause of the world, since nature’s own transformations are sufficient; the Yuktidīpikā argues against a creator; and the late Sāṃkhyasūtra (1.92) declares that God’s existence is not established (īśvarāsiddheḥ). Later interpreters moved the other way: the Bhagavad Gītā had already set Sāṃkhya’s categories within a theistic framework, and Vijñānabhikṣu (16th century) read the system theistically. The case shows that “orthodoxy” (āstikya) was defined by acceptance of Vedic authority rather than by theism, although Sāṃkhya’s own commitment to the Veda was limited, as its verdict on ritual shows.

docs.title: 4.11 Sāṃkhya in the Bhagavad Gītā and the Epics
docs.text: The Bhagavad Gītā represents the most influential integration of Sāṃkhya thought into the broader Hindu tradition. The Gītā’s second chapter is titled “Sāṃkhya Yoga” in later colophons, and Sāṃkhya categories recur throughout the text — though “sāṃkhya” in the Gītā often means the path of knowledge in general rather than the classical system. However, the Gītā’s use of Sāṃkhya is not a mere reproduction of the classical system; it involves a creative reinterpretation within a theistic and devotional framework.

docs.title: 4.11.1 Sāṃkhya Categories in the Gītā
docs.text:
The Gītā adopts the Sāṃkhya categories of Puruṣa, Prakṛti and the three guṇas, and lists constituents of the “field” close to the Sāṃkhya principles (13.5–6), but integrates them within a framework that acknowledges a supreme personal God (Kṛṣṇa/īśvara) who transcends both Puruṣa and Prakṛti. In the Gītā’s scheme (7.4–5), the eightfold material nature is God’s “lower nature” (aparā prakṛti), while the living selves constitute the “higher nature” (parā prakṛti). Both are subordinate to the supreme reality of Kṛṣṇa.

The Gītā’s chapters 13, 14, and 18 contain extensive treatments of Sāṃkhya categories. Chapter 13 (Kṣetra-Kṣetrajña Vibhāga Yoga) distinguishes the “field” (kṣetra, corresponding to Prakṛti and its evolutes) from the “knower of the field” (kṣetrajña, corresponding to Puruṣa). Chapter 14 (Guṇa-Traya Vibhāga Yoga) provides a detailed analysis of the three guṇas and their effects on human character and destiny. Chapter 18 classifies knowledge, action, agents, intellect, firmness, and happiness according to the three guṇas.

docs.title: 4.11.2 Sāṃkhya in the Mahābhārata
docs.text: Beyond the Gītā, the Mahābhārata contains several extended discussions of Sāṃkhya, particularly in the Mokṣa-Dharma-Parvan (Book 12, Śāntiparvan). These passages present various forms of Sāṃkhya, some closer to the classical 25-tattva system and others incorporating theistic elements. Some epic passages enumerate a twenty-sixth principle (the “awakened” or supreme self beyond the individual puruṣa), and others present different evolutionary schemas, testifying to the diverse forms that Sāṃkhya thought assumed before its crystallization in Īśvarakṛṣṇa’s Sāṃkhyakārikā.

docs.title: 4.12 Critics and Comparisons
docs.text:
Sāṃkhya’s most persistent critics were the Vedāntins, who shared its interest in consciousness and liberation but rejected its dualism (Table 4.6).

Table 4.6. Sāṃkhya vs. Advaita Vedānta: Key Differences Issue Sāṃkhya Advaita Vedānta Ultimate Reality Dualistic: Puruṣa and Prakṛti Non-dual: Brahman alone Number of Selves Many (plurality of Puruṣas) One (Ātman = Brahman) Status of World Real transformation (pariṇāma) of Prakṛti Apparent transformation (vivarta) due to Māyā Causation Satkāryavāda (Pariṇāma) Satkāryavāda (Vivarta) God Not required (nirīśvara) īśvara (Saguṇa Brahman) at empirical level Liberation Discrimination of Puruṣa from Prakṛti Knowledge of identity with Brahman State of Liberation Kaivalya (isolation) Merging into Brahman (or realization of identity)

Śaṅkara devotes considerable effort in his Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya to refuting Sāṃkhya, particularly its claim that unconscious Prakṛti can be the cause of the world. His central argument is: an unconscious cause cannot produce the ordered, purposive, intelligent universe we observe. Only an intelligent, conscious Brahman can be the ultimate cause.

The most frequent modern comparison is with Descartes’ dualism of thinking and extended substance (Table 4.7). Both systems posit two kinds of reality, consciousness and matter, and both must explain how they are related. The differences, however, are deeper than the likeness.

Table 4.7. Sāṃkhya Dualism vs. Cartesian Dualism Feature Sāṃkhya Descartes Consciousness Multiple Puruṣas; passive, witnessing Single mind per person; active, thinking Matter Single Prakṛti; dynamic, self-evolving Mechanical matter; passive, inert Interaction No real interaction; reflection theory Interaction through pineal gland Mind Mind (manas) belongs to matter Mind is separate substance Goal Liberation (kaivalya) through discrimination Knowledge of clear and distinct ideas

A crucial difference is that Sāṃkhya places the mind, ego, and intellect on the side of Prakṛti (matter), not on the side of consciousness. In Descartes, thinking is the essence of mind; in Sāṃkhya, thinking is a material process that merely reflects consciousness. Sāṃkhya thus avoids the Cartesian problem of how thought interacts with extension, since thinking is itself material; but it faces the parallel problem of how an unchanging consciousness can be related to, and “illuminate”, a material mind.

The system’s influence was wide. Patañjali’s Yoga took over its metaphysics (Chapter 5); the Carakasaṃhitā (Śārīrasthāna 1) presents a Sāṃkhya-like scheme of twenty-four principles that differs from the classical one, evidence of the variety of Sāṃkhya before Īśvarakṛṣṇa, and medical writers classified minds as sāttvika, rājasa and tāmasa (Volume 13, Āyurveda); the three guṇas became a common idiom of Indian culture; and Śaṅkara’s Advaita, while rejecting the dualism, absorbed much of the vocabulary.

docs.title: 4.13 An Assessment
docs.text:
Sāṃkhya is the first fully systematic metaphysics in the Brahmanical tradition, and its strengths are those of a system. From a single starting point — the difference between what is conscious and what is not — it derives an account of the world’s structure, of the mind, of rebirth and of liberation, and it argues for each step. Its placing of intellect, ego and mind on the side of matter anticipates, in its own terms, the thought that cognition is a natural process, while its insistence that awareness itself is something else poses the problem of consciousness in a sharp form. Its theory of causation gave Indian philosophy one of its two great alternatives, and its three constituents gave Indian culture a lasting vocabulary of temperament and value.

Its weaknesses were pointed out by its classical critics, and they remain. The relation between self and nature — how mere proximity can set nature in motion, how an inactive consciousness can be “reflected” in an unconscious intellect, how an unconscious nature can act for a purpose — is described by analogies rather than explained. The arguments for many selves show that experiences are many, not obviously that selves are. And the account of liberation, on which nothing happens to the self at all, raises the question of what, on this system, the inquiry announced in its first verse was for. The Vedāntins’ answer, that consciousness must also be the cause of the world, and the Yoga answer, that a special self, īśvara, can guide the process, are both responses to these gaps.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Yoga — The Discipline of Union and Liberation
docs.text:
The Defining Sūtra

yogaś citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind (citta). — Yoga Sūtra 1.2

docs.title: 5.1 Historical Background
docs.text:
The word yoga is derived from the Sanskrit root yuj — “to yoke”, “to unite”, “to discipline.” Meditative and ascetic practices are attested in early Buddhist and Jain texts and in the middle Upaniṣads (Kaṭha, Śvetāśvatara); claims that yoga goes back to the Indus civilisation rest on ambiguous seal images and remain speculative. The philosophical system of Yoga was codified by Patañjali in the Yoga Sūtra, a work of 195 or 196 aphorisms (Maas 2013; Bryant 2009).

Historical Note: Patañjali

Later tradition reveres Patañjali as an incarnation of Ādiśeṣa, the serpent on whom Viṣṇu reclines, and a popular invocation verse of uncertain origin praises him as the one who removed the impurities of the mind through yoga, of speech through grammar, and of the body through medicine:

yogena cittasya padena vācāṃ malaṃ śarīrasya ca vaidyakena yo ’pākarot taṃ pravaraṃ munīnāṃ patañjaliṃ prāñjalir ānato ’smi

This identification of the author of the Yoga Sūtra with the grammarian Patañjali (author of the Mahābhāṣya, mid-2nd century BCE) is traditional; most modern scholars regard them as different people. Philipp Maas has argued that the sūtras and the commentary traditionally ascribed to “Vyāsa” form a single work, the Pātañjala Yogaśāstra, composed c. 325–425 CE; this is now the most widely accepted dating (Maas 2006, 2013).

docs.title: 5.1.1 Key Texts and Commentaries
docs.text:
Table 5.1 lists the major texts of the tradition.

Table 5.1. Major Texts of the Yoga Tradition Text Author Date Significance Yoga Sūtra Patañjali c. 325–425 CE (Maas) 195/196 aphorisms Yoga Bhāṣya “Vyāsa” (possibly Patañjali himself) same work, per Maas Primary commentary Vivaraṇa attributed to Śaṅkara (disputed) c. 8th c. CE or later Sub-commentary on the Bhāṣya Tattva­vaiśāradī Vācaspati Miśra 9th or 10th c. CE Sub-commentary on the Bhāṣya Rāja­mārtaṇḍa Bhoja 11th c. CE Independent commentary Yogavārttika Vijñānabhikṣu 16th c. CE Vedāntic interpretation

docs.title: 5.2 Yoga and Sāṃkhya: Metaphysical Foundations
docs.text:
Yoga is traditionally paired with Sāṃkhya as its practical counterpart. While Sāṃkhya provides the theoretical framework (the 25 tattvas, the Puruṣa-Prakṛti dualism), Yoga provides the practical methodology for achieving the discriminative knowledge (viveka-jñāna) that leads to liberation.

The key difference: Yoga introduces īśvara (God) as a special Puruṣa (Yoga Sūtra 1.24; see Section 5.9). For this reason, Yoga is called seśvara Sāṃkhya (Sāṃkhya with God). Patañjali’s īśvara, however, is not a creator but a supreme teacher and object of meditation (Bronkhorst 1981).

docs.title: 5.3 The Structure of the Yoga Sūtra
docs.text:
The Yoga Sūtra is divided into four chapters (pādas; Table 5.2):

Table 5.2. The Four Pādas of the Yoga Sūtra Pāda Name Sūtras Content I Samādhi Pāda 51 Nature of Yoga, types of samādhi, obstacles, and īśvara II Sādhana Pāda 55 Practice: kleśas, kriyā-yoga, the first five limbs III Vibhūti Pāda 55/56 Supernatural powers (siddhis) and inner limbs IV Kaivalya Pāda 34 Absolute liberation

docs.title: 5.4 Citta and Its Modifications (Vṛttis)
docs.text:
The central concern of Yoga is the mind (citta) and its modifications (vṛttis). Patañjali names five (Yoga Sūtra 1.6): valid cognition (pramāṇa, comprising perception, inference and testimony), error (viparyaya), conceptual construction without a real object (vikalpa), sleep (nidrā) and memory (smṛti). The list is striking for what it includes. Valid knowledge, the goal of the other schools’ epistemologies, is here one fluctuation among others, to be stilled along with error and sleep; and sleep is a modification, not an absence of mind, because on waking we remember having slept well or badly. All five are restrained through practice (abhyāsa) and dispassion (vairāgya) (1.12).

The Yoga Bhāṣya also classifies the mind by its states (bhūmis), from the scattered to the fully stilled (Table 5.3).

Table 5.3. The Five States (Bhūmis) of the Mind in Yoga State Sanskrit Dominant Guṇa Characteristics Scattered Kṣipta Rajas Agitated, distracted, restless; mind jumps from object to object Dull Mūḍha Tamas Torpid, sleepy, confused; prone to delusion Partially focused Vikṣipta Rajas + Sattva Occasionally focused but easily distracted; the ordinary state One-pointed Ekāgra Sattva Steadily focused on one object; proper state for dhyāna and samādhi Ceased Niruddha Beyond guṇas All modifications have ceased; the state of asamprajñāta samādhi

Only the last two states — ekāgra and niruddha — are properly “Yogic.” The entire eight-limbed practice is designed to progressively refine the mind from its habitual scattered or dull state to the one-pointed and eventually ceased state.

docs.title: 5.5 The Five Kleśas (Afflictions)
docs.text:
Patañjali’s diagnosis of why the mind is restless is given in his list of the afflictions:

The Five Kleśas

avidyāsmitā-rāga-dveṣābhiniveśāḥ kleśāḥ The afflictions are: ignorance, ego-sense, attachment, aversion, and clinging to life. — Yoga Sūtra 2.3

Ignorance (avidyā) is the root; ego-sense (asmitā) is the identification of the seer with the instrument of seeing, the self with the intellect; attachment and aversion follow pleasure and pain; and clinging to life (abhiniveśa) is the fear of death present even in the wise. Yoga Sūtra 2.4 calls ignorance the “field” (kṣetra) of the other four, which may be dormant, attenuated, interrupted or active, and 2.5 defines it:

Definition of Avidyā

anityāśuci-duḥkhānātma-su nitya-śuci-sukhātma-khyātir avidyā Avidyā is the seeing of the non-eternal as eternal, the impure as pure, the painful as pleasurable, and the non-self as the self. — Yoga Sūtra 2.5

docs.title: 5.6 The Yoga Theory of Karma and Rebirth
docs.text:
The afflictions drive action, and action leaves its mark. Patañjali states (Yoga Sūtra 2.12–13) that the stock of karmic residues (karmāśaya) is rooted in the afflictions and that, as long as the root remains, it ripens in three ways: as the type of birth (jāti), the span of life (āyus) and the quality of experience (bhoga), pleasant or painful according to merit and demerit (2.14). The Bhāṣya distinguishes karma to be experienced in the present life from karma to be experienced in a future one, and karma whose fruition is fixed from karma whose fruition is not. The cycle is shown in Figure 5.1.

Figure 5.1. The cycle of affliction, action, residue and fruition in the Yoga Sūtra (2.3–14), and its interruption by discriminative discernment (simplified)

The scheme raises the question whether a life determined by past karma leaves room for choice. The Yoga Sūtra does not pose the question in those terms, and it is better not to force a modern problem of free will on it; what it does say is that the residues ripen only so long as their root, ignorance, remains, so that the practice of discrimination is itself the way out of the cycle.

docs.title: 5.7 Aṣṭāṅga Yoga — The Eight Limbs
docs.text:
The best-known part of Patañjali’s system is the aṣṭāṅga yoga (Yoga Sūtra 2.29) — the eight “limbs” of disciplined practice leading to kaivalya (liberation). Although it is the most famous section today, it occupies only part of the text, and some scholars think it was integrated from an older source (Figure 5.2).

Figure 5.2. The Eight Limbs (Aṣṭāṅga) of Patañjali’s Yoga

docs.title: 5.7.1 The Outer Limbs
docs.text:
The first two limbs are ethical. The restraints (yama) are non-violence, truthfulness, not stealing, sexual continence and non-possessiveness (2.30), which Patañjali calls a “great vow” when they are kept without exception of birth, place, time or occasion (2.31); the observances (niyama) are purity, contentment, austerity, study and devotion to īśvara (2.32). Posture (āsana) is defined in three words:

Definition of Āsana

sthira-sukham āsanam Posture should be steady and comfortable. — Yoga Sūtra 2.46

The regulation of the breath, defined as the interruption of the movement of inhalation and exhalation (Yoga Sūtra 2.49). Patañjali distinguishes external, internal and suspended operations, regulated by place, time and number, and a “fourth” that goes beyond the external and internal (2.50–51); it removes the covering of the inner light and makes the mind fit for concentration (2.52–53). Later texts describe these as exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka) and retention (kumbhaka).

Health and Safety Note

This chapter describes classical texts; it is not a manual of practice. Prolonged breath retention (kumbhaka) and other intensive breathing techniques can be hazardous, especially for people with heart or lung conditions, high blood pressure, epilepsy, or during pregnancy. The classical texts themselves warn that wrongly practised prāṇāyāma causes disease (e.g. Haṭhayogapradīpikā 2.16). Anyone wishing to practise should seek qualified instruction and medical advice.

Sense-withdrawal (pratyāhāra, 2.54), the fifth limb, is the turning of the senses away from their objects, often illustrated by the Bhagavad Gītā’s image (2.58) of a tortoise drawing in its limbs.

docs.title: 5.7.2 The Inner Limbs
docs.text:
Saṃyama — The Integrated Practice

  • Dhāraṇā (Concentration) — Binding the mind to one place, object, or idea (Yoga Sūtra 3.1)

  • Dhyāna (Meditation) — The uninterrupted flow of cognition towards the chosen object (Yoga Sūtra 3.2)

  • Samādhi (Absorption) — When meditation shines forth as the object alone, as if empty of its own form (Yoga Sūtra 3.3)

The combined practice of these three on any object is called saṃyama (3.4). Through mastery of saṃyama, the yogin attains the light of insight (prajñāloka, 3.5).

docs.title: 5.8 Types of Samādhi
docs.text:
Patañjali (1.17) says that samprajñāta samādhi, concentration with cognitive content, is accompanied by gross reflection (vitarka), subtle reflection (vicāra), joy (ānanda) or the sense of “I am” (asmitā). Separately (1.41–44) he describes four “coalescences” (samāpatti) of the mind with its object, which the commentators map on to the first two of these: with a gross object, first mixed with word and concept (savitarka) and then the object alone (nirvitarka); and with a subtle object such as the subtle elements, first with reflection on space and time (savicāra) and then the object alone (nirvicāra). Beyond these lies the objectless, “seedless” samādhi (asamprajñāta, nirbīja), in which all content ceases; discriminative discernment between sattva and the self (2.26) is the means to it, and it leads to isolation (Figure 5.3).

Figure 5.3. A simplified scheme of samādhi in Patañjali’s Yoga: the four “coalescences” with an object (Yoga Sūtra 1.42–44) lead, through discriminative discernment and the “cloud of dharma”, to the objectless, seedless samādhi and to isolation; the order of the lower row follows the Bhāṣya on 1.2

docs.title: 5.9 The Concept of īśvara in Yoga
docs.text:
īśvara in Yoga

kleśa-karma-vipākāśayair aparāmṛṣṭaḥ puruṣa-viśeṣa īśvaraḥ īśvara is a special Puruṣa, untouched by afflictions, actions, their results, and latent impressions. — Yoga Sūtra 1.24

Patañjali teaches that īśvara-praṇidhāna (devotion to God) is a direct and effective means to samādhi. The sacred syllable Oṃ is the designator (vācaka) of īśvara (Yoga Sūtra 1.27).

docs.title: 5.10 The Vibhūti Pāda: Supernatural Powers (Siddhis)
docs.text:
The third chapter of the Yoga Sūtra describes extraordinary powers (vibhūtis, siddhis) that arise from saṃyama on particular objects: knowledge of past and future from saṃyama on the three kinds of transformation (3.16), of the cries of all creatures from saṃyama on the distinction of word, meaning and idea (3.17), of previous births from saṃyama on latent impressions (3.18), invisibility from saṃyama on the form of the body (3.21), and omniscience from saṃyama on the distinction between sattva and the self (3.49). In the middle of this list Patañjali adds a warning:

Warning Against Siddhis

te samādhāv upasargā vyutthāne siddhayaḥ These [powers] are obstacles to samādhi, though they are accomplishments in the worldly state. — Yoga Sūtra 3.37

The siddhis are not the goal of Yoga; they are by-products of practice that can become obstacles if the practitioner becomes attached to them. True Yoga aims at kaivalya, not supernatural powers.

docs.title: 5.11 Kaivalya — Absolute Liberation
docs.text:
The ultimate goal of Yoga is kaivalya — the absolute isolation of Puruṣa from Prakṛti, the establishment of consciousness in its own essential nature.

Definition of Kaivalya

svarūpa-pratiṣṭhā vā citi-śaktir iti [Liberation is the return of the guṇas to their source,] or the establishment of the power of consciousness in its own nature. — Yoga Sūtra 4.34 (second half)

docs.title: 5.12 The Yoga Theory of Perception and Consciousness
docs.text: The Yoga Sūtra presents a model of how consciousness, mind and objects interact to produce experience.

docs.title: 5.12.1 Yogic Perception (Yogi-Pratyakṣa)
docs.text: One of Yoga’s epistemological contributions is the concept of yogi-pratyakṣa (yogic perception) — a form of direct, non-sensory cognition available to the advanced practitioner in the state of samādhi. Unlike ordinary perception, which requires the mediation of the sense organs, yogic perception involves the direct apprehension of reality by the purified buddhi, illuminated by the light of Puruṣa.

docs.title: 5.13 Yoga and the Bhagavad Gītā
docs.text:
The Bhagavad Gītā uses yoga more broadly than Patañjali, for several paths to the highest goal: karma-yoga, the path of action without attachment to results (“karmaṇy evādhikāras te mā phaleṣu kadācana”, 2.47); bhakti-yoga, loving surrender to the Lord (“sarva-dharmān parityajya mām ekaṃ śaraṇaṃ vraja”, 18.66); jñāna-yoga, discrimination between the real and the unreal; and the meditative discipline of its sixth chapter (the label “Rāja Yoga” for this path is later).

The Gītā’s synthesis is significant because it opens the highest goal to householders acting in the world; it even declares (9.32) that women, vaiśyas and śūdras — whom the verse, on a common reading, includes among those “of sinful birth” (pāpayonayaḥ) — can reach it through devotion, while at the same time insisting (3.35, 18.47) that each should perform the duties of his own social station.

docs.title: 5.14 Comparative Analysis: Yoga and Buddhist Meditation
docs.text:
The parallels between Patañjali’s Yoga and Buddhist meditation practice have been extensively discussed by scholars (Table 5.4):

Table 5.4. Comparison of Yogic and Buddhist Meditation Frameworks Aspect Patañjali’s Yoga Buddhist Meditation Goal Kaivalya (isolation of Puruṣa) Nirvāṇa (cessation of craving) Metaphysics Puruṣa-Prakṛti dualism Anātman (no permanent self) Path structure Aṣṭāṅga Yoga (8 limbs) Aṣṭāṅgika Mārga (8-fold path) Concentration Dhāraṇā / Dhyāna / Samādhi Samādhi / Jhāna Mindfulness Implicit in pratyāhāra and dhāraṇā Satipaṭṭhāna (four foundations) Ethical base Yama-Niyama Śīla (morality)

docs.title: 5.15 Later Yoga: Haṭha and Rāja Yoga
docs.text:
From about the 11th century CE a new body of texts, beginning with the Amṛtasiddhi and culminating in Svātmārāma’s Haṭhayogapradīpikā (15th century), taught haṭha techniques — postures, breath-retention, bandhas and mudrās — that Patañjali treats only briefly or not at all. These texts also adopted the doctrine of kuṇḍalinī and of cakras and nāḍīs, which is not found in the Yoga Sūtra but comes from Śaiva Tantric traditions of the later first millennium; the number and arrangement of the cakras vary between texts, and modern correlations of cakras with endocrine glands are 20th-century innovations (Mallinson and Singleton 2017). The Haṭhayogapradīpikā (1.2) says that it teaches haṭha “solely for the sake of Rāja Yoga” (kevalaṃ rājayogāya haṭhavidyopadiśyate); there “Rāja Yoga” means the state of samādhi, and its identification with Patañjali’s system became standard only with Svāmī Vivekānanda’s Rāja Yoga (1896).

The practices of the eight limbs, the obstacles and remedies of Yoga Sūtra 1.30–39, Kriyā Yoga, prāṇāyāma and the haṭha tradition are treated in detail in Vol. 5 of this series, Yoga Taraṅgiṇī; this chapter has concentrated on Yoga as a philosophical system.

docs.title: 5.16 Yoga’s Enduring Relevance
docs.text:
Patañjali’s Yoga became, especially from the 19th century, a reference point for modern yoga worldwide, although modern posture-based yoga owes more to later haṭha traditions and to 20th-century innovation than to the Yoga Sūtra. Its analysis of the mind and of the afflictions continues to be studied by philosophers and psychologists; claims about the health benefits of modern practices are a matter for clinical research and are not assessed in this volume.

Its philosophical framework is Sāṃkhya’s (Chapter 4); its parallels with Buddhist meditation are taken up again in Chapter 10, and the status of yogic perception in Chapter 13.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Pūrva Mīmāṃsā and the Grammarians — Vedic Hermeneutics and the Philosophy of Language
docs.text:
Opening Sūtra

athāto dharma-jijñāsā Now, therefore, the inquiry into dharma (duty/righteousness). — Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 1.1.1 (Jaimini)

docs.title: 6.1 Historical Background and Significance
docs.text:
The word mīmāṃsā means “deep reflection” or “critical investigation.” Pūrva Mīmāṃsā (Prior Investigation) is also known simply as Mīmāṃsā or Dharma-Mīmāṃsā (Investigation into Dharma). It is called “prior” (pūrva) because it investigates the earlier portions of the Vedas — the Saṃhitās and Brāhmaṇas — which deal with ritual action (karma-kāṇḍa), as distinct from Uttara Mīmāṃsā (Vedānta), which investigates the later portions (Upaniṣads) dealing with knowledge (jñāna-kāṇḍa).

Historical Note: Maharshi Jaimini

The Mīmāṃsā Sūtra is ascribed to Jaimini. It is the longest of the darśana sūtras, comprising about 2,700 aphorisms (counts vary) arranged in twelve chapters (adhyāyas). Tradition makes Jaimini a disciple of Vyāsa. The text is usually dated to c. 2nd century BCE (estimates range from the 3rd to the 1st century BCE); it grew out of the ritual exegesis of the Śrautasūtras and itself cites earlier teachers such as Bādari and Bādarāyaṇa.

docs.title: 6.1.1 Major Texts and Commentators
docs.text:
Table 6.1 lists the major texts and commentators.

Table 6.1. Major Texts of the Mīmāṃsā Tradition Text Author Date Significance Mīmāṃsā Sūtra Jaimini c. 2nd c. BCE c. 2,700 foundational aphorisms Śābarabhāṣya Śabara c. 200–400 CE (estimates vary) Oldest surviving commentary; earlier ones (Upavarṣa, Bhavadāsa) are lost Ślokavārttika, Tantravārttika, Ṭupṭīkā Kumārila Bhaṭṭa c. 600–650 CE Sub-commentaries on Śabara; founding works of the Bhāṭṭa school Bṛhatī and Laghvī Prabhākara 7th c. CE Sub-commentaries on Śabara; founding works of the Prābhākara school Vidhiviveka, Mīmāṃsā­nukramaṇī Maṇḍana Miśra late 7th – 8th c. CE Bhāṭṭa; theory of injunction Ṛjuvimalā, Prakaraṇapañcikā Śālikanātha c. 8th–9th c. CE Prābhākara commentator and systematiser Śāstra­dīpikā Pārthasārathi Miśra c. 11th c. CE Influential Bhāṭṭa exposition Mīmāṃsā­nyāya­prakāśa; Artha­saṃgraha Āpadeva; Laugākṣi Bhāskara 17th c. CE Introductory manuals

This chapter treats Mīmāṃsā together with the philosophy of the Grammarians (Section 6.18), its chief rival on the nature of words and sentences.

docs.title: 6.2 Two Sub-Schools: Bhāṭṭa and Prābhākara
docs.text: The Mīmāṃsā tradition divides into two major sub-schools named after their foundational teachers, Kumārila Bhaṭṭa (the Bhāṭṭa school) and Prabhākara (the Prābhākara school). They differ on the number of pramāṇas, the theory of error, the way cognition is known, and the analysis of sentence meaning; their differences are set out in Table 6.6 below.

docs.title: 6.3 The Concept of Dharma
docs.text:
For Mīmāṃsā, dharma is the central concept, and the second sūtra defines it:

Definition of Dharma

codanā-lakṣaṇo ’rtho dharmaḥ Dharma is a beneficial thing (artha) that is known through Vedic injunction (codanā). — Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 1.1.2

The definition has two parts, and both matter. Dharma is a good (artha), something that leads to a desirable result; and it is known through injunction (codanā) and through nothing else. It is suprasensible (atīndriya): no perception shows that a sacrifice leads to heaven, and no inference from perception could establish it. The Veda is therefore the only authority on dharma, and the Veda’s injunctions (vidhi), above all those prescribing ritual (yajña), are the primary means of knowing and fulfilling it. Everything else in the system — the theory of the Veda’s authorlessness, the doctrine that knowledge is intrinsically valid, the hermeneutic rules — serves to make this claim defensible.

docs.title: 6.4 Vedic Sentences and Injunctions
docs.text:
Mīmāṃsā classifies the sentences of the Veda by their function (Table 6.2).

Table 6.2. Types of Vedic Statements According to Mīmāṃsā Type Sanskrit Description and Example Injunction Vidhi Commands to perform an action: “One who desires heaven should perform the Agnihotra” Prohibition Niṣedha Commands to refrain: “One should not harm any living being” Explanatory Arthāvāda Passages that praise or condemn, motivating the performance of rituals Mantra Mantra Sacred formulae recited during rituals Name Nāmadheya Names of rituals and their components

Among these, vidhi (injunction) is the most important, as it alone communicates dharma. The other types of sentences serve a subordinate function in relation to the injunctions.

Injunctions are themselves of four kinds: the originative injunction (utpatti-vidhi), which establishes a rite; the injunction of application (viniyoga-vidhi), which assigns a detail to a rite; the injunction of eligibility (adhikāra-vidhi), which states who is qualified to perform it; and the injunction of performance (prayoga-vidhi), which fixes the order of its acts.

The question of eligibility (adhikāra) is discussed at length in the sixth book of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra. There Jaimini rejects the view, ascribed to Bādari, that all four varṇas are eligible for Vedic rites, and excludes śūdras; a wife is eligible only jointly with her husband. These rulings, elaborated by Śabara, shaped the Brahmanical restriction of Vedic ritual and learning by caste and gender.

docs.title: 6.5 Principles of Interpretation
docs.text:
Mīmāṃsā developed an extensive set of interpretive rules (nyāyas) for resolving conflicts and ambiguities in the Veda. Its own best-known ranking of evidence (Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 3.3.14; 3.3.13 in some editions) concerns how a subsidiary element is assigned to its principal. It lists six means — direct statement (śruti), the indicatory power of a word (liṅga), syntactic connection (vākya), context (prakaraṇa), position (sthāna) and name (samākhyā) — and rules that in case of conflict each is stronger than those after it. Other general rules are listed in Table 6.3.

Table 6.3. Key Mīmāṃsā Hermeneutical Principles (Nyāyas) Principle Sanskrit Name Application Primary vs. secondary meaning Mukhya-artha / Gauṇa-artha Words should be interpreted in their primary (literal) sense unless this leads to absurdity Context determines meaning Prakaraṇa The meaning of a sentence is determined by its textual context Avoiding contradiction Virodha-parihāra Vedic texts should be interpreted so as to remove apparent contradictions between them Specific overrides general Sāmānya-viśeṣa A specific rule takes precedence over a general rule in case of conflict Exclusive specification Parisaṅkhyā A statement that excludes unmentioned alternatives (“five five-nailed animals may be eaten” excludes other five-nailed animals) Presumptive reasoning Arthāpatti When a Vedic statement appears contradictory, one may postulate an unstated fact

Vedāntins later adapted the method to the Upaniṣads, asking not how a ritual detail fits its rite but what the purport of a whole passage is. They used six indicators (liṅgas) of purport, shown in Figure 6.1; the same concern with method divided the Vedānta schools themselves (Section 8.7).

Figure 6.1. The six indicators (liṅgas) of the purport of a text, a Mīmāṃsā-derived scheme used especially by Vedāntins

docs.title: 6.6 Epistemology: The Six Pramāṇas
docs.text: The Bhāṭṭa school accepts six means of knowledge, a list later adopted by Advaita Vedānta: perception, inference, testimony — of which the Veda is the supreme case — comparison, postulation (arthāpatti) and non-apprehension (anupalabdhi); the Prābhākara school accepts the first five. Postulation is the assumption of an unperceived fact needed to reconcile two known facts that would otherwise conflict. Two classic examples are used: Devadatta is known to be alive but is not at home, so one postulates that he is somewhere else; and Devadatta is fat but does not eat by day, so one postulates that he eats at night. The Naiyāyikas argued that postulation is only a kind of inference; the Mīmāṃsakas replied that it proceeds from a conflict, not from a mark, and that its conclusion is reached by the need to explain, not by a pervasion. Non-apprehension, defended by Kumārila as an independent means for knowing absence, is discussed below.

docs.title: 6.6.1 Svataḥ-Prāmāṇya — The Self-Validity of Knowledge
docs.text:
One of Mīmāṃsā’s most important epistemological contributions is the doctrine of svataḥ-prāmāṇya, the intrinsic validity of knowledge. Every cognition is to be presumed valid unless shown otherwise. Its validity arises from the same conditions that produce the cognition itself, while its invalidity is due to extraneous factors — a defect in the sense organ, or a later cognition that sublates it. Applied to the Veda, the principle has a striking result: since the Veda has no author, there is no author whose ignorance or deceit could introduce a defect, and so nothing could ever overturn its injunctions.

This doctrine stands in contrast to the Nyāya position of parataḥ-prāmāṇya (extrinsic validity), which holds that the validity of a cognition is established by something outside it, such as successful action. The debate over validity (prāmāṇyavāda) became one of the central controversies of Indian epistemology (Taber 2005; Mohanty 2000).

docs.title: 6.7 The Doctrine of Apauruṣeyatva — The Authorless Vedas
docs.text:
The most characteristic Mīmāṃsā doctrine is that the Veda is apauruṣeya, not composed by any person, human or divine. It is eternal, transmitted from teacher to pupil without a beginning; its seers (ṛṣis) saw its mantras but did not make them; and because it has no author it cannot contain the errors, biases or deceptions that any author, even a divine one, might introduce. The argument is largely negative.
