No author of the Veda is remembered, though the authors of other texts are; the tradition of its recitation has no known beginning; and the claim that God composed it cannot be established, since there is no evidence for a creator (see below).

Buddhist and Jain critics replied that an unbroken tradition of transmission proves nothing about authorlessness, and that a text whose meaning depends on human interpreters inherits their fallibility; Nyāya held instead that the Veda is reliable because God is its author. This is a doctrine of faith in the sense that it is not a historical claim: modern scholarship treats the Vedic texts as compositions of many poets over many centuries.

docs.title: 6.8 Language: Words, Meanings and Sentences
docs.text:
The authorless Veda requires a theory of language to match. For Mīmāṃsā the relation between a word and its meaning is innate (autpattika, Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 1.1.5), not established by any person; words are eternal, and what is produced and perishes is only the audible sound that manifests them; the primary meaning of a word is a universal (ākṛti, jāti), not a particular; and a word is nothing but its phonemes in a fixed order, so that the Grammarians’ sphoṭa is unnecessary (Section 6.18). Mīmāṃsā thus disagrees with the Nyāya view that the word–meaning relation is a convention (saṅketa) established by God; it needs no God to establish language, which fits its general theology.

How do words combine into the meaning of a sentence? The two sub-schools gave rival answers. For Kumārila’s school (abhihitānvaya-vāda) the words first express their own meanings, which are then related to one another to give the meaning of the sentence; the conditions of that relating are expectancy, semantic fitness and contiguity, the same conditions Nyāya used (Section 2.7). For Prabhākara’s school (anvitābhidhāna-vāda) words never convey isolated meanings; each expresses its meaning already as connected with the meanings of the others, so that the sentence-meaning is not a later synthesis but the primary unit of communication. Prabhākara’s argument is from learning: a child learns words by watching elders respond to whole commands — “bring the cow”, “take away the horse” — and so learns each word only as a part of a connected meaning. Modern scholars have compared the dispute with the question whether sentence meaning is built compositionally from word meanings or whether the sentence is primary; Kumārila’s view is broadly compositional, Prabhākara’s more contextual (Matilal 1990). The Grammarian Bhartṛhari took the more radical view that the sentence is an indivisible unit.

docs.title: 6.9 Mīmāṃsā’s Theory of the Self (Ātman)
docs.text: Both Mīmāṃsā sub-schools affirm the existence of a permanent, eternal self (ātman), but they differ significantly in their understanding of its nature and how it is known.

docs.title: 6.9.1 Kumārila’s View
docs.text: For Kumārila, the self is an eternal, all-pervading knowing subject (jñātṛ) that is both the agent of action and the experiencer of its fruits. Cognition is an activity or modification of the self that arises when it is joined with the mind (manas) and the senses, not a fixed, ever-present essence; later Bhāṭṭas describe the self as partly insentient and partly conscious (jaḍa-bodhātmaka), and in dreamless sleep it persists without cognitions. The self is the object of the “I”-notion (ahaṃ-pratyaya); cognitions themselves are not self-revealing but are known indirectly.

docs.title: 6.9.2 Prabhākara’s Tripuṭī Theory
docs.text:
Prabhākara holds a more radical view: every act of cognition is a tripuṭī-pratyakṣa (triple awareness). In every cognition, three things are simultaneously revealed: (1) the object known, (2) the cognition itself, and (3) the self as the knower. The self is thus not known through a separate act of introspection but is revealed in every cognitive act (Table 6.4).

Table 6.4. Mīmāṃsā Views on the Self Compared with Other Schools School Nature of Self How Self Is Known Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā Eternal substance whose cognitions are changing modes As the object of the “I”-notion (ahaṃ-pratyaya) Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā Substance revealed in every cognition Tripuṭī-pratyakṣa (triple awareness) Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika Substance inferred from its qualities Inference from mental states Advaita Vedānta Pure consciousness; self-luminous Self-revealing (svaprakāśa) Buddhism No permanent self (anātman) Self is a construct of aggregates

docs.title: 6.10 The Question of God in Mīmāṃsā
docs.text:
Classical Pūrva Mīmāṃsā is remarkable among Indian schools for its explicit rejection of a creator God. An authorless Veda needs no divine author; ritual action, through the unseen potency it produces (apūrva), needs no divine dispenser of its fruits; and Kumārila argues (Ślokavārttika, Sambandhākṣepaparihāra) that there is no evidence that the world ever began, and that a creator’s motive for making a world full of suffering cannot be explained.

Mīmāṃsā is nonetheless classified as āstika because it upholds Vedic authority. The Vedic deities (devatās) are recipients of offerings, but Śabara treats a deity as little more than that to which the offering is made, as named in the Vedic text. Some late Mīmāṃsakas (e.g. Āpadeva and Laugākṣi Bhāskara, 17th century), influenced by Vedānta, recommended dedicating ritual to īśvara.

docs.title: 6.11 The Mīmāṃsā Theory of Apūrva: A Detailed Analysis
docs.text: The concept of apūrva (the unprecedented, the transcendent potency) is one of the most philosophically original contributions of Mīmāṃsā. It addresses a fundamental problem: how does a ritual action performed in the present produce a result (such as the attainment of heaven) that manifests only in the distant future, perhaps after death? The temporal gap between the action and its fruit requires a mediating principle.

docs.title: 6.11.1 The Nature of Apūrva
docs.text:
Apūrva is the suprasensible potency that is generated by the correct performance of a Vedic ritual. It resides in the soul (ātman) of the performer and connects the ritual action with its eventual fruit. The term apūrva literally means “that which did not exist before” — it is a new entity brought into being by the ritual that did not exist prior to the performance (Table 6.5).

Table 6.5. Different Interpretations of Apūrva in Mīmāṃsā Thinker Interpretation Description Śabara Postulated potency Since the act perishes but its fruit comes later, an unseen potency must be postulated (by arthāpatti) to link them Kumārila Capacity in the agent A real capacity (yogyatā, śakti) produced in the sacrificer by the ritual act Prabhākara The “to-be-done” Apūrva is the kārya or niyoga expressed by the injunction itself, which impels the agent and bears fruit

The concept of apūrva serves a function analogous to the concept of adṛṣṭa (unseen merit/demerit) in the Vaiśeṣika system, but with an important difference: whereas adṛṣṭa is a general metaphysical principle, apūrva is specifically tied to Vedic ritual action and derives its authority from the Vedas themselves. This anchoring in Vedic authority gives Mīmāṃsā’s account a character of its own: the efficacy of ritual is not a matter of natural causation but of transcendent ordinance embedded in the eternal structure of the Vedas.

docs.title: 6.11.2 Apūrva and the Problem of Delayed Causation
docs.text: How can a force generated at one time persist, without any visible substrate, until it produces its effect long afterwards? Kumārila’s answer is that apūrva is a real capacity of a kind of its own, not reducible to ordinary physical causation, which persists in the self of the sacrificer as the potency of a seed persists until conditions are right for it to sprout. Critics, Buddhist and Vedāntin, objected that an entity postulated solely to make the injunctions come true can hardly confirm them; the Mīmāṃsaka replied that it is postulated, by arthāpatti, from the conjunction of two things he takes as known: that the Veda’s injunctions are true, and that the ritual act itself perishes at once.

docs.title: 6.12 The Analysis of Ritual Structure
docs.text: Mīmāṃsā’s analysis of Vedic ritual is extraordinarily detailed, amounting to a grammar of ritual action. The Mīmāṃsakas define a sacrifice (yāga) by three elements: a substance (dravya) offered, a deity (devatā) to whom it is offered, and the act of relinquishment (tyāga) by which the sacrificer gives up the substance to the deity. A full description of any rite has to specify more: its purpose, the person eligible to perform it, the formulae recited and the order of its acts. These further items are not a classical enumeration but a convenient summary of what the injunctions of a rite have to settle.

docs.title: 6.12.1 Prakṛti and Vikṛti: Model and Modified Rituals
docs.text:
One of Mīmāṃsā’s most powerful analytical tools is the distinction between prakṛti (model/archetype) rituals and vikṛti (modified/derivative) rituals. A prakṛti ritual is one that is described in full detail in the Vedic texts. A vikṛti ritual is one that is only partially described, with the understanding that the missing details are to be supplied by reference to the prakṛti. This principle of atideśa (analogical extension) allows the vast number of Vedic rituals to be systematized under a relatively small number of archetypes.

The distinction between archetype and modification, with its rules for when an extension is valid and when it is not, is one of the most systematic achievements of Mīmāṃsā reasoning (Jha 1942).

docs.title: 6.13 Kumārila Bhaṭṭa: The Great Defender of the Vedas
docs.text:
Kumārila Bhaṭṭa (c. 600–650 CE) is arguably the most important figure in the history of Mīmāṃsā after Śabara. His three surviving works — the Ślokavārttika, Tantravārttika and Ṭupṭīkā, all sub-commentaries on Śabara — constitute a comprehensive defence of Vedic authority, above all against Buddhist epistemology (Taber 2005).

Kumārila argued for the authorlessness of the Veda together with the intrinsic validity of cognition; against the Buddhists, that determinate perception grasps real objects with their properties and that universals are real and identical-in-difference with their instances; that error consists in misapprehending one real thing as another (viparītakhyāti); that the self is the object of the “I”-notion, and that a cognition is not self-revealing but is known by postulation from the “knownness” (jñātatā) it produces in its object; and that non-apprehension (anupalabdhi, also called abhāva-pramāṇa), already listed by Śabara, is an independent means of knowing absence.

docs.title: 6.13.1 Kumārila’s Critique of Buddhism
docs.text: Later Brahmanical hagiographies portray Kumārila as the destroyer of Buddhism. Historians reject this picture: Buddhist philosophy flourished for five centuries after him (Dharmakīrti, Śāntarakṣita, Ratnakīrti and others answered him), and the decline of Buddhism in India had complex institutional causes. His main arguments included: Against the Buddhist denial of the self, he argued that moral responsibility is impossible if no one endures to reap what was sown; against momentariness, that recognition of the same object over time refutes it; against apoha, that knowing “this is a cow” cannot be merely knowing “this is not a non-cow”; and against the Buddhist claim to an omniscient teacher, that no human being, the Buddha included, can be shown to know dharma directly, so that a human scripture cannot have the authority of the authorless Veda.

docs.title: 6.14 Prabhākara: An Alternative Mīmāṃsā Voice
docs.text:
Prabhākara (c. 7th century CE), the founder of the second major Mīmāṃsā sub-school, differed from Kumārila on several points (Table 6.6).

Table 6.6. Key Differences Between Bhāṭṭa and Prābhākara Schools Issue Bhāṭṭa (Kumārila) Prābhākara Number of pramāṇas Six (including anupalabdhi) Five (absence is known by perceiving the bare locus) Theory of error Viparītakhyāti (misapprehension) Akhyāti (non-apprehension; failure to discriminate) Validity of knowledge Intrinsic validity; invalidity established extrinsically by sublation or defects Every cognition is valid as far as it goes How cognition is known Inferred (by postulation) from the “knownness” of the object Self-luminous; reveals itself, its object and its subject (tripuṭī) Self-knowledge Self is the object of the “I”-notion Self is revealed in every cognition as its subject What an injunction expresses The productive force (bhāvanā) of the verb The “to-be-done” (kārya, niyoga), identified with apūrva Sentence meaning Abhihitānvaya: words first denote, then their meanings are connected Anvitābhidhāna: words denote meanings already connected

docs.title: 6.14.1 Prabhākara’s Akhyāti Theory of Error
docs.text: The akhyāti (non-apprehension) theory of error is Prabhākara’s best-known contribution. According to this theory, error is not a case of apprehending something wrongly but a case of failing to distinguish two valid cognitions:

docs.title: 6.15 Mīmāṃsā and the Theory of Speech Acts
docs.text: Modern scholars have compared Mīmāṃsā’s analysis of Vedic sentences with the speech act theory of J.L. Austin and his successors. An injunction (vidhi) does not describe a state of affairs but directs the hearer to act, much as Austin’s “performative” utterances do things rather than report them; and Kumārila’s account of bhāvanā, the productive force expressed by the verbal ending, is an analysis of how a sentence can move a hearer to action. The comparison is illuminating only as an analogy: the Mīmāṃsakas were concerned with the authority of an authorless text, not with the conventions of everyday speech, and their division of the Veda into injunction, explanatory passage (arthāvāda) and ritual formula (mantra) does not map neatly on to any modern classification of speech acts.

docs.title: 6.16 The Mīmāṃsā Debate with Vedānta
docs.text:
Tradition pairs the “prior” and “later” Mīmāṃsās as complementary inquiries into the two portions of one Veda (Section 6.1; Chapter 1). In practice the pairing concealed sharp disagreements:

  1. The purpose of the Vedas: Mīmāṃsā holds that the primary purpose of the Vedas is to prescribe karma (ritual action); Vedānta holds that the primary purpose is to reveal Brahma-jñāna (knowledge of the Absolute)

  2. Ritual vs. knowledge: Mīmāṃsā regards ritual action as the means to the highest good; Śaṅkara’s Advaita regards knowledge alone as liberating, with karma serving only a preparatory role

  3. The status of Upaniṣadic statements: Mīmāṃsā treats Upaniṣadic passages about Brahman as arthāvāda (explanatory glorifications of ritual); Vedānta treats them as the highest revelation

  4. The nature of mokṣa: For Mīmāṃsā, liberation comes through the cessation of all karmic results after the exhaustion of dharma and adharma; for Vedānta, liberation comes through immediate Self-knowledge

Both sides could cite the Bhagavad Gītā. Those who held that action and knowledge must be combined appealed to its statement that Janaka and others “attained perfection through action alone” (3.20); Śaṅkara read the verse as describing action that purifies the mind and so prepares for knowledge, not action that liberates. The pairing of the two Mīmāṃsās as complementary inquiries was thus a claim made from the Vedāntin side, and the Mīmāṃsakas did not accept its terms.

docs.title: 6.17 Mīmāṃsā’s Influence on Law and Culture
docs.text: The rules developed for interpreting Vedic injunctions were applied systematically to the smṛtis, producing a long tradition of legal interpretation. The Dharmaśāstra commentators — Viśvarūpa, Vijñāneśvara (author of the Mitākṣarā), Aparārka and Jīmūtavāhana (author of the Dāyabhāga) — all used Mīmāṃsā principles: that a specific provision overrides a general one, the distinction between restrictive and exclusive specification (niyama, parisaṅkhyā), and postulation to fill gaps. A few judgments of the Supreme Court of India, notably by Justice Markandey Katju in the 2000s, have invoked Mīmāṃsā maxims alongside the common-law canons, although modern Indian statutory interpretation rests mainly on the common-law tradition. Vedāntins from Śaṅkara onwards adopted the school’s hermeneutic tools; its debates on language shaped grammar; and it remains the theoretical basis of the Vedic ritual still performed in some families. Its use in law is treated in Volume 18 (Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra).

docs.title: 6.18 The Grammarians: Bhartṛhari and the Philosophy of the Word
docs.text: The schools discussed in this volume were not the only Brahmanical traditions to be regarded as darśanas. Mādhava’s Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha (14th century) includes a “Pāṇini-darśana”, the philosophy of the Grammarians (vaiyākaraṇas), and their theory of language was the chief rival of the Mīmāṃsā view just described. This section gives a brief account; grammar itself is treated in Vol. 10 of this series.

docs.title: 6.18.1 From Pāṇini to Patañjali
docs.text: Pāṇini’s grammar (c. 4th century BCE) was followed by Kātyāyana’s critical vārttikas (c. 3rd century BCE) and Patañjali’s Mahābhāṣya (mid-2nd century BCE). Already in these works philosophical questions appear: Kātyāyana’s first vārttika opens by taking the relation of word and meaning to be “established” (siddhe śabdārthasambandhe), and Patañjali reports a debate over whether a word denotes a universal (the view of Vājapyāyana) or an individual (the view of Vyāḍi). Patañjali also uses the term sphoṭa for the word as distinct from the audible sound (dhvani) that manifests it.

docs.title: 6.18.2 Bhartṛhari
docs.text:
The great philosopher of the school is Bhartṛhari, author of the Vākyapadīya (“On Sentence and Word”), in three books. He was once dated to the 7th century on the basis of the Chinese pilgrim Yijing’s report, and identified with the poet of the Śatakatraya; because Dignāga (c. 480–540) already quotes him, he is now dated to c. 5th century CE, and the identification with the poet is doubtful (Iyer 1969; Coward and Kunjunni Raja 1990). The first book opens:

The Word-Brahman

anādinidhanaṃ brahma śabdatattvaṃ yad akṣaram vivartate ’rthabhāvena prakriyā jagato yataḥ Brahman, without beginning or end, whose essence is the Word, the imperishable, which appears in the form of objects, and from which the world proceeds. — Vākyapadīya 1.1

Bhartṛhari’s central doctrines are:

  • Śabdabrahman: ultimate reality is of the nature of the Word, and the world is its appearance (vivarta); this is an early use of the term vivarta, later central to Advaita.

  • Language and cognition: there is no cognition in the world that is not accompanied by language; all knowledge appears “as if interpenetrated by the word” (anuviddham iva jñānaṃ sarvaṃ śabdena bhāsate, Vākyapadīya, book 1).

  • Sphoṭa: the meaning-bearing word or sentence is a single, partless entity (sphoṭa) that is manifested by the sequence of sounds but is not identical with them; the hearer grasps it as a whole once the last sound has been heard.

  • Sentence holism: the primary unit of meaning is the sentence (vākya-sphoṭa), whose meaning is grasped in a single flash of understanding (pratibhā); words and their meanings are abstractions reached by analysis (apoddhāra).

  • Levels of speech: Bhartṛhari distinguishes articulated speech (vaikharī), the intermediate, mental sequence (madhyamā), and undivided “seeing” speech (paśyantī). Later Kaśmīrī Śaivas added a fourth, parā. These levels are a theory of the Grammarians, not a doctrine of the Vedas themselves.

docs.title: 6.18.3 Critics and Influence
docs.text: Mīmāṃsakas (Kumārila in the Ślokavārttika) and Naiyāyikas rejected the sphoṭa as an unnecessary entity: the word, they argued, is simply the series of phonemes, and the last phoneme, together with the traces left by the earlier ones, conveys the meaning (varṇavāda). It is therefore a mistake — found in some popular works — to ascribe the sphoṭa doctrine to Mīmāṃsā; it belongs to the Grammarians, against whom Mīmāṃsā argued. Dignāga’s apoha theory was developed partly in dialogue with Bhartṛhari. Later Grammarians such as Kauṇḍa Bhaṭṭa (17th century) and Nāgeśa (c. 1700) restated the doctrine in Navya-Nyāya terms. Bhartṛhari’s ideas also shaped Kaśmīrī Śaiva philosophy of speech and, through the Grammarians’ notion of manifestation (dhvani), Ānandavardhana’s theory of suggestion in poetics (Matilal 1990; Coward and Kunjunni Raja 1990).

docs.title: Chapter 7: Vedānta — Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita and Dvaita
docs.text:
Invocation from Brahma Sūtra

athāto brahma-jijñāsā Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman. — Brahma Sūtra 1.1.1 (Bādarāyaṇa)

docs.title: 7.1 Introduction: The End of the Vedas
docs.text:
Vedānta literally means “the end of the Vedas” (veda + anta), referring both to the Upaniṣads as the concluding portions of Vedic literature and to the “culmination” or “ultimate purport” of Vedic teaching. It is also known as Uttara Mīmāṃsā (the Later Investigation), dealing with Brahma-jñāna (knowledge of the Absolute) as Pūrva Mīmāṃsā deals with dharma (ritual duty).

In the second millennium CE Vedānta became the dominant framework of Brahmanical theology, and in the modern period it has often been presented, somewhat misleadingly, as the essence of “Hindu philosophy” as a whole. Its interpretations range from the non-dualism of Śaṅkara to the dualism of Madhva (Deutsch 1969; Comans 2000).

docs.title: 7.2 The Triple Foundation and the Central Questions
docs.text:
All Vedānta schools accept three foundational texts, the prasthāna-traya: the Upaniṣads, the revealed basis, especially the ten principal ones (Īśa, Kena, Kaṭha, Praśna, Muṇḍaka, Māṇḍūkya, Taittirīya, Aitareya, Chāndogya and Bṛhadāraṇyaka); Bādarāyaṇa’s Brahma Sūtra, about 555 sūtras in four chapters (the count varies between commentators), which systematises the Upaniṣadic teaching and is so terse that it cannot be understood without a commentary; and the Bhagavad Gītā. The founders of the major schools established their authority by commenting on these texts: Śaṅkara and Madhva on all three, Rāmānuja on the Brahma Sūtra and the Gītā, expounding the Upaniṣads in his Vedārthasaṅgraha. Figure 7.1 shows a manuscript page of one of the principal Upaniṣads.

Figure 7.1. A Devanāgarī manuscript page of the Praśna Upaniṣad (1.6–10) with marginal glosses. Surviving Indian manuscripts are mostly only a few centuries old; the Upaniṣads were transmitted orally long before they were written down Photo: Ms Sarah Welch, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Vedānta asks what Brahman, the ultimate reality, is; what the individual self (jīva) and the world (jagat) are; how the three are related; and what liberation is and how it is attained. Since the texts speak both of identity (“That thou art”) and of difference (“two birds, close companions”), the answers depend on how they are read, and the different answers generate the schools (Figure 7.2).

Figure 7.2. The Three Major Schools of Vedānta

docs.title: 7.3.1 The Life and Legacy of Śaṅkara
docs.text:
Historical Note: Śaṅkara (c. 700–750 CE; older conventional dating 788–820)

Śaṅkara is the most influential exponent of Advaita, though he was not its founder: Gauḍapāda’s Māṇḍūkya Kārikā (c. 6th century) already teaches non-dualism. Most recent scholars date Śaṅkara to c. 700–750 CE. The dates 788–820, long repeated in textbooks, are an older conventional dating, which nineteenth-century scholars took from a late traditional source; the monastic (maṭha) traditions themselves give quite different dates, some of them centuries BCE. The hagiographies (Śaṅkaradigvijaya texts, mostly 14th century or later) say he was born at Kālaḍi in Kerala, died at 32, and founded four monasteries; these accounts are legendary in detail (Comans 2000). His authentic works include the commentaries on the Brahma Sūtra, the principal Upaniṣads and the Bhagavad Gītā, and the Upadeśasāhasrī. Hundreds of other works are ascribed to him; most scholars regard popular texts such as the Vivekacūḍāmaṇi and Ātmabodha as later works by authors of his school.

docs.title: 7.3.2 The Core Doctrine: Brahman Alone Is Real
docs.text:
The essence of Advaita is often summarised in a famous half-verse, popularly attributed to Śaṅkara but found only in later works of doubtful authorship:

A Traditional Summary of Advaita

brahma satyaṃ jagan mithyā jīvo brahmaiva nāparaḥ Brahman is the (sole) Reality; the world is appearance (mithyā); the individual soul is none other than Brahman itself. — Later Advaita tradition

docs.title: 7.3.3 Brahman and Īśvara
docs.text: Brahman is the sole, non-dual, infinite, conscious reality. Śaṅkara distinguishes Brahman without attributes (nirguṇa), the unconditioned reality beyond all predication, from Brahman with attributes (saguṇa), Brahman as conceived through the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of māyā. The latter is īśvara, the personal God who creates, sustains and dissolves the world. Īśvara is not an illusion — he is the highest reality within the empirical order — but he is not the ultimate reality either: when Brahman is known, the distinction between īśvara and the individual self dissolves, and only Brahman without attributes remains. The individual self, in turn, is in essence identical with Brahman; its apparent individuality is due to the superimposition of body, mind and senses on the pure self.

docs.title: 7.3.4 The Doctrine of Adhyāsa (Superimposition)
docs.text:
Śaṅkara’s whole enterprise rests on the concept of superimposition. His preamble to the Brahmasūtrabhāṣya, the Adhyāsabhāṣya, describes it as the fundamental human error from which worldly experience, bondage and suffering arise:

Adhyāsa

…satyānṛte mithunīkṛtya ‘aham idam’ ‘mamedam’ iti naisargiko ’yaṃ lokavyavahāraḥ …coupling the real and the unreal, [people engage in] this natural, everyday usage: “I am this”, “this is mine”. — Śaṅkara, Brahmasūtrabhāṣya, introduction (Adhyāsabhāṣya)

Superimposition is the appearance, in the form of memory, of something previously seen in something else. In its cosmic form it runs both ways: the properties of the self — consciousness, being — are attributed to the not-self, the body and mind, and the properties of the not-self — finitude, change, suffering — are attributed to the self. This mutual superimposition (itaretarādhyāsa) is shown in Table 7.1.

Table 7.1. The Structure of Adhyāsa (Superimposition) in Advaita Direction What Is Superimposed Result Self on not-Self Consciousness attributed to body/mind “My body is conscious”; “My mind knows” Not-Self on Self Limitation attributed to Ātman “I am limited”; “I suffer”; “I will die” Properties of one sense-object on another Shell mistaken for silver “This is silver” (when it is shell) Dream objects on waking Dream experience taken as real Confusion of dream and waking states

Śaṅkara argues that this superimposition is naisargika (natural/innate) and anādi (beginningless). It is not the result of any particular event or act of will but is the fundamental structure of unenlightened experience. All worldly transactions — cognitive, practical, and ritual — presuppose this superimposition. Even the Vedic injunctions (“one should perform the Agnihotra”) operate within the domain of adhyāsa, for they address an agent who identifies himself with a body. The purpose of Vedānta is to remove this beginningless superimposition through the knowledge of the identity of Ātman and Brahman.

Śaṅkara’s argument for the doctrine is an argument from the structure of experience. Every cognition, action and ritual presupposes a knower who takes himself to be embodied, and so presupposes the confusion of self and body; yet the self, which is pure consciousness, cannot really be a body. Since the confusion is present in all experience, it cannot be removed by any experience of the ordinary kind, but only by the knowledge of the self’s identity with Brahman that the Upaniṣads give. Critics asked how something that is never an object — the self — can have anything superimposed on it, since superimposition requires an object present to the senses; Śaṅkara replied that the self is not wholly unknown, since it is the object of the notion “I”, and that space, which is not perceived, is still said to be blue.

docs.title: 7.3.5 Māyā and Avidyā
docs.text: The world-appearance arises from ignorance (avidyā), which later Advaitins also call māyā. Śaṅkara himself speaks mostly of ignorance and superimposition; the systematic doctrine that ignorance is anirvacanīya — neither real (sat) nor unreal (asat), but false (mithyā) — was developed by his near-contemporary Maṇḍana Miśra and by his successors (Padmapāda, Prakāśātman and others). In the developed doctrine māyā is the indescribable power of Brahman through which the world-appearance is projected. It has two functions, concealment (āvaraṇa) of Brahman’s true nature and projection (vikṣepa) of the manifold world, as Sadānanda’s Vedāntasāra (15th century) puts it; it is beginningless but can be ended by knowledge; and, consisting of the three guṇas, it is the material cause of the world at the empirical level. Its status — neither real nor unreal — is a category of its own, and it was the target of Rāmānuja’s criticisms (Section 7.5).

docs.title: 7.3.6 The Three Levels of Reality
docs.text:
Śaṅkara distinguishes the standpoint of ultimate truth (paramārtha) from that of everyday transaction (vyavahāra); later Advaitins formalised the distinction as three levels of reality. Brahman alone is absolutely real (pāramārthika), never sublated by any further knowledge. The world of everyday experience, including bodies, selves and īśvara, is empirically real (vyāvahārika): real within its own domain — fire burns and walls resist us, whatever our philosophy — but sublated by the knowledge of Brahman. Individual errors such as the snake seen in a rope, or the objects of a dream, are merely apparent (prātibhāsika), and are sublated even within ordinary experience (Figure 7.3).

Figure 7.3. The Three Levels of Reality (Sattā-Traya) in Advaita Vedānta

The Advaita theory of error follows from this picture. When one mistakes a shell for silver, the silver is neither absolutely real, since it is contradicted on closer examination, nor absolutely unreal, since it was genuinely experienced; it is indescribable (anirvacanīya) in terms of real and unreal. The same logic is then extended to the world-appearance as a whole. This theory, anirvacanīyakhyāti, is compared with the theories of error of the other schools in Chapter 13 (Table 13.4).

docs.title: 7.3.7 The Great Sayings (Mahāvākyas)
docs.text:
All Vedānta schools engage with the “great sentences” of the Upaniṣads (Table 7.2), and their readings of them are a test of their methods.

Table 7.2. The Four Mahāvākyas Mahāvākya Source Meaning Prajñānaṃ brahma Aitareya Up. Consciousness is Brahman Ahaṃ brahmāsmi Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. I am Brahman Tat tvam asi Chāndogya Up. That thou art Ayam ātmā brahma Māṇḍūkya Up. This Self is Brahman

The Advaita interpretation, systematised by Sureśvara and later authors, uses the technique of “implication that partly gives up and partly keeps” the primary meaning (jahad-ajahal-lakṣaṇā, also called bhāga-lakṣaṇā). In “That thou art”, the primary meaning of “That” is īśvara, God with māyā, and of “thou” the individual self with its limitations. To identify these would be absurd, like identifying a king with a beggar. The sentence therefore asserts the identity of what is common to both, pure consciousness, dropping the incompatible features — omniscience on one side, ignorance on the other — as one does in “this is that Devadatta”, where the person seen now and the person seen before are identified while the differences of place and time are set aside. For Śaṅkara the sentence thus directly asserts the identity of the self with Brahman. Rāmānuja takes it to assert the inseparability of the self, as body, from Brahman, as its soul, and insists on the primary meaning throughout; Madhva reads it as asserting that the self is dependent on and different from Brahman, and one Mādhva reading divides the words to give “thou art not that” (atat tvam asi). The reasons for these differences of method are discussed in Chapter 8 (Section 8.7).

docs.title: 7.3.8 Liberation and Jīvanmukti
docs.text: Liberation, for Advaita, is not the attainment of something new but the realisation (avagati) of what one has always been, Brahman. It comes from knowledge, which arises through hearing the teaching of the great sayings (śravaṇa), reflection that removes doubts (manana) and sustained contemplation (nididhyāsana). Because liberation is knowledge, it can occur while the body still lives. On the dawn of knowledge one is liberated at once, though the body continues, like a potter’s wheel turning after the push has stopped, until the karma that has already begun to bear fruit (prārabdha) is exhausted. The one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) has no sense of “I” or “mine”, is indifferent to praise and blame, acts without personal motive, and “sees the same in a learned brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog and a dog-eater” (Bhagavad Gītā 5.18); no new karma accrues to him. At the fall of the body comes liberation without a body (videhamukti), which is not a new state but the end of the last appearance of individuality.

docs.title: 7.4 Advaita after Śaṅkara: The Later Schools and the Dialectical Turn
docs.text: Śaṅkara left many questions open, and his successors answered them in different ways. Over the next eight centuries Advaita became a scholastic tradition with its own sub-schools, its own technical vocabulary, much of it borrowed from Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā, and a long controversy with the Dvaita school of Madhva. This section outlines that development; the difference between the Bhāmatī and Vivaraṇa schools on the locus of ignorance is summarised in Volume 2 (Upaniṣad Dīpikā), and is only recalled here (Potter 1981).

docs.title: 7.4.1 Maṇḍana, Sureśvara and Padmapāda
docs.text:
Three near-contemporaries of Śaṅkara shaped what came after. Maṇḍana Miśra, a Mīmāṃsaka who also wrote on Advaita, is the author of the Brahmasiddhi, whose four sections deal with Brahman, with reasoning (tarka), with injunction (niyoga) and with the attainment of liberation. Its section on reasoning argues that perception grasps only bare being and cannot grasp difference, since difference is relative to something else and so cannot be presented in a single perception; the plurality of the world is therefore not established by perception, and scripture’s teaching of non-duality is not contradicted by it. Maṇḍana held that ignorance belongs to the individual selves, not to Brahman (“the defilement by ignorance belongs to the jīvas, not to Brahman”); that the verbal knowledge given by the Upaniṣads is indirect and must be made direct by sustained meditation (prasaṅkhyāna); and that ritual action can assist the rise of knowledge. Later tradition identified him with Sureśvara, saying that he took that name after Śaṅkara defeated him in debate; most modern scholars reject the identification, since the two hold different views.

Sureśvara, Śaṅkara’s pupil, wrote the Naiṣkarmyasiddhi (“The Establishment of Actionlessness”) and long verse commentaries (vārttikas) on Śaṅkara’s commentaries on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Taittirīya Upaniṣads. Against Maṇḍana he held that the Upaniṣadic sentence itself produces immediate knowledge, so that no further meditation is needed; that action has no place in the attainment of liberation; and that the individual self is a “semblance” (ābhāsa) of consciousness in the intellect — a view later called ābhāsavāda. Padmapāda, another pupil, commented on the opening of Śaṅkara’s Brahmasūtrabhāṣya in the Pañcapādikā. He described ignorance as a beginningless, insentient power that is the material of the world-appearance, and so opened the way for the doctrine of a “root ignorance” (mūlāvidyā). Prakāśātman’s Pañcapādikāvivaraṇa developed this into the Vivaraṇa school, for which Brahman itself is the locus and the object of ignorance and the individual self is Brahman’s reflection in ignorance (pratibimbavāda). Vācaspati Miśra’s Bhāmatī, a sub-commentary on Śaṅkara (9th or 10th century), followed Maṇḍana instead: ignorance resides in the individual selves, and the self is Brahman as delimited by ignorance, like space enclosed in a pot (avacchedavāda).

docs.title: 7.4.2 Śrīharṣa and the Critique of Definitions
docs.text:
From the eleventh century Advaitins increasingly met the Naiyāyikas on their own ground. The most original of them was Śrīharṣa (12th century), poet of the Naiṣadhīyacarita at the court of Kanauj, whose Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya (“The Sweets of Refutation”) is a systematic attack on the Nyāya definitions of the means and objects of knowledge (Granoff 1978; Phillips 1995). His method is close to that of vitaṇḍā (Section 13.8): he does not defend a rival theory of the means of knowledge but shows, case by case, that each proposed definition of valid cognition, of perception, of inference, of causality or of difference either fails to cover what it should or covers what it should not. Difference is a favourite target. One of his arguments runs as follows. If difference were the very nature of the things that differ, then a thing would be different by its own nature, and to grasp the thing would be to grasp it as different from everything — which no one does; if difference were a property over and above the things, it would itself have to differ from them, and a regress follows. Śrīharṣa concludes that the world of difference is indefinable (anirvacanīya), which is exactly what the Advaitin says of it.

Śrīharṣa also faced the obvious objection: how can an Advaitin, who holds that the means of knowledge are not ultimately real, take part in debate at all? His answer is that debate requires only that both parties accept the means of knowledge for the purposes of the debate, as a matter of practice (vyavahāra), not that they hold them to be ultimately real. The argument made Advaita a formidable dialectical opponent and provoked the Navya-Nyāya reply: much of Gaṅgeśa’s effort to define his terms with exact limitors (Section 2.11) can be read as a response to Śrīharṣa’s challenge (Phillips 1995). A little later (probably in the 13th century) Citsukha’s Tattvapradīpikā continued the critique of Nyāya categories and gave a careful definition of the self-luminosity of consciousness: it is that which is fit to be treated as immediately present while never being an object of cognition.

docs.title: 7.4.3 The Controversy with Dvaita
docs.text:
The longest controversy of late Vedānta was with the followers of Madhva (Section 7.6). Jayatīrtha (14th century) had systematised Madhva’s arguments in his Nyāyasudhā; Vyāsatīrtha (c. 1460–1539), the leading Mādhva scholar at the Vijayanagara court, then wrote the Nyāyāmṛta, a detailed refutation of Advaita that used the methods of Navya-Nyāya (Stoker 2016). Its first target was the Advaita claim that the world is false (mithyā). Vyāsatīrtha examined each definition of falsity that the Advaitins had proposed and argued that each either applies to Brahman as well, or fails to apply to the world, or involves a contradiction. He also posed a dilemma: the world’s falsity must itself be either real or false. If it is real, there is a second reality besides Brahman and non-duality is lost; if it is false, the world is not false after all, and so is real.

The Advaita reply was Madhusūdana Sarasvatī’s Advaitasiddhi (16th or 17th century), one of the most technical works in Indian philosophy (Gupta 2006). It opens by defending, against the Nyāyāmṛta, five definitions of falsity drawn from earlier Advaitins: that which is not the locus of either being or non-being; that which is the counterpositive of an absence, in all three times, in the very locus where it appears; that which is removed by knowledge; that which is the counterpositive of an absolute absence residing in its own locus; and that which is other than the real. To the dilemma, Madhusūdana answers that the falsity of the world is itself false (mithyātvam api mithyā), and argues at length that this does not make the world real. The debate continued for generations: Rāmācārya’s Taraṅgiṇī defended Vyāsatīrtha, and Brahmānanda Sarasvatī’s commentaries defended Madhusūdana. Madhusūdana was also a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, whose Bhaktirasāyana treats devotion as a rasa; the combination shows that the Advaita of this period was not hostile to bhakti.

docs.title: 7.4.4 Diversity within Late Advaita
docs.text: The tradition never settled into a single doctrine. Appayya Dīkṣita (16th century) collected its disagreements in the Siddhāntaleśasaṃgraha — on the locus of ignorance, on whether there is one individual self or many, on whether the self is a reflection, a semblance or a delimitation of Brahman, and on how verbal testimony produces liberating knowledge. At one extreme Prakāśānanda (probably 16th century) defended the view that there is only one individual self and that the world exists only in being perceived (dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda), as in a dream. At the other, Dharmarāja Adhvarin’s Vedāntaparibhāṣā (17th century) worked out an Advaita epistemology that accepts the six means of knowledge of the Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsakas for everyday purposes (Chapter 6) and adopts Navya-Nyāya terminology; it became, with Sadānanda’s Vedāntasāra, a standard textbook. Through such works, and through the modern Vedānta movements described in Chapter 8 and Volume 24, late scholastic Advaita shaped the picture of Indian philosophy that reached the modern world (Ganeri 2011).

docs.title: 7.5 Viśiṣṭādvaita — Rāmānuja’s Qualified Non-Dualism
docs.text:
Historical Note: Rāmānuja (traditionally 1017–1137 CE)

Rāmānuja, born according to tradition at Śrīperumbudūr (Tamil Nadu), was the most formidable philosophical challenger to Advaita. The traditional lifespan of 120 years is doubted, and some scholars place him c. 1077–1157. He built on the work of Yāmunācārya and on the devotional poetry of the Āḻvārs, several of whom were not brahmins. He authored the Śrībhāṣya (commentary on the Brahma Sūtra), the Gītābhāṣya and the Vedārthasaṅgraha, and organised the Śrī Vaiṣṇava tradition (Carman 1974).

docs.title: 7.5.1 Method and Core Doctrines
docs.text:
Rāmānuja’s method is a scriptural realism. All Upaniṣadic statements are to be taken as referring to real things, not explained away as figurative or provisional; and when the texts predicate both unity and plurality of Brahman, both are literally true, by “co-ordinate predication” (sāmānādhikaraṇya): two words with different meanings can refer to one thing, as “the blue lotus” refers to one lotus qualified by blueness. Brahman, accordingly, is not without attributes but possesses infinite auspicious qualities (kalyāṇa-guṇas), and is identified with Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu. The selves and the world are real and are related to Brahman as body to soul (śarīra-śarīri-bhāva): a body, in Rāmānuja’s definition, is whatever a conscious being supports, controls and uses for its own purposes, and in that sense everything is the body of God, who is its inner controller (antaryāmin). Brahman is therefore a “qualified” (viśiṣṭa) unity, one whole whose real modes (prakāra) are the selves and the world. The selves are many, eternal, atomic and conscious, distinct from one another and from God though wholly dependent on him (Table 7.3). God is not conditioned by māyā but is the master of primordial nature; Rāmānuja rejects outright the Advaita distinction between a higher, attributeless Brahman and a lower, personal God.

Table 7.3. Three Categories of Reality in Viśiṣṭādvaita Category Sanskrit Characteristics God īśvara (Nārāyaṇa) Supreme, independent, infinite, possessing all auspicious qualities; the inner controller (antaryāmin) of all Souls Cit (Jīvas) Atomic, conscious, eternal, many; dependent on God; either bound (baddha), liberated (mukta), or ever-free (nitya) Matter Acit (Prakṛti) Unconscious, real, ever-changing, the material for God’s creative activity; also eternal and dependent on God

docs.title: 7.5.2 The Paths to Liberation
docs.text:
Liberation, for Rāmānuja, is not identity with God but the self’s realisation of its true nature as God’s servant (śeṣa), in eternal communion with him and in the bliss of service (nitya-kaiṅkarya); it comes only after death, since Rāmānuja rejects liberation while living. The Śrī Vaiṣṇava tradition recognises two paths to liberation:

  1. Bhakti-Yoga (The Path of Devotion) — The path expounded in Rāmānuja’s commentaries: karma-yoga and jñāna-yoga prepare the way for bhakti, continuous loving meditation on God, which is open to the twice-born who are qualified for Vedic study

  2. Prapatti / Śaraṇāgati (Total Surrender) — Complete self-surrender to God’s grace, open to all regardless of caste, learning or merit. It is expressed in the Śaraṇāgatigadya ascribed to Rāmānuja, and became the central path for later teachers

Those later teachers — Vedānta Deśika and Piḷḷai Lokācārya above all — read the Gītā’s “Abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in me alone” (18.66) as the carama-śloka, the “final verse” that authorises prapatti in place of the demanding discipline of bhakti-yoga. Rāmānuja’s own commentary on the verse is more cautious and offers more than one explanation of it; the doctrinal weight placed on it is a development of the following centuries, and it later divided the Vaḍakalai and Teṅkalai branches of the tradition over the role of the soul’s own effort.

docs.title: 7.5.3 Rāmānuja’s Critique of Advaita
docs.text:
In the Śrībhāṣya Rāmānuja raises seven objections against the Advaita doctrine of avidyā, known as the saptavidha anupapatti (seven untenabilities):

  1. Āśraya — Avidyā can have no locus: not Brahman, which is pure knowledge, nor the jīva, which is itself a product of avidyā

  2. Tirodhāna — Avidyā cannot conceal Brahman, whose very nature is self-luminous

  3. Svarūpa — Its nature cannot be stated: if real, non-dualism fails; if unreal, it can do nothing

  4. Anirvacanīyatva — Something “neither real nor unreal” is a contradiction

  5. Pramāṇa — No valid means of knowledge establishes such an avidyā

  6. Nivartaka — No knowledge can remove it, since knowledge of an attributeless Brahman is impossible

  7. Nivṛtti — Its cessation is impossible, since what is beginningless and positive cannot be destroyed by knowledge

docs.title: 7.6 Dvaita — Madhva’s Dualism
docs.text:
Historical Note: Madhva (c. 1238–1317 CE)

Madhva (Ānandatīrtha; the Mādhva tradition dates him 1199–1278), born near Uḍupi in Karnataka, propounded the most thoroughgoing realist and dualist interpretation of Vedānta. His works, traditionally counted as thirty-seven, include commentaries on the prasthānatraya. His philosophy is also called Tattvavāda (the doctrine of reality) (Sharma 1962).

docs.title: 7.6.1 The Five-fold Difference (Pañca-Bheda)
docs.text:
The hallmark of Dvaita is its assertion of five real and eternal differences (Figure 7.4):

Figure 7.4. The Five-fold Difference (Pañca-Bheda) of Dvaita Vedānta

docs.title: 7.6.2 Core Doctrines of Dvaita
docs.text:
For Madhva, Viṣṇu alone is independent (svatantra); everything else is dependent (paratantra). God is the efficient cause of the world but not its material cause, which is primordial nature, lest God be subject to change. The world is not false but real, though dependent on God. The selves are eternally distinct from God and from one another, and they are graded: there is a natural hierarchy (tāratamya) among all beings, with Viṣṇu supreme, Lakṣmī next, then Brahmā and Vāyu, the other gods in descending order, human selves according to their innate fitness (svābhāvika yogyatā), and matter at the bottom. The hierarchy is eternal, the inherent nature of each being, and not the result of karma. Liberation is attained only through God’s grace, earned by devotion, and consists in the vision and service of God; in it the selves keep their individuality and their rank. Even more controversial was Madhva’s division of souls into three eternal classes (Table 7.4).

Table 7.4. Madhva’s Three Classes of Souls Class Sanskrit Destiny Fit for liberation Mukti-yogya These souls will eventually attain eternal bliss in the presence of Lord Viṣṇu through bhakti and divine grace Eternally transmigrating Nitya-saṃsārī These souls will continue in the cycle of saṃsāra forever, never attaining liberation nor being condemned Destined for darkness Tamo-yogya These souls are destined for eternal damnation (andha-tamas), having an intrinsic nature opposed to God

This doctrine of eternal damnation for some souls is distinctive among Indian schools (Jains, too, hold that some souls, the abhavya, can never be liberated, but not that they are damned) and was sharply criticised by other Vedāntins.

docs.title: 7.7 The Three Schools Compared
docs.text:
Table 7.5 compares the three schools point by point, and Table 7.6 their conceptions of liberation.

Table 7.5. Comparison of Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita, and Dvaita Topic Advaita Viśiṣṭādvaita Dvaita Brahman Nirguṇa (attributeless) Saguṇa (with infinite qualities) Lord Viṣṇu (supreme person) God Brahman as conditioned by māyā; real only empirically Brahman itself, the inner controller of all Wholly independent; efficient cause only World Mithyā (apparent) Real (body of Brahman) Real (dependent) Jīva Identical with Brahman Mode (prakāra) and body of Brahman Eternally distinct Relation Identity Qualified unity Difference Ācārya Śaṅkara Rāmānuja Madhva Date c. 700–750 CE (older conventional dating 788–820) traditionally 1017–1137 CE traditionally 1238–1317 CE (some scholars 1199–1278) Table 7.6. The Concept of Liberation Across Vedānta Schools Aspect Advaita Viśiṣṭādvaita Dvaita Nature of mokṣa Realisation of identity with Brahman Eternal communion with God in Vaikuṇṭha Vision and service of God in eternal bliss Means Knowledge alone Bhakti culminating in prapatti (surrender) Bhakti with divine grace (prasāda) State of the liberated Pure consciousness; no individuality Retains individuality; enjoys God’s presence Retains individuality; ranked in bliss Liberation while living Yes (jīvanmukti) Rejected; liberation follows death Final liberation only after death; one who has the direct vision of God lives out his remaining karma, a state some Mādhva authors compare to liberation while living

The three schools are often presented as a neat spectrum, from an impersonal Absolute above a personal God, through a personal God who is both transcendent and immanent, to a personal God utterly sovereign and other. The picture is useful for orientation but misleading if taken as complete: Chapter 8 describes schools that do not fit on a single line between identity and difference, and Śaiva theologians built non-dualisms and dualisms of their own (Chapter 12). What the three share is narrower: the authority of the prasthāna-traya, the reality of liberation, and the conviction that ritual action alone cannot reach the highest good. On almost everything else they argued that the others had misread scripture.

docs.title: 7.8 Vedānta and Modern Philosophy
docs.text: Vedānta’s influence on modern philosophical thought — both in India and internationally — has been substantial. Several areas of contemporary philosophy find resonance with Vedāntic insights.

docs.title: 7.8.1 Vedānta and Consciousness Studies
docs.text:
The “hard problem of consciousness” — explaining why and how subjective experience arises from physical processes — has emerged as one of the central questions in contemporary philosophy of mind. Vedānta, particularly Advaita, approaches this problem from a radically different starting point: rather than trying to derive consciousness from matter, it begins with consciousness as the foundational reality and asks how the appearance of matter arises within consciousness.

Some contemporary philosophers have compared the Advaita view that consciousness (cit) is not produced by any physical or mental process with modern views that treat consciousness as fundamental rather than emergent. Such comparisons are suggestive, but the Advaita claim rests on scriptural exegesis and an analysis of the self-luminosity of awareness, not on the arguments of modern philosophy of mind.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Other Schools of Vedānta and Related Theologies
docs.text:
Form after Form

rūpaṃ rūpaṃ pratirūpo babūva tad asya rūpaṃ praticakṣaṇāya He became form after form; each form of His is for the purpose of making Him known. — Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19

docs.title: 8.1 Introduction: Beyond the Three Great Schools
docs.text:
While Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita, and Dvaita are the most widely known Vedānta schools, the Vedāntic tradition is far richer than these three alone. Several other ācāryas offered their own interpretations of the prasthānatraya, most of them within Vaiṣṇava devotional traditions, and Śaiva theologians developed parallel systems (Figure 8.1).

Figure 8.1. A rough, simplified placing of Vedānta schools between non-dualism and dualism

docs.title: 8.2 The Early Bhedābheda Tradition
docs.text: The Bhedābheda (difference-and-non-difference) tradition has ancient roots that predate the major ācāryas. Bhāskara (c. 8th–9th century CE) and Yādava Prakāśa (11th century CE) are among the earliest exponents whose works survive; Bhartṛprapañca, an earlier Vedāntin criticised by Śaṅkara, is known only from quotations.

docs.title: 8.2.1 Bhāskara’s Aupādhika-Bhedābheda
docs.text: Bhāskara, a slightly younger contemporary or successor of Śaṅkara, argued that the jīva is both identical with and different from Brahman, depending on the perspective. When considered in its essential nature, the jīva is identical with Brahman; when considered as conditioned by its upādhis (limiting adjuncts), it is different. Crucially, Bhāskara held that the upādhis are real, not illusory as in Advaita. The difference between the jīva and Brahman is therefore a real difference, not an apparent one.

docs.title: 8.2.2 Yādava Prakāśa’s Svābhāvika-Bhedābheda
docs.text:
Yādava Prakāśa, who was according to tradition an early teacher of Rāmānuja before the latter developed his own system, held that Brahman naturally (svābhāvika) transforms itself into the jīvas and the world. The difference and non-difference are both natural and real: just as the ocean is both identical with and different from its waves, Brahman is both identical with and different from its transformations (Table 8.1).

Table 8.1. Variants of the Bhedābheda Position Thinker Date Position Key Distinction Bhartṛ­prapañca pre-Śaṅkara (date uncertain) Early bhedābheda Brahman transforms into the world Bhāskara c. 8th–9th c. CE Aupādhika-bhedābheda Real upādhis cause real difference Yādava Prakāśa 11th c. CE Svābhāvika-bhedābheda Natural transformation of Brahman Nimbārka c. 12th–13th c. CE (disputed) Dvaitādvaita Sun and rays analogy Caitanya / Jīva G. 16th c. CE Acintya bhedābheda Inconceivable simultaneous identity and difference

The later schools described in this chapter can be read as successive answers to the question the early Bhedābheda left open: if Brahman is both identical with and different from the world, what kind of relation is that, and how can it be stated without contradiction?

docs.title: 8.3 Dvaitādvaita — Nimbārka’s Dualistic Non-Dualism
docs.text:
Historical Note: Nimbārka (date disputed; often placed c. 12th–13th century CE)

Nimbārka (also known as Niyamānanda), said by tradition to have come from the Telugu-speaking region, propounded the Dvaitādvaita (Dualistic Non-dualism) school. His followers place him much earlier than modern scholars do. He is regarded by his followers as an incarnation of the divine Sudarśana Cakra. His primary work is the Vedānta-Pārijāta-Saurabha, a commentary on the Brahma Sūtra.

For Nimbārka, Brahman is Kṛṣṇa, with Rādhā as his eternal consort and power (śakti). There are three realities — conscious selves (cit), unconscious matter (acit) and God — and the selves and the world are both different and not different from God, as the sun’s rays are distinct from the sun yet inseparable from it, or as a spider’s web is both different from and one with the spider that is its material and efficient cause. The selves are atomic, many and dependent on God. Liberation is reached by a combination of action, knowledge and devotion, with special emphasis on self-surrender (prapatti), and consists in the enjoyment of God’s company. Nimbārka’s answer to the Bhedābheda question is that difference and non-difference are both natural and real, because the world’s dependence on God is itself a kind of non-difference: what cannot exist apart from another is not wholly other than it.

docs.title: 8.4 Śuddhādvaita — Vallabha’s Pure Non-Dualism
docs.text:
Historical Note: Ācārya Vallabha (1479–1531 CE)

Vallabhācārya, a Telugu Brahmin who became one of the most influential Vaiṣṇava teachers, propounded Śuddhādvaita (Pure Non-dualism). His primary work is the Aṇubhāṣya on the Brahma Sūtra. He founded the Puṣṭi-Mārga (Path of Grace), one of the major devotional traditions of western India.

Vallabha’s non-dualism is “pure” (śuddha) because it dispenses with māyā. Brahman is Kṛṣṇa, who is being, consciousness and bliss (sat-cit-ānanda). The world is real, not false: it is a real transformation (pariṇāma) of Brahman himself, arising from his own will and delight, and Brahman remains unchanged in becoming it, as gold remains gold in the ornaments made from it. The individual self is a part (aṃśa) of Brahman, identical with him in nature but limited in scope; its bliss is obscured, not by māyā, but by the Lord’s own power of concealment (tirodhāna), and liberation is the restoration of that bliss by his grace (puṣṭi). Grace, not effort, is what counts. The highest goal is loving service (sevā) of Kṛṣṇa, and the initiation of “connection with Brahman” (brahma-sambandha) formally dedicates the devotee’s body, mind, possessions and self to him.

Vallabha argued against both his great predecessors. Against Śaṅkara: if Brahman is pure bliss, why would it project an illusion of suffering? Māyā is then inexplicable, and it is simpler to hold that the world is a real expression of Brahman’s bliss. Against Rāmānuja: if the world is God’s body, God is limited by it, as a soul is by its body; the relation of part and whole, Vallabha held, keeps the identity of nature without that limitation. Vallabha himself, however, classified souls by type — those of grace (puṣṭi), of rule (maryādā) and of the worldly “stream” (pravāha) — so that not all are equally destined for the highest devotion.

docs.title: 8.5 Acintya Bhedābheda — Caitanya’s Inconceivable Difference-and-Non-difference
docs.text:
Historical Note: Śrī Kṛṣṇa Caitanya Mahāprabhu (1486–1534 CE)

Caitanya Mahāprabhu, born in Navadvīpa (Bengal), is revered by his followers as an incarnation of Lord Kṛṣṇa Himself. Though he left no philosophical writings of his own, his teachings were systematized by the six Gosvāmīs of Vṛndāvana, particularly Jīva Gosvāmī in his Ṣaṭ-Sandarbha; in the 18th century Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa wrote the school’s commentary on the Brahma Sūtra, the Govinda-Bhāṣya.

The Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavas gave the Bhedābheda question its most radical answer: the relation between God, the selves and the world is one of simultaneous difference and non-difference that is “inconceivable” (acintya) — not contradictory, but beyond the reach of reasoning, and known only from scripture. Brahman is Kṛṣṇa himself, not an avatāra of Viṣṇu but the Lord in his original form (svayaṃ bhagavān). The relation is explained through Kṛṣṇa’s powers (śaktis), of which three are primary (Figure 8.2). A power is neither identical with nor different from the one who has it, and so, through his powers, God is both one with and other than the world and the selves.

Figure 8.2. The Three Śaktis (Energies) of Kṛṣṇa in Acintya Bhedābheda

The tradition, drawing on Sanskrit poetics as well as Vedānta, also developed a theology of the relationships (rasas) between the devotee and God (Table 8.2). Liberation is not release but pure love of God (prema), the highest attainment.

Table 8.2. The Five Primary Rasas in Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava Theology Rasa Relation Nature Exemplar Śānta Neutral appreciation Peaceful contemplation of God’s greatness The four Kumāras Dāsya Servitude Loving service with awe and reverence Hanumān Sakhya Friendship Intimate friendship and equality Śrīdāmā, Arjuna Vātsalya Parental love Protective nurturing love for God as child Yaśodā, Nanda Mādhurya Conjugal love The highest and most intimate loving exchange Rādhā, the gopīs

Each successive rasa is considered more intimate and more complete than the preceding one, with mādhurya rasa being the summit of devotional experience.

docs.title: 8.6 Śaiva Vedānta and the Śaiva Siddhānta
8.6.1 Śivādvaita — Śrīkaṇṭha’s Śaiva Vedānta
docs.text: Śrīkaṇṭha (date disputed, c. 11th–14th century) authored a commentary on the Brahma Sūtra from a Śaiva perspective, interpreting Brahman as Śiva in a manner close to Rāmānuja’s qualified non-dualism. Appayya Dīkṣita (16th century) defended it in his Śivārkamaṇidīpikā, although he himself was an Advaitin. The Vīraśaiva theologian Śrīpati (c. 14th century) wrote the Śrīkarabhāṣya, expounding “śakti-qualified non-dualism” (Śaktiviśiṣṭādvaita).

docs.title: 8.6.2 Śaiva Siddhānta
docs.text: Śaiva Siddhānta is not a school of Vedānta but an Āgamic theology. Its Sanskrit form (Sadyojyotis, Rāmakaṇṭha, Bhoja, late 7th to 11th centuries) is pluralist and realist, and its Tamil form, founded on Meykaṇṭār’s Civañāṉapōtam (13th century), became a major theology of Tamil Śaivism. Both recognise three eternal categories: the Lord (pati, Śiva), souls (paśu) and bonds (pāśa). The philosophy of the Sanskrit Siddhānta is examined in Chapter 12; Śaiva and Śākta traditions as a whole are treated in Vol. 6 of this series. The non-dual Śaiva philosophy of Kashmir, which engaged with Advaita and offered a dynamic alternative to it, is treated in the same chapter (Section 12.6).

docs.title: 8.7 The Hermeneutical Methods of the Vedānta Schools
docs.text:
A central reason for the diversity of Vedānta sub-schools lies in the different hermeneutical methods employed to interpret the Prasthāna-Traya. The Upaniṣads contain statements that appear to affirm both identity (“Tat tvam asi” — That thou art) and difference (“dvā suparṇā sayujā sakhāyā” — Two birds, close companions). How these apparently contradictory statements are reconciled determines the philosophical position of each school (Table 8.3).

Table 8.3. Hermeneutical Methods of the Major Vedānta Schools School Method How Identity and Difference Statements Are Reconciled Advaita Mukhya-gauṇa Identity statements are primary (mukhya); difference statements are secondary (gauṇa) or refer to the empirical level Viśiṣṭādvaita Samānā­dhi­karaṇya Both are literally true: identity and difference coexist because the jīva is Brahman’s attribute; co-ordinate predication Dvaita Priority of difference texts Difference statements are primary; identity statements express similarity or dependence, not ontological identity Śuddhādvaita Aṃśa-aṃśin Jīva as part (aṃśa) of Brahman (whole, aṃśin); identity as sharing the same nature, difference as limited scope Acintya B.A. Śakti-śaktimad Identity and difference coexist inconceivably through the relation of energy (śakti) to the energetic (śaktimān)

The disagreement turns largely on implied meaning (lakṣaṇā). When the primary meaning (vācyārtha) of a word leads to absurdity or contradiction, an interpreter may resort to an implied meaning (lakṣyārtha). The Advaitins do so in reading “That thou art” (Section 7.3.7); Rāmānuja insists on primary meaning throughout and argues that the sentence directly affirms the self’s oneness with Brahman as body with soul. Behind this lies a deeper question: what counts as an absurdity that licenses departure from the literal sense? An Advaitin finds absurdity in identifying God and the individual self; a Viśiṣṭādvaitin finds none, given the body–soul relation; a Dvaitin finds it in any statement of identity at all. The same texts, accepted by all, yield different systems because the schools bring different views of what the texts could possibly mean. The Vedāntins made these commitments explicit and argued about them, which is why their commentaries are works of philosophy and not only of exegesis.

docs.title: 8.8 Modern Vedānta
docs.text:
In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries Vedānta, above all Advaita, was reinterpreted by thinkers writing in English and in dialogue with Western philosophy and Christianity. Svāmī Vivekānanda (1863–1902), the disciple of Rāmakṛṣṇa, preached a “practical Vedānta”: the realisation that all beings are Brahman should lead not to withdrawal from the world but to service of humanity as worship of God — service of God in the form of the poor (daridra-nārāyaṇa). He presented all religions as paths to the same truth, systematised karma, bhakti, rāja and jñāna yoga as complementary disciplines suited to different temperaments, and argued that Vedānta demands the removal of social inequality, since all beings share the same divine essence.

Śrī Aurobindo (1872–1950) developed an evolutionary metaphysics. The Absolute (saccidānanda) has “involved” itself in matter, and evolution is its progressive self-revelation through matter, life and mind towards a “Supermind”, a truth-consciousness that links the infinite with the finite; his Integral Yoga aims not at escape from the world but at its transformation, and the goal is a divine life on earth. He criticised classical Advaita for its world-negation and argued that the Upaniṣads affirm both the transcendence and the immanence of Brahman. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan (1888–1975) gave an Advaita interpretation of Indian thought as a whole in dialogue with Western idealism, and his histories did much to fix the image of Indian philosophy as essentially spiritual that this volume questions (Chapter 1). Krishna Chandra Bhattacharyya (1875–1949), the most original of them, developed an interpretation of Advaita in dialogue with Kant, notably in The Subject as Freedom (1930): he distinguished bodily, psychic and spiritual levels of subjectivity, each involving a deeper freedom of the subject from its objects, by a method sometimes compared with phenomenology but developed largely independently of Husserl.

docs.title: 8.9 Comparison and Common Ground
docs.text:
Table 8.4 compares the schools discussed in this chapter.

Table 8.4. Comprehensive Comparison of Vedānta Sub-Schools Topic Dvaitādvaita Śuddhādvaita Acintya B.A. Śivādvaita Founder Nimbārka Vallabha Caitanya / Jīva G. Śrīkaṇṭha Brahman Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa Śiva World Real, dependent Real, part of God Real (energy of God) Real Jīva–Brahman Different & identical Part of Brahman Inconceivably both Dependent Mokṣa path Bhakti + jñāna Puṣṭi (grace) Prema-bhakti Śiva-bhakti Liberation Eternal service Loving service Prema (divine love) Union with Śiva

The schools share the authority of the prasthāna-traya, the reality of Brahman as the ultimate cause, the eternity of the individual self, the possibility of liberation, and the importance of hearing scripture and of spiritual discipline. They did not regard their disagreements as complementary perspectives: each argued that the others misread scripture. Modern Hindu thinkers have often cited the Gītā in support of a more inclusive reading:

The Gītā on the Ways to God

ye yathā māṃ prapadyante tāṃs tathaiva bhajāmy aham mama vartmānuvartante manuṣyāḥ pārtha sarvaśaḥ In whatever way people approach Me, in that same way do I favour them. People everywhere, O Pārtha, follow My path. — Bhagavad Gītā 4.11

docs.title: Chapter 9: Cārvāka — The Philosophy of Materialism
docs.text:
A Cārvāka Verse

yāvaj jīvaṃ sukhaṃ jīven nāsti mṛtyor agocaraḥ bhasmībhūtasya dehasya punarāgamanaṃ kutaḥ As long as you live, live happily; nothing escapes the eye of death. Once the body is reduced to ashes, how can it ever return? — Verse ascribed to the Cārvākas in Mādhava’s Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha, ch. 1 (the variant “ṛṇaṃ kṛtvā ghṛtaṃ pibet”, “borrow and drink ghee”, appears among the verses that close the same chapter)

docs.title: 9.1 Introduction: The Dissenting Voice
docs.text: In the Indian philosophical tradition the part of the materialist critic was played by the Cārvāka school, also known as Lokāyata (“prevalent among the people”, or “the worldly philosophy”) and as Bārhaspatya, after the legendary teacher Bṛhaspati. The name “Cārvāka” is of uncertain origin — it has been explained, probably fancifully, as cāru (pleasing) + vāk (speech), or as the name of a teacher — and is relatively late; older sources speak of Lokāyata. Hostile authors identified Bṛhaspati with the preceptor of the gods, who was said to have taught materialism deliberately to mislead the demons. The school is the most radical of the traditions Brahmanical authors called nāstika: it rejects not only the authority of the Veda but also the soul, God, karma, rebirth and any reality beyond the material world.

docs.title: 9.2 Sources and History
docs.text:
Historical Note: A Largely Lost Tradition

The foundational text of the school, a sūtra work ascribed to Bṛhaspati, is lost, together with its commentaries. About thirty of its aphorisms and some verses survive as quotations, which have been collected and studied by Ramkrishna Bhattacharya (Bhattacharya 2011). Most of our knowledge comes from opponents: Mādhava’s Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha (14th century), which devotes its first chapter to the Cārvākas; Haribhadra’s Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya (8th century); Śāntarakṣita’s Tattvasaṅgraha with Kamalaśīla’s commentary (8th century); and Jayanta Bhaṭṭa’s Nyāyamañjarī (9th century), which distinguishes “cunning” (dhūrta) from “educated” (suśikṣita) Cārvākas. One work from the materialist milieu survives complete, Jayarāśi Bhaṭṭa’s Tattvopaplavasiṃha (see below). The picture given by opponents is certainly partial and often hostile, and the task of a modern account is to recover the Cārvāka arguments from it.

Materialist and sceptical thought in India is old. The Buddhist Sāmaññaphala Sutta reports the materialist Ajita Kesakambalī, a contemporary of the Buddha, who taught that a person is made of four elements and is annihilated at death (on the other teachers of that text, see Section 1.3.4), and the Pāyāsi Sutta records a sceptical prince who tried to test the existence of the soul by experiment. The epics contain speeches arguing materialist positions, such as Jābāli’s in the Rāmāyaṇa, and the Arthaśāstra (1.2) lists Lokāyata, with Sāṃkhya and Yoga, as a form of critical inquiry (ānvīkṣikī). Vedic hymns such as the Nāsadīya express doubt about the origin of the world, but that is scepticism, not materialism.

docs.title: 9.2.1 Jayarāśi and the Tattvopaplavasiṃha
docs.text: The Tattvopaplavasiṃha (“The Lion that Overthrows All Principles”) of Jayarāśi Bhaṭṭa (c. 8th century CE) was rediscovered in the 20th century and published in 1940 in the Gaekwad’s Oriental Series. Jayarāśi invokes Bṛhaspati at the outset, but his work is a thoroughgoing scepticism rather than a positive materialism. He examines in turn the definitions of perception and other means of knowledge offered by the Naiyāyikas, Buddhists, Mīmāṃsakas, Sāṃkhyas and Jains, and argues that none of them can be defended. Since no means of knowledge is established, no “principles” (tattvas) are established either — not even the four elements of the materialists. Everyday life, however, goes on undisturbed: in a famous phrase, worldly practices are “delightful when not examined” (avicāritaramaṇīya). Eli Franco’s study has made the work central to the modern understanding of Indian scepticism (Franco 1987).

docs.title: 9.3 Knowledge: Perception and the Problem of Inference
docs.text:
The most famous Cārvāka thesis, as reported by opponents, is that perception is the only means of knowledge (Figure 9.1). Testimony is rejected because a speaker may be ignorant, deceived or deceitful, and the Veda has no special authority; comparison and the other means are reducible to perception or invalid. The serious work, however, was done in the critique of inference.

Figure 9.1. The early Cārvāka epistemological position as reported by its opponents (later Cārvākas accepted inference about perceptible things)

The argument, as Mādhava reports it, runs as follows. An inference depends on pervasion (vyāpti): one may infer fire from smoke only if one knows that wherever there is smoke there is fire. How is that known? Not by perception, which grasps only the cases before us, not all smoke past, present and future. Not by inference, since that inference would need a pervasion of its own, and a regress follows. Not by testimony, which on the Vaiśeṣika view is itself a form of inference, and on any view depends on knowing that the speaker is reliable. And the opponents’ own condition for a sound pervasion — that it be free of any hidden condition (upādhi) on which the concomitance really depends, as the smoke of a fire depends on wet fuel — cannot be shown to be met, since a condition may be present without being perceived. The relation of smoke to fire is therefore at best a matter of probability, and the inference to what cannot be perceived — a soul, a future life, God — has no support at all.

docs.title: 9.3.1 Objections and Replies
docs.text:
The other schools answered this critique, and it is the exchange, not the critique alone, that shows what was at stake. The answers are summarised in Table 9.1.

Table 9.1. Responses to the Cārvāka Critique of Inference School Response Nyāya Vyāpti is known from repeated observation of co-presence together with the absence of any observed counterexample, supported by tarka (reasoning showing that denying the vyāpti leads to absurdity); Navya-Nyāya adds an extraordinary perception of the universals smokeness and fireness (sāmānyalakṣaṇā) Buddhism (Dharmakīrti) Vyāpti is guaranteed by an essential connection (svabhāva-pratibandha) between reason and conclusion: either identity of nature (tādātmya) or causation (tadutpatti) Mīmāṃsā The Cārvāka himself uses inference in arguing against inference — a self-defeating move. The proposition “only perception is valid” cannot itself be established by perception alone Jainism Vyāpti is known by a distinct means of knowledge, tarka or ūha (inductive reasoning), not through exhaustive enumeration

The most common objection was that the Cārvāka refutes himself: to argue that inference is invalid he must infer, and the universal proposition “only perception is valid” cannot itself be perceived. The Cārvākas had two replies. The first was to qualify the thesis. Later Cārvākas, notably Purandara (c. 7th century), whose view Kamalaśīla reports, accepted inference about matters that can in principle be perceived — smoke and fire, the kind of thing on which everyday life depends — and rejected only inference to what lies beyond any possible perception (Bhattacharya 2011). On this position the charge of self-refutation simply misses its target: the Cārvāka uses only the kind of inference he accepts. The second reply was methodological. A critic who shows that the opponent’s own principles do not support the opponent’s conclusion is drawing out consequences (prasaṅga), not putting forward a thesis of his own; this was Jayarāśi’s procedure, and it anticipates the Madhyamaka and Advaita defences of refutation without a thesis (Section 13.8).

The positive accounts of pervasion met rejoinders too. Nyāya held that pervasion is known from repeated observation together with the absence of any observed counter-example, supported by suppositional reasoning (tarka) and, in Navya-Nyāya, by an extraordinary perception of the universals smokeness and fireness. The Cārvāka could answer, and the reported arguments imply, that no counter-example so far is not the same as none, that suppositional reasoning itself presupposes some pervasion, and that the extraordinary perception was introduced precisely because ordinary perception could not do the work. Dharmakīrti’s appeal to an essential connection of identity or causation (Chapter 10) moves the problem rather than solving it, for the Cārvāka can ask how causal connections themselves are known, if not from observed regularities. The exchange is summarised, with the other main points of dispute, in Figure 9.2.

Figure 9.2. Four objections to the Cārvāka and the replies reported in the sources (simplified)

The argument is often compared with David Hume’s problem of induction (1739). The comparison is apt in one respect and misleading in another. Like Hume, the Cārvāka denies that any number of observed instances can guarantee a universal rule. Unlike Hume, who concluded that inductive inference rests on custom but did not propose to abandon it, the Cārvāka in Purandara’s form draws a line within inference itself: inference is acceptable where its conclusion could be checked by perception and unacceptable where it could not. That is closer to a verification principle than to Humean scepticism, and it explains why the debate in India was not about induction in general but about the unseen — the self, karma and the other world.

docs.title: 9.4 Metaphysics: Matter Alone Is Real
docs.text:
The Cārvākas recognised four elements — earth, water, fire and air — as the constituents of everything; ether (ākāśa) was rejected by some of them because it is not perceptible. Consciousness is not a separate substance, as in Nyāya or Sāṃkhya, but a property that arises from the elements when they combine in the form of a living body. The surviving aphorisms put it thus:

Consciousness from Matter

pṛthivy āpas tejo vāyur iti tattvāni tebhyaś caitanyam kiṇvādibhyo madaśaktivat Earth, water, fire and air are the principles. From them arises consciousness, like the power of intoxication from yeast and other ingredients. — Aphorisms of the lost Bṛhaspati sūtra, as quoted by opponents

The self, accordingly, is nothing but the body. In Mādhava’s summary, “the self is simply the body qualified by consciousness” (caitanyaviśiṣṭadeha evātmā), and the Cārvāka appealed to ordinary speech in support: we call ourselves fat or thin, or say that we are walking, attributing to the self what belongs to the body. There is no God; things act according to their own nature (svabhāva) — fire is hot and water cool, and no one made them so. There is no karma and no rebirth: when the body dies, the person ceases to exist, and heaven and hell are inventions. Not all materialists, however, identified the self with the gross body. Later Vedāntic doxography distinguishes several positions by what they took the self to be (Table 9.2).

Table 9.2. Varieties of Cārvāka / Lokāyata Thought Position View on Self Details Dehātma­vāda Body is the self The gross physical body is the self; death is the end of the person Indriyātma­vāda Senses are the self The sense organs constitute the self; a variant materialist position Prāṇātma­vāda Life-breath is the self The vital force (prāṇa) is the self; slightly more refined materialism Mana-ātma­vāda Mind is the self The internal organ (manas), itself regarded as material, is the self

docs.title: 9.4.1 The Debate over Consciousness
docs.text:
Here too the opponents’ objections and the Cārvāka replies are best read together. The first objection was that consciousness differs in kind from matter, so that no arrangement of unconscious elements can produce awareness.
