The Cārvāka reply is the analogy of the aphorism: the intoxicating power of liquor is present in none of its ingredients, yet arises when they are fermented together; a property absent from the parts can belong to their combination. The reply had force against the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣikas in particular, who themselves held that wholes have qualities their parts lack and that heat produces new qualities in fired clay (Chapter 3). The second objection was that a corpse has all the elements of the body and no consciousness. The reply was that consciousness belongs to the body in a particular state, the living body with its breath and organisation, not to the elements as such. A third objection appealed to rebirth: a newborn infant seeks the breast, which shows a desire learned in a previous life. The Nyāya Sūtra itself records an answer of the materialist kind, that the infant moves towards the breast by its nature, as iron moves towards a magnet, and then argues against it (3.1.21–24). Dharmakīrti pressed the most systematic objection: each moment of consciousness must have a prior moment of consciousness as its material cause, so that consciousness cannot begin from the body and must continue beyond it (Chapter 10); the Cārvāka view is precisely that the body is consciousness’s material cause.

Neither side could claim a decisive victory. The opponents’ strongest point was the apparent difference in kind between awareness and anything physical; the Cārvākas’ was that every case of consciousness we know of depends on a living body, and that the appeal to a difference in kind assumes what it needs to prove. Modern philosophy of mind continues the same dispute between emergentist and dualist accounts with far more developed arguments, and the classical exchange is best read as an early round of it, not as settled in either direction.

docs.title: 9.5 Ethics: The Pursuit of Happiness
docs.text: If there is no soul, no karma and no other world, the purpose of life is happiness in this one. The Cārvākas, as their opponents report them, recognised only pleasure (kāma) and wealth (artha) as human goals, and dismissed dharma and liberation as fictions. The obvious objection, made by almost every other school, was that pleasure is always mixed with pain, so that a wise person should seek the end of pain rather than pleasure. Mādhava reports the Cārvāka reply: one does not throw away rice because it comes in a husk, or refuse fish because they have scales and bones; one takes the good and removes what is not. The objection that a life of pleasure “leads to suffering” begs the question in the context of this debate, since it presupposes the karmic and otherworldly consequences that the Cārvāka denies. The reply also shows that Cārvāka ethics need not be crude hedonism: it is a prudential ethics of enjoyment with care, and Jayanta’s distinction between “cunning” and “educated” Cārvākas suggests that some of them held a considered moral view, not merely licence.

docs.title: 9.6 Critique of Vedic Rituals and Priesthood
docs.text:
Cārvāka’s critique of Vedic religion is sharp and often satirical:

  • If the sacrificial animal reaches heaven when killed in a ritual, why don’t the priests sacrifice their own fathers?

  • If śrāddha (ancestral rites) nourish the dead, why do travellers take provisions for the road? Their relatives could simply make offerings for them at home

  • “The three authors of the Vedas were buffoons, knaves and demons” (trayo vedasya kartāro bhaṇḍa-dhūrta-niśācarāḥ), who invented rituals to earn their livelihood

These satirical verses are quoted in the Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha. However unfair they may be, they forced the orthodox schools to defend their doctrines.

docs.title: 9.7 The Cārvāka in Indian Thought
docs.text:
Mādhava’s Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha begins with the Cārvākas and arranges the systems in an ascending order, each criticised from the standpoint of the next, that points towards Advaita Vedānta (the work itself ends with Yoga; for Śaṅkara’s system the reader is referred elsewhere). The Cārvāka texts were not preserved, and the school survived chiefly as a target of refutation. Yet the target shaped those who aimed at it. The insistence on perceptual evidence forced Nyāya, Buddhist and Jain logicians to state how pervasion is known; the attack on the soul made the arguments for a self explicit; the satire of ritual pressed the Mīmāṃsakas to defend the authority of the Veda; and the fact that the other schools spent so much effort refuting the Cārvākas is the best evidence of their intellectual seriousness.

Modern readers have compared the school with empiricism, positivism, Epicurean ethics and the Enlightenment critique of religion. Such comparisons are suggestive but should not obscure the differences. The Cārvāka was defined by its opposition to specifically Indian doctrines — karma, liberation, Vedic authority — and it took part in the common culture of debate rather than standing outside it. In the twentieth century Marxist and rationalist scholars such as Debiprasad Chattopadhyaya (Lokāyata, 1959) revived interest in it as an Indian materialist heritage (Chattopadhyaya 1959), and the philological work of Franco and Bhattacharya has since separated what can be known of the school from what its opponents imagined (Franco 1987; Bhattacharya 2011).

docs.title: Chapter 10: Buddhist Philosophy — The Middle Way
docs.text:
The Dhammapada

sabbapāpassa akaraṇaṃ, kusalassa upasampadā sacittapariyodapanaṃ, etaṃ buddhāna sāsanaṃ To refrain from all evil, to cultivate the good, to purify one’s mind — this is the teaching of the Buddhas. — Dhammapada 183

docs.title: 10.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Buddhist philosophy (Bauddha darśana) is one of the richest and longest-lived traditions of Indian thought. For more than fifteen hundred years Buddhist thinkers in India debated among themselves and with Brahmanical and Jain opponents, and many of the central problems of Indian philosophy — the nature of the self, the reality of universals, the criteria of valid knowledge, the analysis of causation — were set by Buddhist arguments. Indian Buddhism also gave rise to the philosophical traditions of Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia, Tibet, China, Korea and Japan.

This chapter outlines the early teachings, the Abhidharma schools, the two great Mahāyāna philosophies (Madhyamaka and Yogācāra), and the epistemological school of Dignāga and Dharmakīrti, before turning to ethics, the debate with Brahmanical schools, and the decline of Buddhism in India. Buddhist and Jain traditions as religions and institutions are treated in Vol. 4 of this series (Gethin 1998; Williams and Tribe 2000; Siderits 2007).

Brahmanical authors classified Buddhism as nāstika because it does not accept the authority of the Veda. Buddhists did not use this label of themselves; they saw their teaching (dharma) as the rediscovery, by an awakened human being, of the way things are.

Historical Note: The Buddha — The Awakened One

Siddhārtha Gautama of the Śākya clan was born, according to tradition, at Lumbinī (in present-day Nepal). Most scholars now favour a “short chronology” placing his death c. 400 BCE (lifetime c. 480–400 BCE); older scholarship followed the “long chronology” (c. 563–483 BCE), and the traditional Theravāda dating is 624–544 BCE. According to the traditional accounts he renounced household life, practised severe asceticism, abandoned it as fruitless, and attained awakening (bodhi) under a tree at Bodh Gayā. He then taught for some forty-five years in the Ganges plain. His teachings were transmitted orally and later written down in Pali (the Tipiṭaka of the Theravāda) and in Sanskrit and other Indian languages, much of which survives only in Chinese and Tibetan translation.

Figure 10.1 shows the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gayā.

Figure 10.1. The Bodhi tree beside the Mahābodhi temple at Bodh Gayā, the traditional site of the Buddha’s awakening Photo: Sumitsurai, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 10.2.1 The Four Noble Truths (Catvāry Āryasatyāni)
docs.text:
According to tradition, the Buddha’s first sermon (the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, Saṃyutta Nikāya 56.11) taught a “middle way” between sensual indulgence and self-mortification, and four truths:

The Four Noble Truths

  1. Duḥkha (Suffering) — Life, as ordinarily lived, is characterized by suffering and unsatisfactoriness: birth, ageing, sickness, death, separation from the loved, and, in short, the five aggregates of grasping

  2. Samudaya (Origin) — Suffering arises from tṛṣṇā (craving, “thirst”) — craving for sensual pleasure, for existence, and for non-existence

  3. Nirodha (Cessation) — Suffering can cease; nirvāṇa (“blowing out” of greed, hatred and delusion) is attainable

  4. Mārga (Path) — The Noble Eightfold Path (āryāṣṭāṅgika mārga) is the way to cessation

docs.title: 10.2.2 Dependent Origination (Pratītyasamutpāda)
docs.text:
For the philosophers, dependent origination is the doctrine on which everything else turns, since it replaces both a permanent self and a creator with a network of conditions. Its abstract formula recurs throughout the early discourses (its place in the Buddha’s teaching as a religious path is described in Vol. 4, Buddha–Jina Prabhā):

Dependent Origination

imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti, imassuppādā idaṃ uppajjati imasmiṃ asati idaṃ na hoti, imassa nirodhā idaṃ nirujjhati When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases. — e.g. Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.21; Majjhima Nikāya 38

Nothing that we experience exists independently; everything arises in dependence upon conditions. Applied to the human situation, the principle is set out in a chain of twelve links (nidānas), which later tradition interpreted as spanning three lives (Table 10.1):

Table 10.1. The Twelve Links of Dependent Origination No. Sanskrit Pali Meaning 1 Avidyā Avijjā Ignorance (of the four truths) 2 Saṃskāra Saṅkhāra Volitional formations 3 Vijñāna Viññāṇa Consciousness 4 Nāmarūpa Nāmarūpa Name-and-form (mind and body) 5 Ṣaḍāyatana Saḷāyatana The six sense-bases 6 Sparśa Phassa Contact 7 Vedanā Vedanā Feeling 8 Tṛṣṇā Taṇhā Craving 9 Upādāna Upādāna Grasping 10 Bhava Bhava Becoming 11 Jāti Jāti Birth 12 Jarāmaraṇa Jarāmaraṇa Ageing and death

docs.title: 10.2.3 The Three Marks and the Five Aggregates
docs.text:
All conditioned things share three marks (trilakṣaṇa):

  1. Anitya (Pali anicca, impermanence) — All conditioned phenomena are impermanent

  2. Duḥkha (dukkha, unsatisfactoriness) — All conditioned phenomena are unsatisfactory

  3. Anātman (anattā, non-self) — No phenomenon is a permanent, unchanging self

The doctrine of anātman is the most philosophically consequential Buddhist teaching, directly challenging the ātman doctrines of the Upaniṣads, Sāṃkhya, Nyāya and Vedānta. A person is analysed into five aggregates (skandhas): material form (rūpa), feeling (vedanā), perception or recognition (saṃjñā), volitional formations (saṃskāra) and consciousness (vijñāna). In the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta (Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.59) the Buddha argues that none of these can be the self: each is impermanent, and each is subject to affliction and not under our control, whereas a self would be permanent and under our control. Nor is there a self apart from them.

The best-known illustration is the chariot simile, used by the nun Vajirā in the Saṃyutta Nikāya (5.10) and developed in the Milindapañha: just as “chariot” is a name for an assemblage of parts, none of which is the chariot, so “person” is a conventional designation for the aggregates. The person is real as a convention, not as an ultimate entity. Buddhism thus steers a “middle way” between eternalism (śāśvatavāda, a permanent self) and annihilationism (uccheda­vāda, nothing continues). Karma, defined as intention (cetanā, Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.63), connects one life to the next through a causal stream, without a transmigrating self.

The Buddha also refused to answer certain speculative questions — whether the world is eternal, whether the soul is the same as the body, whether the Tathāgata exists after death — declaring them “undetermined” (avyākṛta) and unprofitable for the path.

docs.title: 10.3 Early Schools and the Abhidharma
docs.text: Within two centuries of the Buddha’s death the community had divided, first into the Sthaviras (“Elders”) and the Mahāsāṅghikas, and later into the traditional “eighteen schools”. Their disputes concerned monastic discipline and doctrine, and their most important philosophical achievement was the Abhidharma (“higher teaching”): the systematic analysis of experience into its ultimate constituents, the dharmas.

docs.title: 10.3.1 The Abhidharma Project
docs.text: Abhidharma thinkers distinguished conventional truths, which concern composite things like persons and chariots, from ultimate truths, which concern the momentary dharmas of which composites are made. Each dharma is defined by its “own nature” (svabhāva) or own characteristic. The Pali Abhidhamma of the Theravāda (seven canonical books, interpreted by Buddhaghosa in the 5th century CE and summarised in later manuals such as Anuruddha’s Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha) recognises four kinds of ultimate reality: consciousness (citta), mental factors (cetasika), matter (rūpa) and nibbāna.

docs.title: 10.3.2 Sarvāstivāda (Vaibhāṣika)
docs.text:
The Sarvāstivāda school, powerful in north-western India and Kashmir, is named after its thesis that “everything exists” (sarvam asti) in all three times: past and future dharmas exist as well as present ones. Its followers argued that past dharmas must exist because they can be objects of cognition and because past actions bear fruit. The great commentary, the Mahāvibhāṣā (c. 2nd century CE), gave the school its later name, Vaibhāṣika. The Sarvāstivādins classified 75 dharmas in five groups (Table 10.2):

Table 10.2. The Seventy-five Dharmas of the Sarvāstivāda Group Number Content Rūpa (matter) 11 Five sense organs, five sense objects, and “unmanifest” matter Citta (mind) 1 Consciousness Caitasika (mental factors) 46 Feeling, perception, intention, attention, faith, greed, hatred, etc. Cittaviprayukta saṃskāra (forces dissociated from mind) 14 Acquisition, origination, duration, decay, impermanence, life-force, etc. Asaṃskṛta (unconditioned) 3 Space and two kinds of cessation (one of them nirvāṇa)

docs.title: 10.3.3 Sautrāntika and the Doctrine of Momentariness
docs.text:
The Sautrāntikas (“those who follow the sūtras”) rejected the Sarvāstivāda thesis: only the present moment exists, and dharmas perish as soon as they arise. They held that we never perceive external objects directly; consciousness takes on the “form” (ākāra) of the object, and the object itself is inferred as the cause of that form. The doctrine of universal momentariness (kṣaṇikavāda) became a hallmark of later Buddhist philosophy: since destruction needs no cause, whatever exists perishes in the very moment after it arises. Later epistemologists argued that to exist is to be causally efficacious (arthakriyā), and that only momentary things can be efficacious; Ratnakīrti (11th century) summarised the thesis as “whatever exists is momentary”.

Vasubandhu’s Abhidharmakośa (c. 4th–5th century CE), whose verses summarise Vaibhāṣika doctrine while its auto-commentary (bhāṣya) often criticises it from a Sautrāntika standpoint, became the standard Abhidharma textbook in India, Tibet and East Asia (Gold 2015).

docs.title: 10.3.4 The Personalists (Pudgalavāda)
docs.text: One group of schools, the Vātsīputrīyas and Sāmmitīyas, held that there is a “person” (pudgala) that is neither identical with nor different from the aggregates — a position they thought necessary to explain memory, karma and rebirth. Other Buddhists regarded this as a covert return to the self; Vasubandhu devoted the ninth chapter of the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya to refuting it. The Sāmmitīyas were nonetheless among the largest schools of India, according to the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang (7th century).

docs.title: 10.4 The Major Philosophical Schools in Later Classification
docs.text:
Later Indian and Tibetan doxographies, and Brahmanical surveys such as the Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha, reduced the variety of Buddhist thought to four “schools”. The scheme is a simplification, but it is widely used (Figure 10.2):

Figure 10.2. The four Buddhist “schools” of later doxography (a simplification of a much more varied tradition)

docs.title: 10.5.1 The Mahāyāna
docs.text: From around the 1st century BCE new sūtras appeared that presented themselves as the word of the Buddha and taught the path of the bodhisattva, who seeks full Buddhahood for the sake of all beings, rather than the arhat’s personal liberation. The earliest of these, the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā) sūtras, taught that all dharmas, including those of the Abhidharma lists, are “empty” (śūnya). Mahāyāna was for centuries a minority movement within monasteries that also housed non-Mahāyāna monks.

docs.title: 10.5.2 Nāgārjuna
docs.text:
Nāgārjuna (c. 2nd century CE), probably a monk of south India, gave the doctrine of emptiness philosophical form in the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā (“Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way”, 27 chapters) and shorter works such as the Vigrahavyāvartanī (Garfield 1995; Westerhoff 2009). His target is the Abhidharma notion of svabhāva, “own-being” or intrinsic nature. If a thing had intrinsic nature, it would be independent of causes and conditions; but everything that exists arises dependently; therefore nothing has intrinsic nature. The work opens with a fourfold denial of origination:

The Opening Verse of the Madhyamaka

na svato nāpi parato na dvābhyāṃ nāpy ahetutaḥ utpannā jātu vidyante bhāvāḥ kva cana ke cana Not from themselves, not from another, not from both, nor without a cause do any entities whatever, anywhere, ever arise. — Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 1.1

Nāgārjuna’s characteristic method is to show that every view which assumes intrinsic natures — about causation, motion, time, the self, the aggregates, even nirvāṇa — leads to absurd consequences (prasaṅga). He often examines four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi): that something is, is not, both, or neither, and rejects all four.

Śūnyatā — Emptiness

  • All phenomena (dharmas) are empty (śūnya) of intrinsic existence (svabhāva)

  • Emptiness is not non-existence: things exist conventionally, as dependently arisen

  • Emptiness is dependent origination — two descriptions of the same fact (verse below)

  • Emptiness is itself empty: it is not a hidden absolute behind appearances

  • The two truths: saṃvṛti-satya (conventional truth) and paramārtha-satya (ultimate truth); “without relying on the conventional, the ultimate is not taught” (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 24.10)

Nāgārjuna’s Central Verse

yaḥ pratītyasamutpādaḥ śūnyatāṃ tāṃ pracakṣmahe sā prajñaptir upādāya pratipat saiva madhyamā What is dependent origination, that we declare to be emptiness. It is a dependent designation and is itself the Middle Way. — Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 24.18

Opponents — Naiyāyikas, Mīmāṃsakas and other Buddhists — accused Nāgārjuna of nihilism and of self-refutation: if all statements are empty, so is the statement that all things are empty. In the Vigrahavyāvartanī (verse 29) he replies that he has no thesis of his own (nāsti ca mama pratijñā) that could be refuted; his arguments work by drawing out the consequences of his opponents’ assumptions. The Nyāya Sūtra itself seems to respond to such arguments, which is one reason for dating its final redaction after Nāgārjuna.

docs.title: 10.5.3 Later Madhyamaka
docs.text: Nāgārjuna’s disciple Āryadeva wrote the Catuḥśataka. In the 6th century Bhāviveka argued that Mādhyamikas may advance independent (svatantra) inferences of their own, while Buddhapālita and, in the 7th century, Candrakīrti (Prasannapadā, Madhyamakāvatāra) held that the Mādhyamika should only draw out the absurd consequences (prasaṅga) of others’ views. The labels “Svātantrika” and “Prāsaṅgika” for these positions were coined later in Tibet. Śāntideva (8th century) expressed Madhyamaka ethics and the bodhisattva ideal in the Bodhicaryāvatāra.

docs.title: 10.5.4 Śāntarakṣita and Kamalaśīla
docs.text: Śāntarakṣita (c. 725–788) combined Madhyamaka with Yogācāra and with Dharmakīrti’s epistemology in the Madhyamakālaṅkāra. His Tattvasaṅgraha, with the commentary of his pupil Kamalaśīla, is an encyclopaedic critique of every rival school — Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika categories and theism, Sāṃkhya’s prakṛti, Mīmāṃsā’s authorless Veda and the eternity of sound, Jain anekānta, the Cārvākas, and the Buddhist Personalists — and is one of our best sources for the doctrines of the period. Both men travelled to Tibet, where Śāntarakṣita helped found the first monastery at Samye.

docs.title: 10.6 Yogācāra (Vijñānavāda)
docs.text:
The Yogācāra (“practice of yoga”) school takes its name from the meditative experience of its founders; it is also called Vijñānavāda (“doctrine of consciousness”). Its scriptural basis is the Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra; its classical authors are Asaṅga (Yogācārabhūmi, Mahāyānasaṃgraha) and Vasubandhu (Viṃśatikā, Triṃśikā, Trisvabhāvanirdeśa), traditionally brothers, of the 4th–5th century CE. Some works are ascribed to Maitreya, whom tradition regards as a celestial bodhisattva and some scholars as a human teacher.

Yogācāra: “Mind Only”

  • Vijñaptimātratā (“mere representation”) — What we experience as external objects are representations in consciousness; there are no material objects existing apart from the mind

  • The ālayavijñāna (store-consciousness) — A subliminal stream of consciousness that holds the “seeds” (bīja) left by past actions and experiences, from which future experiences ripen

  • Eight consciousnesses: the five sense-consciousnesses, mental consciousness (manovijñāna), the afflicted mind (kliṣṭa manas) that mistakes the store-consciousness for a self, and the store-consciousness itself

  • The three natures (trisvabhāva): the imagined (parikalpita) nature of subject and object as separate; the dependent (paratantra) nature, the causal flow of experience; and the perfected (pariniṣpanna) nature, the dependent nature empty of the imagined duality

In the Viṃśatikā (“Twenty Verses”) Vasubandhu answers the objection that, if there are no external objects, experience could not be fixed in place and time, shared by several people, or causally effective. Dreams, he replies, show all three features: dream objects appear at particular places and times; hungry ghosts (pretas) collectively see a river of pus where humans see water; and dream experiences can have real bodily effects. He then argues that external objects cannot be made of atoms, since a partless atom cannot combine with others to form an extended body (see Chapter 3).

Whether Yogācāra is an “idealism” in the Western sense is debated by modern scholars: some read it as metaphysical idealism, others as an epistemological or phenomenological analysis of experience that brackets the question of external objects. The school’s doctrine of the reflexive awareness of consciousness (svasaṃvedana) was taken up by Dignāga and Dharmakīrti. Through Xuanzang’s translations, Yogācāra became the basis of the East Asian Faxiang school.

docs.title: 10.7 Buddhist Epistemology: Dignāga and Dharmakīrti
docs.text:
From the 5th century onwards the Buddhist “epistemological school” (pramāṇavāda) transformed Indian philosophy. Its founders were:

  • Dignāga (c. 480–540 CE) — Author of the Pramāṇasamuccaya with its auto-commentary, the Nyāyamukha and the Ālambanaparīkṣā (Hattori 1968; Hayes 1988)

  • Dharmakīrti (6th–7th century; often dated c. 600–660 CE, though some recent scholars place him c. 550–610) — Author of the Pramāṇavārttika, Pramāṇaviniścaya and Nyāyabindu, the most influential work of Buddhist epistemology (Dunne 2004)

Their successors included Dharmottara, Prajñākaragupta, Jñānaśrīmitra and Ratnakīrti (10th–11th centuries), who defended momentariness and the apoha theory against Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā critics.

docs.title: 10.7.1 Two Means of Knowledge for Two Kinds of Object
docs.text:
Dignāga argued that there are exactly two means of knowledge because there are exactly two kinds of object: the unique, momentary particular (svalakṣaṇa), which is real and causally efficacious, and the general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa), which is a mental construction. Perception grasps the first, inference the second.

Buddhist Epistemology

  1. Pratyakṣa (Perception) — “Perception is free from conceptual construction” (pratyakṣaṃ kalpanāpoḍham, Dignāga, Pramāṇasamuccaya 1.3). It is a direct, non-conceptual awareness of the particular. Dharmakīrti adds that it must also be non-erroneous, and recognises four kinds: sense perception, mental perception, reflexive self-awareness (svasaṃvedana) and yogic perception

  2. Anumāna (Inference) — Conceptual, indirect knowledge through a logical mark. Inference grasps a general characteristic, which is a construction, not a real universal; yet it leads indirectly to the real, as when one infers fire and finds it

Testimony and the other pramāṇas of the Brahmanical schools are treated as forms of inference or rejected. Dharmakīrti defines a means of knowledge as “non-deceptive cognition” (pramāṇam avisaṃvādi jñānam, Pramāṇavārttika 2.1), i.e. cognition that does not let us down in practical action.

The definition of perception as kalpanāpoḍha is Dignāga’s, not Nyāya’s; Naiyāyikas such as Uddyotakara and Vācaspati criticised it, though they came to recognise an initial non-conceptual stage (nirvikalpaka) of perception in their own terms.

docs.title: 10.7.2 The Triple Mark of a Valid Reason
docs.text:
Dignāga formulated the conditions of a valid reason as three marks (trairūpya):

  1. Pakṣadharmatva — the reason is present in the subject (smoke is on the hill);

  2. Sapakṣe sattvam — it is present in at least some similar instances (smoke in a kitchen, where there is fire);

  3. Vipakṣe asattvam — it is absent from all dissimilar instances (no smoke in a lake, where there is no fire).

His “wheel of reasons” (hetucakra) systematically classified the nine possible combinations of presence and absence in similar and dissimilar instances, showing which yield valid reasons. Dharmakīrti went further: the third mark can be guaranteed only if the reason is essentially connected (svabhāva-pratibandha) to what is proved, either by identity of nature (tādātmya) — “this is a tree, because it is a śiṃśapā” — or by causation (tadutpatti) — “there is fire, because there is smoke”. To these two kinds of reason he added a third, non-perception (anupalabdhi), for proving absence.

In an argument for others (parārthānumāna), Dignāga required a thesis, a reason and an example; the example statement already contains the universal rule (“wherever there is smoke there is fire, as in a kitchen”), so that the Nyāya’s application and conclusion are redundant. Dharmakīrti held that even the thesis need not be stated: the reason and the pervasion suffice.

docs.title: 10.7.3 The Doctrine of Apoha (Exclusion)
docs.text:
Dignāga’s theory of apoha is a landmark in the philosophy of language:

  • Words do not denote real universals, since there are none

  • A word like “cow” functions by excluding what is not a cow: its meaning is “exclusion of others” (anyāpoha)

  • The theory allows Buddhist nominalism to explain language without positing real universals

Kumārila and the Naiyāyikas objected that knowing “this is not a non-cow” presupposes knowing what a cow is. Dharmakīrti and later Buddhists (Śāntarakṣita, Ratnakīrti) refined the theory, explaining exclusion in terms of conceptual images formed from experiences of particulars that have the same effects.

docs.title: 10.7.4 Rebirth, Omniscience and God
docs.text: The epistemologists also used their logic in defence of Buddhist doctrine. In the second chapter of the Pramāṇavārttika, Dharmakīrti argues against the materialists that consciousness cannot arise from matter alone, since each moment of consciousness must have a prior moment of consciousness as its material cause — hence rebirth. He argues that the Buddha is a reliable authority (pramāṇabhūta) because his teaching on the matters that count for liberation is non-deceptive, and he and his successors rejected Nyāya’s arguments for a creator God.

docs.title: 10.8.1 The Eightfold Path
docs.text:
The Buddhist path to liberation consists of eight factors, grouped into three trainings (Table 10.3):

Table 10.3. The Noble Eightfold Path Training No. Factor Description Prajñā (Wisdom) 1 Samyag-dṛṣṭi Right View 2 Samyak-saṅkalpa Right Intention Śīla (Ethics) 3 Samyag-vāc Right Speech 4 Samyak-karmānta Right Action 5 Samyag-ājīva Right Livelihood Samādhi (Meditation) 6 Samyag-vyāyāma Right Effort 7 Samyak-smṛti Right Mindfulness 8 Samyak-samādhi Right Concentration

docs.title: 10.8.2 The Bodhisattva Path
docs.text: Mahāyāna ethics centres on the bodhisattva, who generates the “mind of awakening” (bodhicitta) and practises six perfections (pāramitās): generosity, ethical conduct, patience, vigour, meditation and wisdom. Compassion (karuṇā) and wisdom (prajñā) are described as the two wings of the path; Śāntideva argues that, since there is no self, there is no reason to prefer my own suffering’s removal to anyone else’s.

docs.title: 10.8.3 Caste and Gender
docs.text: The early texts contain sharp criticism of brahmin claims to superiority by birth. In the Assālāyana Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya 93) and the Vāseṭṭha Sutta the Buddha argues that one is a true brahmin by conduct, not birth, and the order admitted members of all classes. The Vajrasūcī, a critique of caste ascribed to Aśvaghoṣa (attribution disputed), carries the argument further. The Buddha also founded an order of nuns, whose verses survive in the Therīgāthā, one of the earliest collections of women’s religious poetry in the world; the monastic rules, however, subordinated nuns to monks through the “eight heavy rules” (garudhammas). Buddhist societies did not abolish caste or gender hierarchy, but the tradition provided resources for criticising them that B.R. Ambedkar later drew on (Ambedkar 1957; Gethin 1998).

docs.title: 10.9 The Debate with Brahmanical Schools
docs.text: The interaction between Buddhist and Brahmanical philosophers produced some of the finest argumentation in Indian history. Its main issues — the self against the causal stream, real universals against exclusion, enduring things against momentariness, the number of means of knowledge, the intrinsic validity claimed for the Veda, and the existence of God and of an omniscient teacher — are taken up from the Brahmanical side in the chapters on Nyāya (Section 2.9) and Mīmāṃsā (Section 6.13) and compared in Chapter 13. The debate was not one-sided. Dharmakīrti’s successors answered Kumārila and Uddyotakara point by point; Udayana’s Ātmatattvaviveka (“Discrimination of the Truth about the Self”) is largely a refutation of Ratnakīrti and his predecessors; and the Śaiva non-dualists built their theory of the self from Buddhist materials (Chapter 12). The arguments of each side are hard to understand without those of the other (Matilal 1986).

docs.title: 10.10 The Decline of Buddhism in India
docs.text:
Buddhism declined in most of India between the 7th and the 13th centuries, though it survived much longer in Bengal, Bihar, Odisha, Kashmir and the Himalayan regions. Historians attribute the decline to several interacting causes rather than to any single event:

  • Institutional concentration: late Indian Buddhism was concentrated in large monasteries dependent on royal patronage, with relatively weak ties to lay communities; when patronage shifted, these institutions were vulnerable

  • Competition and assimilation: devotional Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava movements and Brahmanical temple religion attracted lay support, and Buddhist practices and figures were absorbed into Hindu worship (the Buddha was even counted as an avatāra of Viṣṇu)

  • Philosophical and polemical pressure: Brahmanical philosophers answered Buddhist arguments in detail, although later hagiographies greatly exaggerate the role of individuals such as Kumārila and Śaṅkara

  • Destruction of monasteries: the great monastic centres of Bihar and Bengal — Nālandā, Vikramaśilā, Odantapurī — were sacked by Turkic armies around 1200 CE, and monks fled to Nepal and Tibet; this ended an already weakened institutional tradition

Buddhism continued in Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia, the Himalayas, Tibet and East Asia. In India it revived in the modern period through the work of Anagārika Dharmapāla’s Maha Bodhi Society (founded 1891) and, above all, through B.R. Ambedkar, who converted to Buddhism at Nagpur on 14 October 1956 together with a very large number of followers, mostly from communities treated as “untouchable”. His The Buddha and His Dhamma presents Buddhism as a rational and egalitarian social philosophy (Ambedkar 1957).

docs.title: 10.11 Legacy and Influence
docs.text: Nāgārjuna’s critique of intrinsic nature is one of the most radical arguments in the history of philosophy, and Dignāga and Dharmakīrti reshaped the agenda of Indian epistemology: Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Jain logic and Kashmiri Śaivism all developed in response to them. Outside India, Buddhist philosophy shaped the intellectual traditions of Tibet, China, Korea, Japan and Southeast Asia, and contemporary philosophers engage its arguments on personal identity, part and whole, consciousness and language (Siderits 2007). Its relations to Yoga (Chapter 5) and to Jain philosophy (Chapter 11) are discussed in those chapters.

docs.title: Chapter 11: Jain Philosophy — The Doctrine of Many-Sidedness
docs.text:
Tattvārthasūtra

parasparopagraho jīvānām Souls render service to one another. — Tattvārthasūtra 5.21

docs.title: 11.1 Introduction: The Path of the Conquerors
docs.text:
The Jain philosophical tradition (Jaina darśana) derives its name from Jina (“conqueror”) — one who has conquered attachment and aversion and attained omniscience. Its followers were earlier called Nirgranthas (“those without bonds”). Like Buddhism, Jainism was classified by Brahmanical authors as nāstika because it does not accept the authority of the Vedas. It developed one of the most systematic metaphysics in India, an original logic of perspectives, and an ethics of non-violence of exceptional rigour (Dundas 2002; Jaini 1979).

Three related doctrines are especially associated with Jain philosophy:

  1. Anekāntavāda — The doctrine that reality is many-sided (“non-one-sidedness”)

  2. Syādvāda — The doctrine of qualified, conditional predication

  3. Nayavāda — The doctrine of partial standpoints

Historical Note: Mahāvīra and the Tīrthaṅkaras

Jain tradition recognises twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras (“ford-makers”) in the present cosmic age. The twenty-second and earlier figures belong to mythic time. The twenty-third, Pārśva, is probably historical and is placed about 250 years before Mahāvīra. The twenty-fourth, Vardhamāna Mahāvīra, was an older contemporary of the Buddha; Jain tradition dates him 599–527 BCE, but most scholars place him later, in the 5th century BCE, in line with the revised chronology of the Buddha. The early Buddhist canon mentions him as Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.

The community later divided into the Śvetāmbaras (“white-clad”) and the Digambaras (“sky-clad”, whose monks go naked), a division that crystallised in the first centuries CE. The Śvetāmbaras preserve a canon of Āgamas in Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit, finally redacted at the council of Valabhī in the 5th century CE; the Digambaras hold that the original canon was lost and rely on later works such as the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and the treatises of Kundakunda.

docs.text:
Table 11.1 lists the major texts and thinkers.

docs.title: 11.2 Umāsvāti and the Tattvārthasūtra
docs.text:
The Tattvārthasūtra (“Sūtra on the Meaning of the Principles”) of Umāsvāti is the only Jain text accepted as authoritative by both Śvetāmbaras and Digambaras, although they read it in slightly different recensions and with different commentaries (the Śvetāmbara Svopajñabhāṣya, ascribed to the author himself, and the Digambara Sarvārthasiddhi of Pūjyapāda). Written in Sanskrit sūtra style, in ten chapters, it did for Jainism what the sūtra texts did for the Brahmanical schools: it summarised the doctrine of the scattered canon in a systematic form (Umāsvāti 1994). It opens:

The Path to Liberation

samyag-darśana-jñāna-cāritrāṇi mokṣa-mārgaḥ Right faith, right knowledge and right conduct together constitute the path to liberation. — Tattvārthasūtra 1.1

These “three jewels” (ratnatraya) must be present together: knowledge without conduct, or conduct without right insight, does not liberate. The work then covers epistemology (ch. 1), the soul (ch. 2), cosmology (chs. 3–4), the non-soul substances (ch. 5), karmic influx and bondage (chs. 6–8), the stopping and shedding of karma (ch. 9) and liberation (ch. 10).

docs.title: 11.3 Jain Metaphysics: The Nature of Reality
11.3.1 Substance, Quality and Mode
docs.text:
Jain ontology is realist and pluralist. Its definition of existence is one of the most characteristic doctrines of the school:

The Definition of Existence

utpāda-vyaya-dhrauvya-yuktaṃ sat What exists is endowed with origination, cessation and permanence. — Tattvārthasūtra 5.29 (5.30 in the Digambara recension)

A substance (dravya) “possesses qualities and modes” (guṇa-paryāyavad dravyam, Tattvārthasūtra 5.37/5.38). A lump of gold is permanent as gold, while its modes — bracelet, necklace — arise and pass away. Against the Buddhists, for whom only momentary events exist, and against the Advaitins, for whom only unchanging being is ultimately real, the Jains held that permanence and change are both real aspects of the same thing. This is the metaphysical basis of anekāntavāda.

docs.title: 11.3.2 The Six Substances
docs.text:
Jainism recognises six substances: soul (jīva) and five kinds of non-soul (ajīva):

  1. Jīva (Soul) — Conscious substance, infinite in number

  2. Pudgala (Matter) — Possessing colour, taste, smell and touch; composed of atoms (paramāṇu) that are all of one kind and combine through their “smooth” and “rough” qualities (snigdha-rūkṣatvād bandhaḥ, Tattvārthasūtra 5.32/5.33); karmic matter is a form of pudgala

  3. Dharma (Medium of motion) — A non-material, all-pervading substance that makes movement possible

  4. Adharma (Medium of rest) — A non-material substance that makes rest possible

  5. Ākāśa (Space) — Provides room for all substances; divided into the inhabited universe (loka) and the empty space beyond it (aloka)

  6. Kāla (Time) — The condition of change; accepted as a separate substance by the Digambaras and by some Śvetāmbaras

The first five are “extended” (astikāya), whence Kundakunda’s title Pañcāstikāyasāra. Dharma and adharma here have unique, non-moral meanings: the universe is finite because these media, which make motion and rest possible, do not extend beyond the loka.

docs.title: 11.3.3 The Soul (Jīva)
docs.text:
The defining characteristic of the soul is upayoga, the active exercise of consciousness in knowing and perceiving (upayogo lakṣaṇam, Tattvārthasūtra 2.8).

Jīva — The Jain Concept of Soul

  • Jīvas are infinite in number, eternal, and distinct from each other

  • Each jīva is intrinsically endowed with infinite knowledge (ananta-jñāna), infinite perception (ananta-darśana), infinite bliss (ananta-sukha) and infinite energy (ananta-vīrya)

  • These qualities are obscured by karmic matter accumulated through beginningless time

  • The jīva is of the same size as its body — expanding or contracting like the light of a lamp in a large or small room

  • Jīvas exist at every level of life: from one-sensed beings (earth-, water-, fire- and air-bodies, plants, and the minute nigoda beings) to five-sensed beings with mind

docs.title: 11.3.4 The Seven Tattvas
docs.text:
The Tattvārthasūtra (1.4) lists seven principles (tattvas): “soul, non-soul, influx, bondage, stoppage, shedding and liberation” (jīvājīvāsrava-bandha-saṃvara-nirjarā-mokṣās tattvam). Some lists add merit (puṇya) and demerit (pāpa) to make nine. The first two are the substances; the remaining five describe the process of bondage and liberation (Figure 11.2).

Figure 11.2. The Seven Tattvas (Fundamental Principles) of Jain Philosophy (Tattvārthasūtra 1.4)

docs.title: 11.3.5 The Jain Theory of Karma
docs.text:
Jain karma theory is unusual in treating karma as a form of subtle matter:

  • Activity of body, speech and mind (yoga) draws in karmic particles (āsrava); the passions (kaṣāya: anger, pride, deceit, greed) make them stick to the soul (bandha)

  • There are eight basic types of karma: knowledge-obscuring (jñānāvaraṇīya), perception-obscuring (darśanāvaraṇīya), feeling-producing (vedanīya), deluding (mohanīya), lifespan-determining (āyuṣka), body-determining (nāma), status-determining (gotra) and obstructive (antarāya). The first, second, fourth and eighth are “destructive” (ghātiyā), since they obscure the soul’s innate qualities

  • Karmic bondage colours the soul, which is described by six “colourations” (leśyās) from black to white

  • Liberation requires both stopping new karmic influx (saṃvara) through vows, vigilance and restraint, and shedding existing karma (nirjarā) through austerity (tapas), including meditation

  • Spiritual progress is mapped in fourteen stages (guṇasthānas), from delusion to omniscience; the liberated soul (siddha) rises to the top of the universe and abides there forever in its innate perfection

The Jains, like the Mīmāṃsakas, reject a creator God: the universe is beginningless and runs by the nature of its substances. Jain authors such as Haribhadra, Hemacandra and Malliṣeṇa criticised the Nyāya arguments for a creator. The perfected souls, and above all the Tīrthaṅkaras, are objects of veneration, but they do not intervene in the world.

docs.title: 11.4 Anekāntavāda: The Many-Sidedness of Reality
docs.text:
Anekāntavāda (literally “the doctrine of non-one-sidedness”) is Jainism’s best-known philosophical contribution. It holds that reality is complex: every real thing has infinitely many characteristics (ananta-dharmātmakaṃ vastu), including some that appear to be opposed, such as permanence and impermanence, identity and difference, existence and non-existence — each in a different respect. The doctrine has roots in the canon, where Mahāvīra answers questions by distinguishing respects (saying, for instance, that a thing is eternal with respect to its substance but not with respect to its modes), and was developed by Siddhasena Divākara, Samantabhadra, Akalaṅka and Haribhadra (Matilal 1981).

Anekāntavāda

  • Reality (vastu) has infinite aspects (ananta-dharma)

  • Any particular judgment grasps only one aspect of reality

  • Ekāntavāda (one-sidedness) — holding that a single perspective captures the whole truth — is rejected

  • Rival philosophies are seen as one-sided absolutisations of partial truths: the Buddhists of change, the Advaitins of permanence, the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣikas of difference

Anekāntavāda is not relativism or scepticism. The Jains held that things really have the many aspects they ascribe to them and that the omniscient Jina knows them all. Nor did they regard every view as equally true: views become false when they claim to be the whole truth. Haribhadra, however, gave the doctrine a notably irenic expression, presenting the rival schools respectfully in his Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya and in other works urging tolerance of different religious paths.

Critics rejected the doctrine as contradictory. The Brahma Sūtra (2.2.33 in Śaṅkara’s numbering, naikasminn asambhavāt) declares that contradictory properties cannot belong to one thing, and Śaṅkara’s commentary ridicules the Jain sevenfold predication; Dharmakīrti and Śāntarakṣita made similar objections. The Jain reply is that there is no contradiction where the properties belong to the thing in different respects.

docs.title: 11.5 Syādvāda: Qualified Predication
docs.text: Syādvāda is the logical expression of anekāntavāda. Every assertion should be qualified by the particle syāt. In ordinary Sanskrit syāt means “it may be”, and the doctrine is sometimes called a “logic of perhaps”; but in Jain usage it means “in a certain respect” or “from a certain standpoint”, and it is usually combined with the particle eva (“definitely”): “in a certain respect, the pot definitely exists” (syād asty eva ghaṭaḥ).

docs.title: 11.5.1 The Sevenfold Predication (Saptabhaṅgī)
docs.text:
Any property can be predicated of a thing in seven ways (Table 11.2):

Table 11.2. The Seven Modes of Predication (Saptabhaṅgī) Mode Sanskrit Form Meaning 1 Syād asty eva In some respect, it is 2 Syān nāsty eva In some respect, it is not 3 Syād asti nāsti ca In some respect, it is and is not (successively) 4 Syād avaktavyam In some respect, it is inexpressible (both affirmed simultaneously) 5 Syād asti cāvaktavyaś ca In some respect, it is and is inexpressible 6 Syān nāsti cāvaktavyaś ca In some respect, it is not and is inexpressible 7 Syād asti nāsti cāvaktavyaś ca In some respect, it is, is not, and is inexpressible

Example: Consider a pot.

  1. From the perspective of its own substance, place, time and state (sva-dravya-kṣetra-kāla-bhāva) — it is: a clay pot, here, now

  2. From the perspective of another substance, place, time or state — it is not: it is not a cloth, not elsewhere, not yet existent before it was made

  3. Taking both perspectives in succession — it both is and is not

  4. Taking both perspectives simultaneously — it is inexpressible, since no single word can express both at once

  5. Modes 5–7 combine the fourth with the first three

The number seven is explained by the three basic predicates (is, is not, inexpressible) and their possible combinations. Modern scholars have compared syādvāda with many-valued and paraconsistent logics; B.K. Matilal and others have argued that it is better understood as a theory of context-relative assertion than as a rejection of the law of non-contradiction (Matilal 1981; Ganeri 2001); see Figure 11.3.

Figure 11.3. The Sevenfold Predication (Saptabhaṅgī) of Jain Logic: each of the seven modes combines one or more of the three basic predicates (filled circle), and each is qualified by syāt, “in some respect”

docs.title: 11.6 Nayavāda: The Theory of Standpoints
docs.text:
A naya is a partial standpoint from which a thing is considered. The Tattvārthasūtra (1.33/1.34) lists five nayas in the Śvetāmbara recension and seven in the Digambara recension; the standard later list of seven is often grouped under two basic standpoints: that of substance (dravyārthika, the first three) and that of modes (paryāyārthika, the last four).

  1. Naigama (Common-sense or teleological) — Considering a thing together with its general and specific features, or by its intended purpose

  2. Saṅgraha (Collective) — Considering the universal nature (e.g. all things as “existent”)

  3. Vyavahāra (Practical) — The conventional, analytic standpoint of daily life

  4. Ṛjusūtra (Straight-thread) — Considering only the present moment

  5. Śabda (Verbal) — Taking words with their grammatical features (tense, gender, number)

  6. Samabhirūḍha (Etymological) — Each word has its own distinct meaning; synonyms are not truly synonymous

  7. Evaṃbhūta (“Such-as-it-is”) — A word applies only when the object is actually performing the activity the word names

Each naya is valid within its own domain but becomes a “false standpoint” (durnaya) when absolutised. Siddhasena Divākara argued in the Sanmatitarka that the rival philosophical systems are precisely such absolutised standpoints — Sāṃkhya taking only the standpoint of substance, the Buddhists only that of modes — and that the Jain teaching is their synthesis; later Jain authors correlated particular schools with particular nayas.

docs.title: 11.7 Kundakunda and the Two Standpoints
docs.text:
The Digambara teacher Kundakunda, whose Prakrit works (Samayasāra, Pravacanasāra, Niyamasāra, Pañcāstikāyasāra) are among the most revered in that tradition, organised Jain teaching around two standpoints: the ultimate or “definitive” standpoint (niścaya-naya) and the conventional standpoint (vyavahāra-naya). From the conventional standpoint, the soul is bound by karma, acts, and enjoys the fruits of its actions; from the ultimate standpoint, the pure soul is nothing but knowledge and perception and is untouched by karma, which is merely matter. Liberation comes from realising the soul’s own pure nature.

This emphasis on the inner, pure self has sometimes been compared with Advaita Vedānta, though the Jain soul remains one among infinitely many and the world remains real. Kundakunda’s teaching inspired later Digambara reform movements — the 17th-century Adhyātma movement associated with the poet Banārsīdās and, in the 20th century, the movement of Kānjī Svāmī — which emphasised inner realisation over ritual. Kundakunda’s dates are much disputed; tradition places him very early, while many scholars date him to the middle of the first millennium CE (Dundas 2002).

docs.title: 11.8.1 The Five Kinds of Knowledge and the Two Pramāṇas
docs.text:
Jain epistemology begins with five types of knowledge (jñāna), already listed in the canon and systematised by Umāsvāti:

Knowledge and the Pramāṇas

mati-śrutāvadhi-manaḥparyaya-kevalāni jñānam tat pramāṇe ādye parokṣam pratyakṣam anyat Knowledge is sensory, scriptural, clairvoyant, mind-reading and omniscient. These are the two means of knowledge. The first two are indirect; the rest are direct. — Tattvārthasūtra 1.9–12

The Five Types of Jain Knowledge

  1. Mati-jñāna — Knowledge through the senses and mind

  2. Śruta-jñāna — Knowledge through words and scripture

  3. Avadhi-jñāna — Clairvoyant knowledge of material things beyond the range of the senses

  4. Manaḥparyaya-jñāna — Direct knowledge of the thoughts of others

  5. Kevala-jñāna — Omniscience: complete, unlimited knowledge of all things in all times

Strikingly, in this canonical scheme sense-knowledge is indirect (parokṣa), because it depends on the senses and mind as instruments; only knowledge that the soul has by itself is direct (pratyakṣa). Thus there are only two pramāṇas, pratyakṣa and parokṣa, in a sense quite different from that of the Brahmanical schools.

docs.title: 11.8.2 The Later Jain Logicians
docs.text:
In debate with Nyāya and Buddhist logicians, Jain thinkers from Siddhasena and Akalaṅka onwards adapted this scheme. Akalaṅka recognised ordinary sense perception as “empirical direct knowledge” (sāṃvyavahārika pratyakṣa), reserving “primary” (mukhya) directness for supersensory knowledge. Indirect knowledge was divided into five kinds (Table 11.3):

Table 11.3. The Five Kinds of Indirect Knowledge (Parokṣa) in Later Jain Logic Kind Sanskrit Description Memory Smṛti Recollection of what was previously experienced; a valid means of knowledge for the Jains, unlike most Brahmanical schools Recognition Pratyabhijñā Synthesis of memory and perception: “this is that”, “this is like that”, “this is different from that”; it includes what Nyāya calls comparison (upamāna) Inductive reasoning Tarka (Ūha) Knowledge of the universal relation (vyāpti) between reason and conclusion Inference Anumāna Knowledge of the conclusion from the reason; the Jains defined a valid reason by a single mark, “inexplicability otherwise” (anyathānupapannatva), rejecting the Buddhist triple mark Testimony Āgama Knowledge from the words of a reliable person, above all the Jina

This classification allowed the Jains to account for the Nyāya pramāṇas within their own scheme: comparison is a form of recognition, and the knowledge of pervasion, which Nyāya struggled to justify, is a distinct means of knowledge. Hemacandra’s Pramāṇamīmāṃsā (12th century) gives the classical statement of this mature Jain logic.

docs.title: 11.8.3 Omniscience
docs.text: The Jains defended the possibility of omniscience (kevala-jñāna) against the Mīmāṃsakas, who denied that any person could know dharma directly, and against Buddhists, who limited the Buddha’s omniscience to what matters for liberation. Since the soul’s nature is knowledge, they argued, the removal of all obscuring karma must leave it knowing everything.

docs.title: 11.9 Jain Ethics: The Path of Ahiṃsā
docs.text:
Jain ethics is centred on five vows, taken in full as “great vows” (mahāvratas) by monks and nuns and in a limited form as “lesser vows” (aṇuvratas) by lay people:

  1. Ahiṃsā — Non-violence (in thought, word and deed; towards all living beings)

  2. Satya — Truthfulness

  3. Asteya — Non-stealing

  4. Brahmacarya — Celibacy (for lay people, chastity)

  5. Aparigraha — Non-possession

Ahiṃsā in Jainism is taken to its most radical extent. Since jīvas exist in earth, water, fire, air and plants, even walking, breathing and eating involve harm. Monks and nuns practise vigilance (samiti) in walking, speaking, eating, handling objects and excretion, and restraint (gupti) of body, speech and mind; lay Jains traditionally avoid occupations involving much harm to life and follow strict dietary rules. The tradition also honours the voluntary fast to death (sallekhanā) undertaken by ascetics or lay people near the end of life, a practice whose legal status has been debated in modern India.

The question of gender divided the sects. Digambaras held that women cannot attain liberation in a female body, since they cannot go naked, while Śvetāmbaras held that they can, and honour Mallī, the nineteenth Tīrthaṅkara, as a woman. In Jain tradition, as today, nuns have generally outnumbered monks. Jainism rejected the Brahmanical claim that birth determines spiritual worth, though Jain lay communities themselves developed caste-like divisions (Jaini 1979).

docs.title: 11.10 Jain Philosophy and Other Schools
docs.text: Jain authors argued on every front. Against Advaita, they held that reality cannot be reduced to one principle and that plurality and change are real; against the Buddhists, that substances endure through their changing modes and that universal momentariness cannot explain memory, karma or bondage; against Sāṃkhya, that the soul is an agent and experiencer, not an inactive witness, and is the same size as its body; against Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, that there is no creator God and that substance and quality are not absolutely distinct; and against Mīmāṃsā, that omniscience is possible and that a sacrifice involving killing cannot be dharma. Over all of these they set the doctrine of many-sidedness as a philosophy of philosophies, which places the partial truths of the other systems within a larger whole. In the seventeenth century Yaśovijaya restated that doctrine in the idiom of Navya-Nyāya (Section 2.11.5).

docs.title: 11.11 Legacy and Continuing Relevance
docs.text: Many-sidedness has been read, especially in modern times, as a philosophical basis for intellectual humility and tolerance, though classically it was also a weapon of debate; the sevenfold predication has interested logicians working on many-valued and paraconsistent systems; and the Jain logicians made original contributions to the theory of inference and the classification of knowledge. Jain non-violence shaped Indian culture — vegetarianism, animal hospitals, the ethics of trade — and influenced M.K. Gandhi, notably through his friend the Jain thinker Śrīmad Rājacandra (Raychandbhai Mehta). Non-violence and non-possession are often invoked in modern environmental ethics, though their classical purpose was the purification of the soul. The Buddhist doctrine of non-self, the Vaiśeṣika categories and the Cārvāka materialism against which Jain authors argued are treated in Chapters 10, 3 and 9.

docs.title: Chapter 12: Śaiva Philosophy — The Siddhānta and the Doctrine of Recognition
docs.text:
Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā

kathaṃ cid āsādya maheśvarasya dāsyaṃ janasyāpy upakāram icchan samastasaṃpatsamavāptihetuṃ tatpratyabhijñām upapādayāmi Having somehow attained the servitude of the great Lord, and wishing to help others too, I establish the recognition of Him, the cause of attaining every fulfilment. — Utpaladeva, Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.1.1

docs.title: 12.1 Introduction: Śaiva Theology as Darśana
docs.text:
The schools treated so far in this volume grew out of the Vedic exegetical and ascetic traditions, or, in the case of the Buddhists, Jains and materialists, defined themselves against them. A further body of philosophy grew out of the revealed scriptures of the Śaivas, the Tantras or Āgamas, which their followers regarded as a revelation of Śiva distinct from, and for initiates superior to, the Veda. From about the end of the seventh century these scriptures acquired learned exegetes who argued for their doctrines in the common language of Indian philosophy — the language of pramāṇa, of pūrvapakṣa and siddhānta, and of the debate with Dharmakīrti’s Buddhist epistemology. Mādhava’s Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha (14th century) gives four of its sixteen chapters to Śaiva systems: the Nakulīśa-Pāśupata, the Śaiva (that is, the Siddhānta), the Pratyabhijñā (“Recognition”) and the alchemical Raseśvara system. The Brahmanical classification into āstika and nāstika (Section 1.3) has no place for them, which is one reason they are often left out of surveys of the “six systems”.

This chapter treats the two Śaiva schools that made the largest contribution to philosophical argument: the dualist Śaiva Siddhānta, and the non-dualist school of Recognition founded by Somānanda and Utpaladeva and systematised by Abhinavagupta. Both reached their classical form in Kashmir between the ninth and eleventh centuries, and they disagreed sharply with each other; the Siddhānta later acquired a distinct Tamil form (Section 12.2.6). The scriptures, ritual, yoga, cosmology of the thirty-six tattvas, the Spanda and Krama traditions and the later history of the Śaiva traditions are described in Volume 6 (Tantra–Āgama); Abhinavagupta’s aesthetics belongs to Volume 8 (Kāvya Kalpalatā). The concern here is with the arguments: what these philosophers held about the self, cognition, causality, relation, bondage and liberation, and why (Sanderson 1988).

An earlier Śaiva system deserves a sentence. The Pāśupatas, the oldest Śaiva ascetic order, possessed a Pāśupatasūtra with a commentary by Kauṇḍinya (the Pañcārthabhāṣya, probably of the mid-first millennium), which organises its teaching under five topics: effect (kārya), cause (kāraṇa), yoga, ritual injunction (vidhi) and the end of suffering (duḥkhānta). Its most debated philosophical thesis was that the Lord acts freely, independently of the karma of souls — a claim that Naiyāyikas and Siddhāntins alike felt obliged to discuss. The Pāśupata tradition itself is treated in Volume 6.

docs.title: 12.2 The Śaiva Siddhānta: A Realist Theology
12.2.1 The Exegetes
docs.text: The Siddhānta, “the established doctrine”, was the mainstream of initiatory Śaivism across India. Its scriptures are the Siddhāntatantras, of which the Mṛgendra, the Kiraṇa, the Mataṅgapārameśvara and the Svāyambhuvasūtrasaṃgraha were the most important for philosophy. Its first great exegete, Sadyojyotis, is now placed in the late seventh or early eighth century (c. 675–725 on Sanderson’s argument); his short treatises — the Nareśvaraparīkṣā (“Examination of the Soul and the Lord”), the Mokṣakārikā, the Paramokṣanirāsakārikā (“Verses Refuting the Liberations of Others”) and the Bhogakārikā — defend the doctrine against Buddhists, Naiyāyikas, Mīmāṃsakas and Sāṃkhyas (Sanderson 2006). In tenth-century Kashmir Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha commented on the Mṛgendra, and his son Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha wrote commentaries on several scriptures and on Sadyojyotis’s Nareśvaraparīkṣā; these are the most philosophically demanding works of the school (Goodall 1998). King Bhoja’s Tattvaprakāśa (11th century) became a standard digest. From the eleventh and twelfth centuries the Siddhānta’s centre moved south, where Aghoraśiva of Cidambaram (12th century) commented on the earlier treatises, and where a Tamil school arose with Meykaṇṭār’s Civañāṉapōtam (Section 12.2.6).

docs.title: 12.2.2 Lord, Souls and Bonds
docs.text:
The Siddhānta recognises three eternal and irreducible categories: the Lord (pati), souls (paśu, literally “beasts”, that is, beings tethered like sacrificial animals) and the bonds (pāśa) that hold them.

The Lord. Śiva is the agent of five acts — emission, maintenance and withdrawal of the world, concealment, and liberation — which the Mṛgendra (Vidyāpāda 2.3) names as the whole of his work. The Siddhāntins argue for his existence in a form close to the Nyāya proof (Section 2.10): the world, being made up of parts and arranged in a particular way, is an effect, and an effect requires an intelligent maker who knows its material. The Mṛgendra adds that this maker must be perfect by nature (svabhāvasiddha), for a maker who had himself become perfect would require a prior maker, and the series would have no end (2.4). Śiva, however, is only the efficient cause of the world. Its material cause is māyā, a real, eternal and insentient substance distinct from him, from which the impure levels of the universe evolve; and the karma of souls is the auxiliary cause that determines what each will experience. Śiva therefore does not transform himself into the world, as the Brahman of some Bhedābheda Vedāntins does (Section 8.2), nor is the world an appearance, as in Advaita.

Souls. Souls are many, eternal and all-pervading, and their nature is consciousness. The Siddhānta’s account of that consciousness is distinctive. “Consciousness has the form of seeing and doing (dṛkkriyā), and it is always present in the self”, says the Mṛgendra (2.5); since scripture describes the liberated soul as “facing in all directions”, the soul is by nature omniscient and omnipotent. This sets the Siddhānta apart from Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, for which consciousness is an adventitious quality that the self acquires only in conjunction with mind and body (Section 2.9), and from Sāṃkhya, whose puruṣa is a witness that does nothing (Chapter 4). In the Siddhānta the self is both knower and agent; what needs explaining is why its knowledge and agency are so limited.

Bonds. The explanation is the bonds. The root bond is mala (“impurity”), also called āṇava mala because it makes the soul an aṇu, a limited being. Mala is a single, beginningless substance (dravya) with many powers, one for each soul, which obstructs the soul’s innate powers of knowing and acting, much as a film covers the eye. To this are added karma and the products of māyā: the body, the faculties and the world, which the Lord supplies so that souls can experience the fruits of their actions and so that, over time, their impurity may “ripen” (malaparipāka). When a soul’s impurity is ripe, the Lord’s power “descends” on it (śaktipāta) and it becomes fit for initiation.

docs.title: 12.2.3 Why Knowledge Alone Does Not Liberate
docs.text:
From these premises follows the thesis for which the Siddhānta was best known among its rivals: liberation requires ritual action, and specifically the initiation (dīkṣā) in which the officiant, as the instrument of Śiva’s power, severs the soul’s bonds. The argument is philosophical, not merely sectarian. Knowledge removes ignorance, and ignorance is a cognitive state. But mala is not a cognitive state; it is a substance. A substance cannot be dissolved by a cognition, any more than a cataract can be cured by understanding what a cataract is. It can be removed only by an action, and the only agent able to act on it is the Lord, who acts through the rite. The Siddhāntins accordingly criticised the Sāṃkhyas, Advaitins and others who taught liberation through knowledge alone; Sadyojyotis’s Paramokṣanirāsakārikā is a review of the liberations proposed by other schools, each rejected as either not final or not liberation.

Liberation, on this view, is not union with Śiva. The soul’s innate omniscience and omnipotence become manifest, so that it becomes “equal to Śiva” (śivasama), but it remains a distinct soul; and, according to most Siddhānta authors, the liberated do not take over the Lord’s cosmic functions. A dualist realism about the world thus goes together with a dualism of souls and God that persists even in release (Goodall 1998).

docs.title: 12.2.4 Scripture and Its Authority
docs.text:
The Siddhāntins also had to defend the authority of their scriptures, and here their opponents were Brahmanical. For the Mīmāṃsā the Veda is valid because it has no author, and therefore no author’s faults (Section 6.7); texts composed by persons, however revered, can have only a derived authority, and Kumārila, in his Tantravārttika (on MS 1.3), counted the Pāśupata and Pāñcarātra teachings, along with Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Buddhist and Jain works, among compositions of this kind that stand outside the Veda. The Śaivas answered on Nyāya rather than Mīmāṃsā principles. A statement is valid, they held, because its speaker is reliable, and no speaker is more reliable than an omniscient Lord; the Tantras are therefore authoritative precisely because they have an author. Many Siddhāntins added that the Veda too was spoken by Śiva, so that the two revelations are not rivals but stages: the Veda for all twice-born men, the Tantras for those whom Śiva’s grace has made fit for initiation. The Naiyāyika Jayanta Bhaṭṭa, writing in late ninth-century Kashmir, discussed whether the Śaiva and Pāñcarātra scriptures could be accepted as valid, and allowed them a place as long as they did not contradict the Veda — a compromise that reflects the social standing these traditions had already won.

The debate mattered because it decided who could be liberated, and how. Initiation into the Siddhānta was open, in principle, to members of all four classes and, with restrictions, to women; the scriptures set the initiate’s ritual duties according to his class, and the high offices of officiant and teacher were in practice reserved largely to Brahmins. The claim that a rite could free a soul regardless of its Vedic eligibility was one reason orthodox Mīmāṃsakas regarded the Tantras with suspicion; the retention of class distinctions within initiation is one reason modern historians do not describe the Siddhānta as a movement against caste (Sanderson 1988).

docs.title: 12.2.5 Rāmakaṇṭha and the Buddhist Denial of the Self
docs.text: The Siddhāntins’ most important philosophical opponents were the Buddhist epistemologists, for whom the self is a construction imposed on a stream of momentary cognitions (Chapter 10). Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha’s reply, studied by Alex Watson, is notable for turning a Buddhist doctrine against the Buddhists (Watson 2006). Dharmakīrti had held that every cognition is aware of itself (svasaṃvedana). Rāmakaṇṭha accepts that awareness is self-revealing, but argues that it is not momentary. What we call different cognitions, he argues, are one continuing awareness distinguished only by the different objects it illuminates; the variety belongs to the objects, not to the awareness. That one continuing awareness is the self. In support he appeals to recognition in the ordinary sense — “I who saw this before now see it again” — which joins two experiences in a single subject, and which a series of discrete momentary cognitions, none aware of another, could not produce. The argument anticipates the Pratyabhijñā’s, and both schools drew on a common Kashmiri debate with the Buddhists; but where Rāmakaṇṭha concluded to an infinite number of permanent selves, the non-dualists concluded to one.

docs.title: 12.2.6 The Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta
docs.text:
In the Tamil country the Siddhānta met a devotional tradition older than itself and was transformed by it. From the seventh to the ninth centuries the Nāyaṉmār poets — Appar, Campantar and Cuntarar, whose hymns form the Tēvāram, and Māṇikkavācakar, author of the Tiruvācakam — sang of Śiva in Tamil as a personal Lord who saves by grace. Their hymns were later gathered, with other works, into a Tamil Śaiva canon of twelve “sacred books” (Tirumuṟai), which includes the Tirumantiram ascribed to Tirumūlar, a long and doctrinally mixed poem whose date is much disputed. When the Sanskrit Siddhānta moved south in the eleventh and twelfth centuries, it found a public for whom Śiva was already known through devotion rather than through ritual theory.

The result was a Tamil theology with its own canon of fourteen treatises, the Meykaṇṭa Cāttiram. Its foundation is Meykaṇṭār’s Civañāṉapōtam (13th century), twelve terse aphorisms in Tamil with brief explanations, traditionally regarded as a rendering of twelve Sanskrit verses said to come from the Raurava Āgama, a claim many scholars doubt. Meykaṇṭār’s pupil Aruṇanti’s Civañāṉa Cittiyār expounds it at length in two parts: a refutation of rival doctrines (parapakkam), which reviews and rejects the materialists, several Buddhist schools, the Jains and others, and a statement of the school’s own position (cupakkam). Umāpati Civācāriyar of Cidambaram (14th century) completed the canon (Dhavamony 1971).

The Tamil school kept the three categories of Lord, souls and bonds, the three impurities and the necessity of grace, but it changed their balance. Where the Sanskrit exegetes made initiation the decisive act and the liberated soul “equal to Śiva” yet distinct (Section 12.2), the Tamil authors stressed Śiva’s grace (aruḷ), which works through the teacher and through the soul’s own devotion, and described liberation as a union in which soul and Lord are “not two” without being one. They called this relation advaita, but meant by it inseparability, not identity: in release the soul does not become Śiva but no longer exists apart from him. The soul itself was described as cat-acattu, “real-unreal”: not real as Śiva is, nor unreal as the bonds are, but taking on the character of whatever it is joined with. The parapakkam literature also gives a Tamil survey of the Indian systems that complements the Sanskrit doxographies of Haribhadra and Mādhava, and, like the Maṇimēkalai before it (Chapter 1), shows that the debate between the darśanas was carried on in Tamil as well as in Sanskrit (Zvelebil 1973).

The Tamil Siddhānta remained the dominant theology of Tamil Śaivism, sustained by non-brahmin monastic institutions (maṭams) such as those at Tiruvāvaṭuturai and Dharmapuram. In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries it became an emblem of the Tamil revival, presented by its English-language interpreters as the original philosophy of the Tamils and set against a Brahmanical Vedānta; that modern use, like the modern use of Advaita described in Chapter 8, tells us more about its time than about the medieval texts.

docs.title: 12.3 Somānanda and the Beginnings of the Recognition School
docs.text:
The school of Recognition (pratyabhijñā) begins with Somānanda (c. 900–950), whose Śivadṛṣṭi (“The Vision of Śiva”) is the first philosophical defence of a strictly non-dual Śaivism (Nemec 2011). Its thesis is that everything is Śiva: not a part, a reflection or a transformation of Śiva, but Śiva himself, possessed of will, knowledge and action. Since each thing is Śiva in full, Somānanda can say that “everything has the nature of everything” (sarvaṃ sarvātmakam); the differences between a pot and a cloth are real as Śiva’s self-expression but do not divide him. The world is therefore neither an illusion, as for the Advaitins, nor the product of an independent material cause, as for the Siddhāntins.

Much of the Śivadṛṣṭi is polemic. Its second chapter is a sustained critique of the Grammarians who, following Bhartṛhari, identified the ultimate reality with speech at its subtle “seeing” level (paśyantī; see Section 6.18). Speech, Somānanda objects, is an instrument, and an instrument presupposes an agent who uses it; to make speech ultimate is to put the instrument before the agent. Later chapters argue against other Śaiva and non-Śaiva positions, and the last gives an account of the lineage through which the non-dual teaching was transmitted. Somānanda’s style is compressed and combative; it was his pupil who turned his “vision” into a systematic argument.

docs.title: 12.4.1 The Work and Its Plan
docs.text:
Utpaladeva (c. 925–975), son of Udayākara and pupil of Somānanda, wrote the Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā (“Verses on the Recognition of the Lord”), with two commentaries of his own: a short Vṛtti, which survives, and a long Vivṛti, of which only fragments survive. He also wrote three short “proofs” (the Siddhitrayī: proofs of the conscious knower, of the Lord, and of relation) and the hymns of the Śivastotrāvalī. The Kārikā has about 190 verses in four sections (adhikāra), set out in Table 12.1; a verse near its close (4.16) presents the work as a new and easy path, already taught by Somānanda in the Śivadṛṣṭi, which Utpaladeva has now “made well-fitted” by reasoning (Torella 1994).

Table 12.1. The plan of Utpaladeva’s Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā (section numbers as in Torella’s edition) Section Verses Main topics 1. Knowledge (jñāna) 1.1–1.8 Purpose; the Buddhist objection (1.2); memory and the synthesis of cognitions (1.3–1.4); light and reflective awareness (1.5); I-awareness and conceptual thought (1.6); unity of the knower (1.7–1.8) 2. Action (kriyā) 2.1–2.4 Time and space as sequence; relation and universals (2.2); the object as a bundle of manifestations, means of knowledge, error (2.3); causality as agency (2.4) 3. Scripture (āgama) 3.1–3.2 The tattvas reinterpreted; Lord and bound soul; the three impurities; states of consciousness 4. Summary (tattvasaṃgraha) 4.1–4.18 The one Lord as the self of all beings; liberation as recognition

The title states the method. Recognition (pratyabhijñā) is the kind of cognition expressed in “this is that same Devadatta”: it does not discover a new object but identifies a present one with what was already known. The Lord, Utpaladeva argues, cannot be proved or disproved in the ordinary way, for he is the knower and agent presupposed by every act of proof: “Who, being conscious, could deny or establish the great Lord, who is the agent, the knower, one’s own self, established from the beginning?” (1.1.2). Yet, through delusion, the Lord is not noticed even though he is constantly experienced (1.1.3). The work therefore does not demonstrate an unknown God; it removes the obstacles to recognising a self that is already manifest, by pointing to its powers of knowing and acting.

docs.title: 12.4.2 The Buddhist Objection
docs.text: Before stating his own view Utpaladeva gives the opponent’s case in full (1.2), and it is the case of Dharmakīrti’s school. There are only two kinds of cognition: perception, which presents the bare particular (svalakṣaṇa), and conceptual thought (vikalpa), which is bound up with words. Neither presents a permanent seer; the notion “I” is about the body. Memory needs no lasting self, for it arises from the latent impression (saṃskāra) left by an earlier experience. Action, which seems to require a single agent persisting through a sequence, is only the arising of different things in different places. Causality is nothing more than “when this is, that comes to be”. Relations are unreal, for a relation would have to reside in two things at once and be dependent on what is already complete; and so the agent, too, is imagined (1.2.1–11).

docs.title: 12.4.3 Memory and the Synthesis of Cognitions
docs.text:
Utpaladeva’s reply begins with memory (1.3–1.4). Grant the Buddhist premise that every cognition is self-revealing and cannot be the object of another cognition. Then a memory, which is itself a new cognition, cannot reach the earlier experience; it can at most resemble it, and an appeal to the latent impression only explains that resemblance, not the memory’s being of the earlier experience. If cognitions were mutually separate and unaware of one another, the whole of everyday life, which rests on joining one cognition to another (anusaṃdhāna), would collapse — unless there is a single Lord, a body of consciousness, who holds the endless forms of the world within himself and has the powers of cognition, memory and exclusion (1.3.6–7). In memory, the earlier experience does not appear as a separate object, like the remembered thing; it appears as “I experienced this before”, taken up into the self (1.4.4). The unity of cognitions at different times is the knower (1.4.3).

This argument resembles the Nyāya argument from memory to a self (Section 2.9), and Utpaladeva knew it. The difference lies in what the self is. For Nyāya the self is a substance in which cognitions occur as qualities; in itself it is unconscious. For Utpaladeva the self is the very consciousness that cognises, and the unity that memory requires is the unity of that consciousness, not of a substrate behind it.

docs.title: 12.4.4 Light and Reflective Awareness
docs.text:
The heart of the work is its account of manifestation (1.5). Whatever appears, appears by being manifest. An object that was not of the nature of light (prakāśa) would remain unmanifest, as it was before it was known; and the light cannot be different from the object, for then the object would still not be manifest (1.5.2–3). Utpaladeva then reviews two Buddhist ways of accounting for the variety of experience. The Sautrāntika infers external objects from the fact that particular appearances arise unbidden; but the inference fails, for an inference can only reach what has been manifest at some time, and an external object, by definition, never has been (1.5.4, 8–9). The Yogācāra explains the variety by the awakening of latent impressions; but then what explains the variety of the awakenings (1.5.5)? Utpaladeva’s own answer is that the Lord, who is consciousness, by his own will manifests outwardly what lies within him, without any material cause, as a yogin creates objects by will alone (1.5.7).

So far the position might seem to be that of the Yogācāra itself, or of Advaita. What distinguishes it is the next step:

Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.5.11

svabhāvam avabhāsasya vimarśaṃ vidur anyathā prakāśo ’rthoparakto ’pi sphaṭikādijaḍopamaḥ They know reflective awareness (vimarśa) to be the very nature of manifestation; otherwise light, though coloured by objects, would be like an insentient crystal.

A crystal takes on the colour of what is placed next to it, but it does not know that it does so. If consciousness were only light — a pure, passive manifesting, like the witness-consciousness of Sāṃkhya or Advaita — it would be no different from such a reflector. What makes light conscious is vimarśa: a reflexive grasp of itself and of its contents, which in its fullest form is the awareness “I”. Utpaladeva’s Vṛtti says that without it there would be no camatkṛti, the savouring wonder of awareness — an idea that Abhinavagupta, under the name camatkāra, was later to apply to aesthetic experience. Consciousness is thus “reflective awareness, the supreme speech arising of its own accord”, and this is its freedom (svātantrya) and its sovereignty (1.5.13). The equation of vimarśa with the highest level of speech borrows Bhartṛhari’s conception (Section 6.18) while rejecting the Grammarians’ view of speech as ultimate in its own right.

Two further arguments complete this part of the work.
