First, against Dharmakīrti’s doctrine that perception is wholly free of conceptual construction, Utpaladeva holds that reflective awareness is present even at the moment of direct perception: otherwise the quick, unreflecting responses of everyday life — running, for instance — could not be explained (1.5.19). Secondly, he distinguishes this awareness from conceptual thought in the Buddhists’ own terms. Conceptual thought, on the Buddhist apoha theory (Section 10.7.3), works by excluding an opposite: to think “pot” is to exclude what is not a pot. The pure “I” has no opposite and excludes nothing; it is therefore not a concept (1.6.1–3). The limited “I” that identifies itself with the body, the breath or the mind is a concept, formed by excluding others; and this, not the self, is what the Buddhists rightly deny (1.6.4–5).

The first section ends by drawing the consequences. Knowing a causal connection from repeated perception and non-perception, sublating a false cognition by a true one, and knowing the absence of a pot on the ground all require a single knower who holds several cognitions together (1.7). “Externality” is simply difference from the knower, and “internality” unity with it (1.8.8): objects are external in so far as they appear as other than the subject, but they have their being within consciousness.

docs.title: 12.4.5 Action, Relation and Causality
docs.text:
The section on action applies the same principle to the categories that the Buddhists had dissolved. Time and space are sequences of manifestations that the Lord projects (2.1). The notions of action, relation, universal, substance, direction and time are true, “because they are stable and serve a purpose”, and they are grounded in what is both one and many (2.2.1): relation is the unity, in a single knower, of things that appear separately (2.2.4). This is a direct answer to Dharmakīrti’s Sambandhaparīkṣā, which had argued that relations cannot be real; Utpaladeva’s Sambandhasiddhi takes up the question at length.

Utpaladeva also offers an original analysis of the object. A thing is a bundle of “manifestations” (ābhāsa) unified in one locus: the same thing can be manifest as long, round, upright, a man, smoke, sandalwood; or as existent, a pot, a substance, gold, bright (2.3.4–5). Each manifestation is a possible meaning of a word, and things perform different functions according to which of their manifestations are in play. The scheme does the work of the Vaiśeṣika universals (Chapter 3) without positing them as entities independent of consciousness. On this basis Utpaladeva defines a means of knowledge as the newly arisen manifestation through which a thing is fixed as “this, of such a kind” (2.3.1); and he concludes that the Lord, who is always manifest, is not the object of any means of knowledge (2.3.16). Error, too, is explained in terms of manifestations. In the shell mistaken for silver there really is a reflective awareness of silver, but the silver is not fixed in the shell, because the place does not agree (2.3.13); error is an incomplete manifestation, not the appearance of something unreal. Abhinavagupta later called this theory apūrṇakhyāti, “incomplete manifestation”, and placed it beside the theories of error described in Table 13.4.

The account of causality (2.4) is perhaps the boldest part of the work. An insentient thing cannot be a cause, for a cause would have to give existence, and what does not exist cannot take on existence while what already exists gains nothing by receiving it (2.4.2–3) — a dilemma that cuts against both the Sāṃkhya and the Nyāya theories of causation (Figure 13.2). Causation is therefore the relation of agent and act: the only true cause is a conscious agent who manifests as his act what was within him. The Lord is the cause even of a sprout; the potter makes a pot only within the order that the Lord has established; and a yogin can produce a pot without clay (2.4.8–10). Dharmakīrti’s formula “when this is, that comes to be” cannot hold between insentient things, each enclosed in itself, for the relation it expresses presupposes someone who connects the two (2.4.14–15).

docs.title: 12.4.6 Bondage and Recognition
docs.text:
The third section reinterprets the Śaiva scriptural categories. The knower is called “Lord” (pati) when the objects are his own limbs, and “bound soul” (paśu) when, through māyā, they appear as separate from him (3.2.3). The three impurities of the Siddhānta are redefined as modes of awareness. The āṇava impurity is twofold: a loss of the freedom of awareness, or a lack of awareness of one’s freedom (3.2.4). The māyīya impurity is the appearance of objects as different from the knower, and the kārma impurity belongs to an agent who acts without awareness of what he is (3.2.5). None of them is a substance.

Liberation follows. One who knows that “all this glory is mine” possesses the Lord’s nature even while concepts continue to arise (4.12); bound and liberated have the same world before them, but the bound see it as utterly different from themselves and the liberated as their own body (4.13). Utpaladeva’s last image is of a woman who has longed for a lover she knows only by report: when he stands beside her he gives her no joy until she recognises him (4.17). So the Lord, though always present as one’s own self, does not bring fulfilment until he is recognised. The Vṛtti on 4.16 draws the conclusion that through recognition alone one is liberated while living.

docs.title: 12.5 Abhinavagupta: Systematiser and Critic
docs.text:
Abhinavagupta (c. 950–1016), the pupil of Utpaladeva’s pupil Lakṣmaṇagupta, wrote two commentaries on Utpaladeva: the Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī on the verses and the much longer Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī on the lost Vivṛti, which is the main source for that work’s arguments. His Tantrāloka, an encyclopaedic exposition of Trika Śaivism, is described in Volume 6. Three of his contributions matter most for philosophy (Pandey 1963; Sanderson 1988).

Knowledge, ritual and the two kinds of ignorance. At the opening of the Tantrāloka (1.36–51) Abhinavagupta settles the dispute with the Siddhānta over knowledge and ritual by distinguishing two kinds of ignorance. “Personal” ignorance (pauruṣa ajñāna) is the impurity itself: a pre-conceptual contraction of the self’s powers of knowing and acting. “Intellectual” ignorance (bauddha ajñāna) is a determinate but mistaken conviction in the intellect, of the form “I am such-and-such, and I know this”. Initiation destroys the first, but the second remains; an initiate who lacks knowledge is liberated only at the death of the body. When intellectual ignorance is removed by knowledge — for which the study of scripture is the chief means — liberation in life is “in the palm of the hand” (1.44). The Siddhānta’s claim for ritual is thus accepted, but subordinated to knowledge.

Impurity without a substance. Abhinavagupta defines the root impurity as the sense of being incomplete (apūrṇaṃmanyatā; Tantrāloka 9.62). It is “real” (vastubhūta), he says, only in the sense that it is Śiva’s own will to conceal himself (9.65–66). The Siddhānta’s independent substance is thereby replaced by a free act of the one consciousness, and the scriptural language of a separate impurity is read as a description of how that act appears to the bound.

Speech and aesthetic experience. Developing Utpaladeva’s identification of vimarśa with the highest speech, Abhinavagupta worked out a correspondence between the phonemes of Sanskrit and the stages of the self-manifestation of consciousness (Volume 6 and Volume 10). His theory that rasa is the savouring (carvaṇā) of a generalised emotion, free of the limits of the individual ego, applies to aesthetic experience the analysis of awareness developed in the Pratyabhijñā (Volume 8).

Abhinavagupta’s pupil Kṣemarāja (early 11th century) condensed the doctrine into the twenty sūtras of the Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya, whose opening sūtras are given in Volume 6; his works made the school’s ideas widely accessible but are less concerned with argument than Utpaladeva’s.

docs.title: 12.6 Dualists and Non-dualists in Debate
docs.text:
The disagreements between the two Śaiva schools, and between both and the Buddhists, can be laid out side by side (Table 12.2). Several are worth stating explicitly.

Table 12.2. Buddhist epistemologists, Śaiva Siddhānta and Pratyabhijñā compared Question Dharmakīrti Śaiva Siddhānta Pratyabhijñā Self A construction on momentary cognitions Many eternal selves, by nature omniscient and omnipotent One consciousness, the Lord, appearing as many knowers Cognition Momentary and self-aware One continuing self-aware awareness, varied by its objects (Rāmakaṇṭha) Light (prakāśa) that is also reflective awareness (vimarśa) World Momentary particulars Real; evolved from māyā, a substance distinct from Śiva Real as the manifestation of consciousness within itself Relation and causality Constructed; “when this is, that comes to be” Real; Śiva is the efficient cause, māyā the material cause Unity in one knower; causality is agency Bondage Craving and ignorance Mala, a beginningless substance Contraction of awareness; the sense of incompleteness Liberation Cessation of the defilements Equality with Śiva, remaining distinct Recognition of oneself as the Lord Means Insight Initiation, as Śiva’s act Recognition; initiation with knowledge

First, both Śaiva schools reject the Buddhist dissolution of the subject, and both use the Buddhists’ own doctrine of self-awareness to do so; the argument from memory and recognition is common to Rāmakaṇṭha and Utpaladeva. They part over its conclusion. For the Siddhānta the self-aware subjects are many and remain many in liberation; for the Pratyabhijñā their plurality is the Lord’s self-limitation. Secondly, they differ over what bondage is, and so over how it is removed. If impurity is a substance, liberation needs a rite; if it is a contraction of awareness, recognition is enough, and ritual becomes a means of producing or expressing it. Thirdly, they differ over the world. The Siddhānta needs māyā as a material cause because it holds that an intelligent being cannot itself be the stuff of the world; the Pratyabhijñā answers that a conscious agent can manifest objects without material cause, as the yogin’s power shows, and that only a conscious agent can be a cause at all.

The Pratyabhijñā’s relation to other non-dualisms is equally instructive. Like the Yogācāra, it denies that there are objects outside consciousness; unlike it, it holds that consciousness is one rather than a stream of moments, that it is reflexively aware of itself as “I”, and that the world it manifests is real. Its differences from Advaita — above all the dynamic, active character of consciousness and the reality of māyā as a power of Śiva — are set out in Table 12.3.

Table 12.3. Kaśmīr Śaivism vs. Advaita Vedānta Issue Kaśmīr Śaivism Advaita Vedānta Ultimate Reality Paraśiva: dynamic, creative consciousness Nirguṇa Brahman: actionless (niṣkriya), attributeless consciousness Status of the world Real manifestation of Śiva’s creative power Mithyā (apparent; ultimately unreal) Māyā One of Śiva’s powers; it conceals but is real Inexplicable; neither real nor unreal Liberation Recognition (pratyabhijñā) of one’s identity with Śiva Knowledge (jñāna) of identity with Brahman Nature of consciousness Dynamic, creative, possessing svātantrya (absolute freedom) Pure witness (sākṣin); actionless

Abhinavagupta’s critique of Advaita centres on the charge that Śaṅkara’s Brahman, being utterly devoid of activity and creative power, cannot adequately explain the dynamic reality of experience. For the Kaśmīr Śaivas, consciousness is not merely a passive witness but an active, creative force (vimarśa) that freely manifests the entire universe within itself, like a mirror reflecting images without being affected by them. The Pratyabhijñā authors argued above all against the Buddhist epistemologists, and their engagement with Advaita was less direct; but the contrast became a commonplace of later writing on both traditions.

Modern interpreters have read Utpaladeva’s argument as a transcendental argument, which shows that the Lord is the condition of the possibility of ordinary cognition and action (Lawrence 1999), and as a careful theory of the relation between self and other (Ratié 2011).

docs.title: 12.7 Legacy
docs.text:
In Kashmir the non-dual tradition continued after Kṣemarāja through commentators such as Jayaratha (13th century), and the Siddhānta flourished in the Tamil country, where Meykaṇṭār and his successors gave it a Tamil theological form (Section 12.2.6). Pratyabhijñā ideas passed into the Śrīvidyā tradition and into Śaiva and Śākta writing across India (Volume 6). Modern study began with the Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies, published at Srinagar from 1911, and with K. C. Pandey’s study of Abhinavagupta (Pandey 1963); critical editions and translations of Utpaladeva (Torella 1994), studies of Somānanda (Nemec 2011) and of the Siddhānta exegetes (Goodall 1998; Watson 2006) have since shown how closely these Śaiva philosophers engaged the Buddhist, Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā debates treated elsewhere in this volume.

The Nyāya arguments for God and the self that the Siddhānta adapts are in Chapter 2; Bhartṛhari’s philosophy of the word, which Somānanda criticises and Utpaladeva adapts, in Chapter 6; Dharmakīrti’s epistemology in Chapter 10; and the Śaiva theories of error and causation are compared with those of the other schools in Chapter 13.

docs.title: Chapter 13: Comparing the Schools — Knowledge, Error, Debate and Conclusions
docs.text:
The Centrality of Pramāṇa

pramāṇato ’rthapratipattau pravṛttisāmarthyād arthavat pramāṇam A means of knowledge is true to its object, since, when an object is known through a means of knowledge, the activity that follows is successful. — Vātsyāyana, Nyāya Bhāṣya, opening sentence

docs.title: 13.1 Introduction: Why Epistemology Became Central
docs.text:
A distinguishing feature of classical Indian philosophy, especially from the middle of the first millennium CE, is the primacy accorded to epistemology. Above all after Dignāga, a philosopher was expected to state the pramāṇas (means of valid knowledge) through which any claim could be justified, and the question “How do you know?” became foundational.

Every school defined its accepted pramāṇas, and much of the inter-school debate revolves around which pramāṇas are valid, how they function, and what they can reveal. This chapter compares the epistemological theories of the major schools (Matilal 1986; Mohanty 2000; Phillips 2012). The earlier chapters have described each school’s means of knowledge in its own setting; this chapter does not repeat those accounts. It asks instead what the schools’ disagreements about knowledge, error and debate show when they are set side by side, and it ends with the volume’s conclusions.

docs.title: 13.2 What Counts as a Means of Knowledge
docs.text:
Indian epistemology works with a set of related terms: valid cognition (pramā), usually defined as cognition that is true to its object (yathārtha); its means or instrument (pramāṇa); its object (prameya); and the knower (pramātṛ). Every school accepted this frame, which is why their disagreements were genuine disagreements and not merely different vocabularies. Table 13.1 sets out which means of knowledge each school accepts, in the terms of the Brahmanical list.

Table 13.1. Pramāṇas accepted by Indian philosophical schools, in the terms of the Brahmanical list School Pratyakṣa Anumāna Śabda Upamāna Arthāpatti Anupalabdhi perception inference testimony comparison postulation non-apprehension Cārvāka \(√\) – – – – – Bauddha \(√\) \(√\) – – – – Vaiśeṣika \(√\) \(√\) – – – – Sāṃkhya \(√\) \(√\) \(√\) – – – Yoga \(√\) \(√\) \(√\) – – – Nyāya \(√\) \(√\) \(√\) \(√\) – – Jaina \(√\) \(√\) \(√\) – – – Prābhākara \(√\) \(√\) \(√\) \(√\) \(√\) – Bhāṭṭa \(√\) \(√\) \(√\) \(√\) \(√\) \(√\) Advaita Vedānta \(√\) \(√\) \(√\) \(√\) \(√\) \(√\) Schools accepting 10 9 7 4 3 2

Simplifications: later Cārvākas accepted inference about perceptible things; the Jains classify knowledge as pratyakṣa and parokṣa, counting inference and testimony as forms of the latter and treating comparison as a form of recognition; Buddhists after Dignāga accept two pramāṇas only.

The table can be read as a series of reductions. Each school that accepts fewer means of knowledge than its neighbour does so by arguing that the extra ones are really forms of those it keeps. The Buddhists and Vaiśeṣikas reduce testimony to inference: a statement is believed because one infers that its speaker is reliable. Nyāya reduces postulation to inference, and the Prābhākara Mīmāṃsakas reduce non-apprehension to perception of the bare locus (Chapter 6). The Jains, with a scheme of their own, absorb comparison into recognition (Chapter 11). The early Cārvāka, finally, reduces everything to perception and challenges even inference (Chapter 9).

What drives the reductions is not a love of economy but what each school needs a means of knowledge to do. Testimony is the clearest case. For the Mīmāṃsā, dharma is known from the Veda and from nothing else, so testimony must be an independent means of knowledge and the Veda’s authority must not depend on any inference about its author. For Nyāya, testimony is independent but its authority does depend on its speaker, which is why Nyāya needs God. For the Buddhists, the Buddha’s word is authoritative because what he taught about liberation can be tested and is not found deceptive, so testimony can be treated as a kind of inference. The dispute about how many means of knowledge there are is in large part a dispute about the authority of scripture, conducted in the language of epistemology.

docs.title: 13.3 Perception and Conceptual Construction
docs.text:
Perception is the one means of knowledge accepted in some form by every school, the sceptic Jayarāśi apart, though the Jains’ canonical scheme counts ordinary sense-cognition as indirect. The schools differ greatly on its nature (Table 13.2).

Table 13.2. Comparative Theories of Perception School Theory of Perception Nyāya Perception arises from sense-object contact; grasps real objects with their qualities and universals; both nirvikalpaka and savikalpaka admitted Vaiśeṣika Similar to Nyāya; emphasises role of manas (mind) as coordinating sense data Sāṃkhya Perception is the function of buddhi (intellect) when modified by the object through the senses; Puruṣa is the witness Yoga Adds yogaja-pratyakṣa (yogic perception) as a valid form of direct knowledge Mīmāṃsā (Bhāṭṭa) Perception grasps real objects with their universals; the cognition itself is not perceived but known by postulation from the “knownness” of its object Mīmāṃsā (Prābh.) Perception involves a tripuṭī (triple relation): knower, knowledge, known Advaita Perception occurs when the antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti (mental modification) takes the form of the object; the consciousness limited by this vṛtti is perceptual knowledge Bauddha Perception is non-conceptual (kalpanā-apoḍha); grasps the unique particular (svalakṣaṇa) Jaina In the canonical scheme, sense-knowledge (mati) is technically indirect, and only avadhi, manaḥparyaya and kevala are direct; later logicians call ordinary perception “empirical direct knowledge” (sāṃvyavahārika pratyakṣa) Cārvāka Perception is the primary (for early Cārvākas the sole) pramāṇa

The decisive line runs between Dignāga and almost everyone else. For Dignāga and Dharmakīrti perception is free from conceptual construction: it grasps only the unique, momentary particular, and everything general — “cow”, “blue”, “pot” — is added by thought (Chapter 10). Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā and the Jains replied that determinate perception grasps real things with real properties; the Naiyāyikas granted an initial non-conceptual stage, but denied that what follows it is construction. The disagreement is not about psychology. It is about whether universals and wholes are real, for if perception presents them they must be; and that is why the theory of perception and the theory of universals were argued together (Section 13.9). The Śaiva non-dualists, adopting the Buddhist analysis of momentary awareness while rejecting its conclusion, gave the dispute a further turn: for Utpaladeva every perception already contains a reflective awareness (vimarśa) that is the root of concept and language (Chapter 12).

docs.title: 13.4 Inference Compared
docs.text:
Inference is accepted by every school except the early Cārvākas, but they disagree on its form and its ground. Nyāya states an argument for others in five members, Dignāga in three, in which the example already contains the universal rule, and Dharmakīrti in effect in two (Figure 13.1).

Figure 13.1. Comparison: the Nyāya five-membered argument and Dignāga’s three-membered argument (in which the example statement includes the universal rule)

The deeper disagreement concerns how pervasion is known. For Nyāya it holds between real universals and is known from repeated observation without counter-example, supported by suppositional reasoning; for Dharmakīrti it rests on an essential connection of identity or causation; for the Jains it is known by a separate means of knowledge, tarka. Each answer was shaped by the Cārvāka challenge (Section 9.3.1), and each reflects its school’s metaphysics: Nyāya’s realism about universals, the Buddhists’ analysis of causation among momentary particulars, and the Jains’ readiness to recognise as many means of knowledge as there are kinds of cognition.

docs.title: 13.5 The Validity of Knowledge: Svataḥ and Parataḥ
docs.text:
A central debate concerned whether the validity of a cognition is intrinsic or extrinsic — whether it arises from, and is known by, the same conditions that produce the cognition itself, or from and by something further (Table 13.3).

Table 13.3. Theories of the Validity and Invalidity of Knowledge School Origin of Validity Origin of Invalidity Mīmāṃsā Intrinsic (svataḥ) Extrinsic (parataḥ) Advaita Vedānta Intrinsic Extrinsic Nyāya Extrinsic (parataḥ) Extrinsic (parataḥ) Buddhism (as classified by Brahmanical doxographers) Extrinsic Intrinsic Sāṃkhya (as classified by Brahmanical doxographers) Intrinsic Intrinsic Jainism Arises from external conditions; known intrinsically in familiar cases and extrinsically in unfamiliar ones The same

The positions are clearer when one asks what each school was afraid of. The Mīmāṃsaka’s fear was a regress: if every cognition needed a second cognition to confirm its validity, that second cognition would need a third, and no one would ever know anything; so validity must be intrinsic, and only invalidity needs a further cause, a defect or a contradicting cognition. The doctrine also protected the Veda, which has no author whose defects could undermine it (Chapter 6). The Naiyāyika’s fear was credulity: if every cognition were valid until refuted, error would be as authoritative as truth until someone happened to notice it. Nyāya therefore held that validity is established extrinsically, typically by the success of the action a cognition prompts, and answered the regress objection by saying that in familiar cases we do not in fact seek confirmation, and that the confirming cognition need not itself be confirmed for the first to be valid. The Jain position, that validity is known intrinsically in familiar cases and extrinsically in unfamiliar ones, is less a compromise than a recognition that both sides had described part of our practice.

docs.title: 13.6 Theories of Error (Khyātivāda)
docs.text:
How is false cognition possible? The question — usually discussed through the example of a shell mistaken for silver — produced a set of theories (Table 13.4) that show the schools’ metaphysics with unusual clarity.

Table 13.4. Theories of Error Across Indian Philosophical Schools Theory School Explanation of Error Akhyāti Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā Failure to discriminate two valid cognitions, a perception of “this” and a memory of silver Anyathākhyāti Nyāya A real object is perceived as other than it is, with the attributes of something real elsewhere Viparītakhyāti Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā Misapprehension of one real thing as another (close to the Nyāya view) Ātmakhyāti Yogācāra Buddhism (as presented by opponents) The mind projects its own content as external Asatkhyāti Madhyamaka Buddhism (as presented by opponents) What is cognised in error is non-existent Anirvacanīyakhyāti Advaita Vedānta The object of error is neither real nor unreal, but indescribable Satkhyāti (Yathārthakhyāti) Viśiṣṭādvaita All cognition apprehends something real; silver is really present in the shell in a small measure Apūrṇakhyāti Pratyabhijñā (Abhinavagupta) An incomplete manifestation, in which the silver is not fixed in its place

The pattern is easy to see once the table is read against the earlier chapters. Realists explain error without admitting any unreal object: for the Prābhākara nothing false is ever cognised, only two true cognitions are not told apart (Chapter 6); for Nyāya the silver is real, but elsewhere; for Rāmānuja it is real even here, since every element contains every other in some measure. Idealists and anti-realists locate the false object in the mind or in nothing. The Advaitin’s “indescribable” silver is the hinge of his whole system, since the same status is then claimed for the world (Chapter 7). A theory of error is thus a test of a metaphysics: it must explain how the mind can present what is not there, without either making error impossible or making all cognition erroneous.

docs.title: 13.7 The Tradition of Debate
docs.text:
Indian philosophy has a long tradition of formal debate (śāstrārtha), shared by Brahmanical, Buddhist and Jain thinkers, in which a proponent (vādin) states a thesis, an opponent (prativādin) challenges it, arguments must be supported by recognised means of knowledge, and an umpire (madhyastha) or assembly (pariṣad) decides. The Nyāya Sūtra distinguishes three kinds of debate (Table 13.5); its list of the points of defeat is described in Chapter 2 (Table 2.6).

Table 13.5. Three Types of Philosophical Debate Type Sanskrit Description Honest debate Vāda Both parties sincerely seek truth; both use valid arguments; the goal is ascertainment of truth Sophistical debate Jalpa One or both parties seek victory rather than truth; use of tricks and quibbles permitted Destructive debate Vitaṇḍā One party only refutes without establishing any positive thesis

docs.title: 13.8 Debating about Debate: Norms, Manuals and Thesis-less Refutation
docs.text: The three kinds of debate in Table 13.5 were not simply a classification; they were a standing problem. Indian philosophers argued about which kinds of debate were legitimate, about what counts as defeat, and about whether one may refute without holding a thesis. Their answers show how closely the ethics of argument was tied to its logic. The setting of debate in education, from the Upaniṣadic contests to the monastic universities, and the medical tradition’s own rules of discussion in the Carakasaṃhitā (Vimānasthāna 8), are described in Volume 22 (Manas and Śikṣā) and Volume 13 (Āyurveda); the concern here is with the theory.

docs.title: 13.8.1 The Nyāya Definitions and the Defence of Wrangling
docs.text:
The Nyāyasūtra defines the three kinds of debate precisely. Vāda is the taking up of a thesis and a counter-thesis in which proof and refutation proceed by the means of knowledge and by suppositional reasoning (tarka), which does not contradict the accepted doctrine, and which uses the five-membered argument (1.2.1). Jalpa has these features but proves and refutes by means of quibbles (chala), false rejoinders (jāti) and points of defeat (1.2.2). Vitaṇḍā is jalpa without the establishment of a counter-thesis: the disputant only attacks (1.2.3). In its fourth book the sūtra adds that discussion (saṃvāda) should be held with pupils, teachers, fellow students and others who seek the good and are free of envy (4.2.47–48), and that it may even be undertaken without a counter-thesis, when one seeks to learn (4.2.49).

Why then teach jalpa and vitaṇḍā at all? The sūtra’s answer is a famous image: they exist “to protect the ascertainment of truth, as a hedge of thorny branches protects the growth of seeds” (4.2.50). When an opponent argues in bad faith, one may answer in kind, “by contending” (4.2.51). The Naiyāyikas thus admitted that victory-seeking debate had a place, but subordinated it to the protection of knowledge already gained. The cost was a complicated apparatus of quibbles, false rejoinders and twenty-two points of defeat (Table 2.6), much of which concerned the debater’s conduct rather than the truth of the thesis.

docs.title: 13.8.2 Buddhist Reform: Dharmakīrti’s Vādanyāya
docs.text: Buddhist thinkers had their own debating traditions. The Pali Kathāvatthu (“Points of Controversy”) records the Theravāda refutation of other Buddhist schools in a formal question-and-answer procedure (Volume 4), and Vasubandhu wrote a manual on the method of debate, the Vādavidhi, known from fragments and quotations. The most radical reform came from Dharmakīrti. His Vādanyāya (“The Logic of Debate”) opens by observing that rogues defeat even an honest reasoner in debate by appealing to false rules, and that the treatise is written to prevent this. It then reduces the grounds of defeat to two: for the proponent, stating what is not a proper part of the proof (asādhanāṅgavacana), and for the opponent, failing to point out a real fault (adoṣodbhāvana). Anything else, Dharmakīrti says, is not accepted as a ground of defeat, because it is not reasonable. Quibbles and false rejoinders are dishonest and should have no place in debate; a debater wins by proving his thesis or by exposing a genuine flaw, and by nothing else. The effect was to make the rules of debate follow from the theory of valid proof, rather than from the conventions of the assembly.

docs.title: 13.8.3 Jain Debate Theory
docs.text: Jain logicians from Akalaṅka (8th century) onwards took a similar line. They refused to allow quibbles and false rejoinders, did not accept vitaṇḍā as a legitimate form of debate, and treated debate as a single kind in which victory consists in establishing one’s own thesis and the opponent’s defeat in his failing to establish his. Later Jain manuals describe debate as having four “limbs” — the proponent, the opponent, the members of the assembly who judge, and the presiding authority who keeps order — and assign to each its duties. The Jains’ doctrine of many-sidedness (Chapter 11) gave them a further reason to distrust a style of argument that aims only at the defeat of the other side.

docs.title: 13.8.4 Can One Refute without a Thesis?
docs.text: The deepest question concerned vitaṇḍā. If a debater only refutes and puts forward no thesis, is he arguing at all? For the Naiyāyikas, vitaṇḍā was parasitic: the critic must at least hold that the opponent’s view is wrong, and so has a thesis after all. Two of the most powerful thinkers in the tradition rejected this. Nāgārjuna, answering an opponent who argued that the claim “all things are empty” is itself either empty and powerless or not empty and self-refuting, replied: “If I had any thesis, this fault would be mine; but I have no thesis, so the fault is not mine” (Vigrahavyāvartanī 29). His arguments are reductions (prasaṅga) of the opponent’s own premises, which commit him to nothing (Section 10.5). Many centuries later the Advaitin Śrīharṣa defended refutation without a counter-thesis in the same spirit, arguing that both parties need only accept the means of knowledge for the purposes of the debate (Section 7.4). Their critics replied that an argument which uses the means of knowledge cannot avoid committing its author to their validity. The dispute, which runs from the early Madhyamaka to late Vedānta, is one of the clearest cases in which Indian philosophers reflected on the presuppositions of argument itself (Matilal 1998; Solomon 1976–1978).

docs.title: 13.9 Universals and Causation
docs.text:
Two metaphysical disputes ran through every epistemological one. On universals, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika held them to be real, eternal entities inhering in individuals; the Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsakas held them real but identical-in-difference with their instances, and made them the primary meaning of words; the Buddhists held them to be constructions, explained by exclusion; the Jains treated universal and particular as two real aspects of one substance; and the Advaitins granted them reality at the empirical level only. On causation, the schools divided into those for whom the effect pre-exists in its cause, either really (Sāṃkhya) or apparently (Advaita), those for whom it is a new beginning (Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika), and the Buddhists, for whom momentary events arise in dependence on conditions without either pre-existing or being new wholes (Figure 13.2).

Figure 13.2. Comparative Theories of Causation in Indian Philosophy

docs.title: 13.10 Conclusion: What the Comparison Shows
docs.text:
Set side by side, the schools described in this volume show several things that no single chapter could.

The first is that they shared a language. From the middle of the first millennium, Brahmanical, Buddhist, Jain, materialist and, later, Śaiva philosophers argued in the same terms — means and objects of knowledge, pervasion and its faults, prior position and conclusion — and before the same kind of audience. Their disagreements were therefore real disagreements, about which each side could be shown wrong, not the incommensurable outlooks of closed “worldviews”. This is the strongest reason to read Indian philosophy as philosophy.

The second is that epistemology and metaphysics were never separate. A school’s theory of perception commits it to a view of universals; its theory of error commits it to a view of what the world is; the number of means of knowledge it accepts encodes its attitude to scripture. The schools knew this, which is why an attack on one part of a system was so often aimed at another.

The third is that the history of Indian philosophy is a history of argument, not a set of fixed systems. Dignāga and Dharmakīrti changed the agenda of every school after them; Kumārila, Uddyotakara and Udayana wrote in reply; the Śaiva non-dualists adapted Buddhist analyses to defend a self; Śrīharṣa’s attack on definitions helped provoke the precision of Navya-Nyāya; and the early-modern logicians of Navadvīpa reworked the categories themselves (Section 2.11.5). Daya Krishna’s complaint, noted in Chapter 1, that the image of six closed “systems” hides this history, is largely borne out by the comparison. So is his doubt about the claim that all Indian philosophy is oriented to liberation. Many schools did frame their inquiries by the highest good, and the framing was not idle; but much of the work compared in this chapter — on validity, on error, on the conditions of debate — was carried on for its own sake, and the materialists rejected the framing altogether. The picture of a uniformly spiritual India and its mirror image, a purely technical one, both oversimplify.

The fourth is that the conventional map distorts the territory in particular ways. The Buddhists and Jains, classed as heterodox, were at the centre of the debate rather than at its edge; the Grammarians and the Śaiva schools, absent from the “six systems”, made some of its most original contributions; and the Cārvākas, known almost only through their opponents, shaped the arguments of everyone who refuted them. The map also leaves out much that this volume could not cover — above all Indo-Islamic thought and much regional-language philosophy (Section 1.17.1).

The fifth is a limit. The debates surveyed here were conducted almost entirely by men, mostly of a few social groups, in Sanskrit and Pali, and the restrictions on who could study and argue shaped what was argued about (Section 1.16.3). A history of Indian philosophy that took account of those excluded from the assembly would look different from this one, and the evidence for writing it is still being gathered.

Finally, the comparison does not produce a winner. On the self, on universals, on the validity of knowledge, on the relation of consciousness to the body, the arguments set out in this volume remain open, and several of them are argued today in very similar terms. That, rather than any claim of priority, is the best case for studying them: not that the ancient schools anticipated modern conclusions, but that they reasoned carefully about questions that are still unresolved.

docs.text:
The quotations from primary texts in this volume follow the standard editions; readers who wish to check them should use the critical editions and translations listed here (full details in the Select Bibliography). Sanskrit verse and sūtra numbers differ between editions, especially for the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra, the Tattvārthasūtra and the Yoga Sūtra.

Nyāya Sūtra and Bhāṣya: translation with the Vārttika by Jha (Jha 1912–1919). Vaiśeṣika Sūtra: Candrānanda’s recension, edited by Jambuvijaya (Jambuvijaya 1961).
